mentions.text: Texture data of the HZSM-5 and the Ti-containing HZSM-5 samples were measured by the N 2 adsorption, as listed in Table 1. It can be seen that both the specific surface areas and pore diameter of 0.99TiO 2 -HZSM-5 sample are slightly lower than that of the HZSM-5, which may be due to the pores of HZSM-5 partly blocking by TiO 2 particles. In contrast, the specific surface areas of 0.99Ti-HZSM-5 sample is a bit higher than that of the HZSM-5, but its pore diameter is a bit lower than the HZSM-5, which could be understood also by the chemical bonding of Ti species to surface oxygen atoms of TiO 2. It should be noted that such a small change of specific surface area and pore size could not induce such a difference in the photocatalytic activity between Ti-HZSM-5 and TiO 2 -HZSM-5, which could be seen from the normalized rates on the two samples. Thus, specific surface area and CO 2 adsorption capacity are not responsible for the difference in photocatalytic activity.

mentions.text: EPR meausrment (Fig. 3, g = 1.992) and the negative shift of Ti 2p spectra (Fig. 4A and B) also revealed the formation of Ti 3+ . Ti 4+ can changes into Ti 3+ by accepting the electron of F -in solution containing HF at a higer temperature [27]. This is similar with Ti 4+ reduced by electron donator, such as H 2 [28]. O vacancies can also induce the formation of Ti 3+ to keep the charge balance. This kind of Ti 3+ will enhance the visible light absorption ( > 400 nm) [29]. However, the UV-vis spectra (Fig. S3) do not show any change in the visible light absorption after calcination except a slight redshift for absorption edge. Thus, Ti 4+ was reduced to Ti 3+ by F -during calcination. Further calcination (4 h) could not enhance the amount of Ti 3+ (Fig. 3) after F -ions were fully removed (2 h Table S1).

The photocatalytic rate is normal lower in the first several hours. During this period, adsorption of CO 2 and H 2 O is the main reaction. Fig. 5A shows the rate of CH 4 production is rapider during first two hours. The higher rate canbe attributed to the function of OH groups. There are lots of OH groups on the TiO 2 surface. The ratio of O to Ti (larger than 2:1,Table S1), FT-IR (Fig. S2) and O 1 s XPS spectra (532 eV) all prove the existence of OH groups. H 2 O decomposes into OH -and H + , then OH -changes into OH ȧfter accepting the photoinduced hole [5]. Thus, OH groups are helpful for the production of CH 4 . To verify the hypothesis, photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 was tested on TiO 2 (calcined at 550 • C for 2 h) without adding water. CH 4 was obtained under this condition (Fig. 5B). To eliminate the effect of organics, CO 2 photoreduction was tested without water and CO 2 . However, no CH 4 was detected. The results prove OH groups can replace H 2 O as the reducer and are benefit for improving the production rate of CH 4 .

OH groups have an affinity for lewis-acidic CO 2 [30,31], thus, can enhance the CO 2 adsorption capacity [12]. Samples without calcination have the highest CO 2 adsorption capacity (Table 1). The adsorption capacity decreases with calcination time lengthening. While the calcination time increased up to 2 h, there is a small peak (Table 1). This is due to the increase in the number of Ti 3+ and O vacancies (Fig. 3), which can enhance the adsorption ability of CO 2 [10]. If further prolong the calcined time to 4 h, O vacancies are filled by the oxygen in air and disappear (Fig. 3). This leads to the reduction of CO 2 adsorption (Table 1). CO 2 adsorption capacity is an important factor affecting CH 4 production.

Fig. 6 is bar graph of CH 4 production. The higher activity for samples calcined for 0.0 h and 0.25 h (Fig. 6 A) come from organics, which is not a photocatalytic activity. To verify the statement, samples were presintered at 450 • C for 10 h to remove organics (Table S1). Sample without further calcination at 550 • C indeed have a lower activity (Fig. S4-0 h). Calcining at 450 • C can remove organic but can not remove superficial F -(Table S1), which is unfavorable for CO 2 reduction [32]. Samples must be calcined at 550 • C to remove F -and organics before measuring the photocatalytic activity. Thus, the higher photocatalytic activity is meaningless, and the reduction in CH 4 production for samples calcined for 0.5 h (Fig. 6A) is due to the removal of organics.

CO 2 adsorption and CH 4 production should further reduce with calcination time lengthen for the reduction in the amount of OH groups. CH 4 production reaches the maximum when calcination time is 2 h. Crystallinity, light absorption, photogenerated carriers separation and CO 2 adsorption all affect the photocatalytic activity. PL spectra is a powerful technique to study the carriers transfer process. All samples have an obvious PL peaks at about 385 nm (Fig. 6B), which is attributed to the band-band emission of TiO 2 [33]. The intensity of PL peak decreases with increasing calcination time and reaches minimum for calcination time 2 h, which means sample calcined for 2 h has the highest utilization of carriers. One reason accounting for the decrease is the removal of surface states as the recombination of carriers. Another reason is the enhancement of CO 2 adsorption capacity. A higher CO 2 adsorption capacity means more reactive sites, that improves utilization efficiency of photogenerated electrons. The intensity of PL peak (Fig. 6B) for samples calcined 1-4 h does show positive correlation with CO 2 adsorption capacity (Table 1) and photocatalytic activity (Fig. 6A). Therefore, CO 2 adsorption can affect CH 4 production by affecting recombination of photogenerated carriers.

mentions.text: -SCH 3 was the strongest functional group causing the remarkably decreased band gap and enhanced photocatalytic performance of UiO-66(SCH 3 ) 2 . Surprisingly, compared to the most representative UiO-66-NH 2 which had no visible light-induced photocatalytic hydrogen generation activity, Pt/ UiO-66-(SCH 3 ) 2 exhibited an efficient hydrogen generation rate of 3871 lmol/g under the same reaction conditions. However, in some reactions, the narrow band gap and excellent visible light harvesting ability of modified UiO-66 does not suggest exceptional photocatalytic performance. Mu et al. [76] synthesized UiO-66 as well as its isostructural derivatives UiO-66-X with NH 2 , Br, (OH) 2 , and (SH) 2 functional group in aromatic ring of the organic linker H 2 BDC for the photodegradation of Rhodamine B (RhB). X-ray diffractometry (XRD) patterns showed that the five samples were isostructural and the substitution of linkers did not affect the crystal structure. Inferred from relevant characterization results, these functional groups were present in the micropores and did not coordinate with metal centers. UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) indicated that the light absorption edges of UiO-66-NH 2 , UiO-66-(OH) 2 and UiO-66-(SH) 2 visibly shifted to the visible light region (Table 1). Although UiO-66-(OH) 2 and UiO-66-NH 2 possessed apparent visible light absorption, both had significantly weaker degradation efficiency than UiO-66-Br and UiO-66 with almost no visible light absorption. Therefore, the light absorption ability of modified UiO-66 was not the decisive factor in determining its photocatalytic activity, other properties should also be taken into account, such as the efficiency of charge separation and potential relationship between the target and modified UiO-66. There are also many relevant reports on ligand modifications of UiO-66 and the corresponding photoresponse ranges are shown in Table 1.

Modified UiO-66 possess superb water stability, high photostability, fast photogenerated charge separation and migration rate, making these materials to be the ideal photocatalysts for boosting the carbon-neutral energy cycle and solving environmental remediation issues. mentions.text: The photocatalytic activities of photocatalysts were first estimated by the photodegradation of NO under visible light illumination. Fig. 2a shows the change of NO removal rate with the increase of irradiation time in the presence of visible light on the difference as-prepared catalysts. The NO removal rates are ignorable in the absence of catalyst under visible light irradiation. Among these prepared samples, the 5-Cu@Cu 2 O sample exhibits the highest catalytic activity, and the photocatalytic oxidation efficiency of NO can achieve 46.4% within 10 min. The above results manifest that the Cu nanoparticles supported on the surface of the Cu 2 O octahedron can significantly improve the catalytic activity of the catalyst, and there is an optimal proportion between them for improving photocatalytic performance. It is reported that the final product of photocatalytic oxidation of NO is nitrate (NO 3 -), but NO 2 as the intermediate products may be generated during the oxidation process [44,45]. The concentration of NO 2 was also tested by NOx analyzer. It can be seen from the results in Table S1 that the NO 2 concentration for the 5-Cu@Cu 2 O is quite low among these samples, reaching 14.6 ppb. It means that the sample is more conducive to deep oxidation. Although the NO 2 concentrations for other samples are higher compared with that of the 5-Cu@Cu 2 O, which is due to the suppression of deep oxidation. However, the NO 2 concentrations are still far lower than the concentration of NO 2 in the air referring to the air quality grade standard in China (the first-grade standard of air quality grade is 0.08 mg/m 3 (i.e., 61.9 ppb)). The Å OH and Å O 2 -radicals produced in the photocatalytic process are two kinds of active species with strong oxidation ability, which can oxidize NO x (NO and NO 2 ) to nitrate without selectivity [46]. To confirm the presence of nitrate, all these five samples after catalytic reactions were gathered and analyzed by FTIR and as shown in Fig. 2b, which displayed that the peak at 1380 cm À1 assigned to the antisymmetric stretching vibration absorption of NO 3 À of 5-Cu@Cu 2 O was stronger than those of the other four samples, suggesting that the NO ? NO 3 À oxidation process on the 5-Cu@Cu 2 O was more favorable [47]. Then, the CO 2 photocatalytic reduction performance is evaluated by detecting carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH 4 ) as the major and minor product of the process, respectively. Fig. 3a and b demonstrate the time courses of photocatalytic CO and CH 4 evolutions, respectively, suggesting the harvest of CO and CH 4 increase with increasing the reaction time. (3) Too many Cu nanoparticles are more likely to cause the recombination of photoinduced electrons and holes in the catalysts, therefore reducing the catalytic performance of the sample (10-Cu@Cu 2 O). The above speculation, such as increased specific surface, effective photogenerated carrier separation, formation of the Cu@Cu 2 O ohmic junction and LSPR of Cu nanoparticles, will be fully proved in the characterization section below. The photocatalytic CO 2 reduction activity of the Cu@Cu 2 O photocatalyst is compared with that of other Cu 2 O-based photocatalysts [32,48,49]. As shown in Table 1, it is found that the photocatalyst prepared in this work has good photocatalytic activity. Further isotope labeling experiment was confirmed that the photocatalytic reduction products (CO and CH 4 ) were indeed produced by CO 2 photocatalytic reduction reaction. The results show that the m/z ratio of the product is properly matched with the CO 2 used (Fig. S1). At the same time, molecular oxygen (O 2 ) was also detected in the GC-MS chromatogram, which could be the product of water oxidation by photocatalytic oxidation. In addition, the reusability of the 5-Cu@Cu 2 O sample was also investigated (Fig. 3c and d). The results show that the performance of the catalyst does not decrease significantly after several continuous catalytic reactions under visible light irradiation, indicating that the sample has sufficient stability. The stability of the recovered samples was further verified by XRD and TEM, as shown in Fig. 3e and f. It was found that the crystal and morphology changes of the 5-Cu@Cu 2 O photocatalyst were negligible, indicating that the photocatalyst had little change.

mentions.text: The thermal decomposition performance of the specimens can be analyzed by TG measurement (Fig. 3). When the temperature gradually rises to 800 C, the weight loss of NiO nanosheets is hardly found [40]. The g-C 3 N 4 nanowires have a sharp weight loss arising from about 450 C to 710 C, owing to its thermal decomposition [40]. For the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 composites, the obvious weight loss in the range of 500-650 C reveals the thermal decomposition of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires. Therefore the contents of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires in the heterojunctions can be easily calculated from the corresponding mass loss over 800 C [41], which is well consistent with the feeding amount of g-C 3 N 4 (Table 1). The above TG results indicate that there is no loss of precursors during the synthesis of the composites.

To prove the photocatalytic performance of the as-synthesized NiO/g-C 3 N 4 heterojunctions, the catalytic reduction properties of CO 2 using similar photocatalysts were compared in Table S1. Various composite photocatalysts can effectively convert CO 2 to corresponding products under their own catalytic conditions. Compared with other composites, the as-prepared NiO/g-C 3 N 4 heterojunctions with the yield rates of 2.75 and 1.79 μmol⋅h -1 ⋅g -1 for CO and CH 4 exhibit satisfactory photocatalytic performance of CO 2 , indicating superior candidate as the sunlight photocatalyst.

tables.caption: The BET specific surface area, pore volume, average pore size and band gap energy of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires, NiO nanosheets and the composites.

mentions.text: According to the BJH approach (inset of Fig. 5), the pore diameters of NC-3 are primarily partitioned into two sorts. One is the mesopore at about 5.0 nm from the surface structure of the sample that may be due to gas escape during heat treatment. The other is the micropore of 30-110 nm, due to the disordered aggregation of nanoparticles. As summarized in Table 2, compared with pure NiO nanosheets (S BET ¼ 13.94 m 2 g -1 ), the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 photocatalysts display a sharp increase in specific surface area and pore volume, and a significant decrease in pore size, which can be further confirmed by Fig. S1. And it becomes larger with the increasing g-C 3 N 4 content, which leads to more reaction active sites in the samples. At the same time the CO 2 adsorption over various samples (Fig. S3) indicates the potential application of NC-3 in the photocatalytic CO 2 reduction. The results are in line with BET analysis discussed above.

Fig. 7a exhibits the UV-vis spectra of NiO nanosheets, g-C 3 N 4 nanowires and the composites in the range of 250-800 nm. Single NiO nanosheets display its intrinsic band gap absorption of NiO at wavelength of about 305 nm [52]. However, single g-C 3 N 4 nanowires show an absorption edge situated at visible light range as presented. Furthermore, compared with NiO nanosheets and g-C 3 N 4 nanowires, the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 photocatalysts exhibit a red shift of the absorption edge, indicating the strong visible light response [54]. The band gaps of NiO and g-C 3 N 4 could be reckoned from the formula (αhv) ¼ A(hv-E g ) n/2 [55]. Moreover, the n value is dependent on the transition type of the semiconductor. And n ¼ 1 represents a direct transition, while n ¼ 4 means an indirect transition [55]. The n value for g-C 3 N 4 and NiO is 4 and 1, respectively. According to the above equation, the band gap energies of pure g-C 3 N 4 nanowires and NiO nanosheets are 2.75 eV and 3.46 eV (Fig. 7b) [40,52], respectively. Moreover on basis on the Tauc plots of the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 photocatalysts, the band gap energies of the composites are shifted to a more visible region with the increasing content of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires (Table 2), leading to more efficient use of visible light. For NC-3, the band gap energy is estimated to be 2.98 eV. The low band gap can promote the excitation of more electrons under irradiation, which may be beneficial to enhance the photocatalytic activity.

Impressively, this optimized Pt-NC/P25-0.5 catalyst outperforms the majority of previously reported state-of-the-art TiO 2 family photocatalysts for CH 4 generation (Table S1). Furthermore, the AQY of the Pt-NC/P25-0.5 catalyst was 0.91% when illuminated with 365-nm monochromatic light. This AQY value is substantially higher than that of many of the previously reported effective catalysts for CH 4 generation [40,[53][54][55][56][57].

The role of the surface area in CO 2 reduction in the case of the proposed photocatalyst system was examined using N 2 adsorption/ desorption measurements. The results are summarized in Table 1. The specific surface area of P25 was determined to be 52.7 m 2 g -1 ; however, the specific surface areas of the fabricated Pt-NC/P25-0.5, Pt-NC/P25-1.0, and Pt-NC/P25-2.0 catalysts were marginally improved to 59.2 m 2 g -1 , 57.9 m 2 g -1 , and 55.6 m 2 g -1 , respectively. Although the fabricated Pt-NC/P25 catalysts exhibited remarkably higher photocatalytic activities than P25, they had marginally larger surface areas, demonstrating that the improved activity of Pt-NC/P25 catalysts cannot be attributed to surface area effects. In addition, the adsorption capacity of CO 2 on the catalyst surface is considered a critical parameter that significantly influences the efficiency of the CO 2 photoreduction process because the retention period of CO 2 molecules on the catalyst surface must be sufficient to allow the process to proceed [40,64]. Fig. 8c shows the CO 2 adsorption isotherms of all the fabricated Pt-NC/P25 catalysts and the P25 counterpart. As observed in Fig. 8c, all the Pt-NC/P25 catalysts have much higher CO 2 adsorption capabilities than the P25 counterpart. Moreover, the Pt-NC/P25-0.5 catalyst has the highest CO 2 adsorption capacity among the examined catalysts, and the trend of CO 2 adsorption capacities is consistent with the photocatalytic activity of the catalysts. The high CO 2 adsorption capacity is apparently due to the high proportion of low coordinated (edge/corner) sites in the sub-nanometer-sized Pt NCs, which have a higher capacity for CO 2 adsorption [32]. Thus, the enhanced CO 2 adsorption of Pt-NC/P25 catalysts over P25 can explain, at least in part, their enhanced photocatalytic activity.

The calculated results show that all the values of E f_X are negative ranging from -4.11 eV to -6.74 eV, much lower than that of C atom in the MoS 2 sheet at about -3.40 eV [49], indicating non-metal atoms X are stable. It should be noticed that the formation energy E f_Sv is positive due to an endothermic process to form an S vacancy, requiring about 5.84 eV external energy (see in SI-Fig. 1). The Gibbs free energy changes (ΔG) of CO 2 reduction to CO on different modified SnS 2 substrates are studied, and the corresponding result is displayed in Fig. 4. For convenience, the detailed calculated result for ΔE ZPE and TΔS of CO 2 reduction to CO is also provided (see in SI-Table 1). It can be found that the rate determining step (RDS) occurs at the first step (*CO 2 →*COOH) with an energy barrier of 2.12 eV at SnS 2 sheet (see black line in Fig. 4 (a)). As S v included, the RDS remains at the first step, but the energy barrier decreases to 1.55 eV. Considering the synergy effect of S v and non-metal atoms X, the energy barrier can be further reduced. For example, it is only about 1.07 eV on O/S v -SnS 2 sheet, half the value of that on pristine case, where the RDS is changed to second step (*COOH→*CO) [1]. In all, O/S v -SnS 2 has an excellent photocatalysis for CO 2 reduction to CO molecule due to the relative low energy barrier as shown in Fig. 4(b). Except for intermediate *COOH, the hydrogenation of CO 2 to *HCOO is also checked, where an extremely large energy barrier of 2.30 eV is found on O/S v -SnS 2 substrate. Therefore, the synergy of S v and atom O has a priority to form CO (g) through *COOH process.

mentions.text: The calculated adsorption energy (E ads ), adsorption distance (d), and charge transfer (Δq) of CO 2 adsorbed on modified SnS 2 structures are summarized in Table 2. As modification is included, the adsorption behavior of CO 2 can be significantly enhanced. Interestingly, it can be found that the strength of CO 2 adsorption is linearly enhanced with the decreasing non-metal atoms X from O to B atom. This unique behavior can be explained by the partial electronic density of state and electron transfer. Relative to CO 2 molecule, the peak of PDOS near the Fermi level for the adsorbed CO 2 is linearly red-shift as the non-metal atoms changing from O to B atoms as shown in IS-Fig. 4, indicating stronger adsorption of CO 2 on B/Sv-SnS 2 than that on O/Sv-SnS 2 . On the other hand, the corresponding electron transfer is examined by analyzing the Bader charge as displayed in Table . 2. The lower E ads can also be reflected by the shorter distance d, where it is about d = 3.35 Å at perfect surface and it decreases to d = 2.99 Å on B/S v -SnS 2 sheet. Therefore, it can be concluded that non-metal atoms X as well as S v can greatly enhance the adsorption ability of CO 2 molecule, paving the way for the sequence reactions. Following, the synergy effect of S v and non-metal atoms X (X = B, C, N, and O) on the activity and product selectivity of CO 2 photoreduction are studied. Applying the Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) developed by Nørskov et al. [46], the conversion of CO 2 to main C 1 products such as CO, HCOOH, and CH 4 molecules are considered. Since the terms of ΔE ZPE and TΔS in ΔG could be affected by functional or box used, thus all the related results in the context are simulated to avoid these issues. The products CO and HCOOH involve two-electron process as: CO 2 + 2H + + 2e -→ CO + H 2 O, and CO 2 + 2H + + 2e -→ HCOOH. Other products HCHO, CH 3 OH, and CH 4 involve four-, six-, and eight-electron process, respectively.

To explain the low energy barrier on C/S v -SnS 2 substrate, the adsorption strength of intermediates *HCOO and *HCOOH are examined, and the corresponding result is shown in Table 4. On the other hand, the E ads of adsorbed *HCOOH is also playing an important role during the reaction process. The strong adsorption of *HCOOH (E ads = -2.87 eV) on B/S v -SnS 2 makes it extremely difficult to desorb from substrate. Thus, a moderate *HCOOH adsorption on C/S v -SnS 2 (E ads = -1.38 eV) is beneficial to desorb. Furthermore, the interaction between *HCOOH and substrates can also be validated by PDOS as shown in IS-Fig. 6. Clearly, the molecular orbital of *HCOOH is slightly overlapped with the C-p y of C/S v -SnS 2 substrates. Therefore, the *HCOOH can be much easier to desorb from C/S v -SnS 2 substrate with a low energy barrier of 0.59 eV. substrates separately occurs at the third, fifth and first step with the energy barrier of 2.05 eV, 1.04 eV and 2.31 eV, respectively. In all, it can be concluded that B/S v -SnS 2 sheet has a priority to form CH 4 with a moderate energy barrier of 1.04 eV (see in Fig. 7(b)), together with the detailed reaction process in Fig. 7(c).

To explain this low energy barrier on B/S v -SnS 2 , the adsorption behavior of intermediates involved in RDS is examined, and the corresponding result is summarized in Table 4. It can be found that the adsorption energy of *HCOO and *HCOOH on B/S v -SnS 2 is extremely low at about -5.03 eV and -2.87 eV, much lower than that on other substrates, consistent with larger charge transfer Δq as shown in SI-Table 2, indicating it is facilitate to form *HCOO and *HCOOH. Similarly, the adsorption of *CHOH and *CH on B/S v -SnS 2 involved in the RDS is also extremely low, with the E ads at about -4.36 eV and -5.41 eV, respectively. It should be noticed that the *CHOH→ *CH is a detaching process, which is an endothermic process, thus it requires to overcome an energy barrier of 1.04 eV.

tables.caption: Comparison of the photocatalytic CO 2 reduction performance of the optimized CdS-P25/ZIF-67 with those of the previous reported photocatalysts.

mentions.text: Fig. 8 demonstrates the photocatalytic CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR) of the composite material CdS-P25/ZIF-67 (20:3) under the illumination of a 300 W xenon lamp (Each catalytic workup in our study were carried out for more than three times. The standard deviation for the tests were less than 3%, suggesting all the tests are reliable [64]. The performance test in Fig. 8a shows that, compared with pure CdS, the CdS-P25 sample shows stronger photocatalytic reduction activity, whilst the ternary hybrid CdS-P25/ZIF-67 presents the optimal photocatalytic behavior. Fig. 8b shows that among all the composite materials prepared, the CdS-P25/ZIF-67 (20:3) composite material has the best catalytic rate, and the yields of CO and CH 4 are 1.49 and 1.58 μmol h -1 , respectively. In terms of the reduction product CO yield, CdS-P25/ZIF-67 (20:3) is about 27.7 times higher than CdS reduction yield. As compared to the reported TiO 2 -based photocatalysts (Table 1), the CO/ CH 4 production given by the optimized CdS-P25/ZIF-67 photocatalyst presents a satisfactory improvement. In addition, as a competing product for the CO 2 RR, H 2 production was measured during the reaction, and the amount is undetectable. Due to the strong interaction between CdS and P25, the liveness of CdS-P25 composites is much higher than that of P25 nanosheets and CdS nanoparticles, which ultimately greatly enhances the ability of photocatalytic CO 2 conversion capacity. Additionally, the special structure of ZIF-67 also inhibits the recombination of electrons and holes. As the content of ZIF-67 in the composite increases from 4.8% to 13.0%, the photocatalytic activity is significantly increased [48]. When the content of ZIF-67 increases to a certain amount, due to the agglomeration of CdS-P25 nanoparticles, the photocatalytic activity is reduced. In order to testify to the steadiness of the ternary hybrid and the carbon source of the product (CO/CH 4 ) during the catalytic usage, a series of control trials were conducted (Fig. 8d). In the absence of either light or photocatalyst, undetectable products are observed after the reaction, suggesting the necessity of the simultaneous presence of both photocatalyst and light to complete the CO 2 reduction. When the reduction system is treated by vacuum (light/vacuum + Cat. + H 2 O), a slight amount of CO is observed. Given that the absolute vacuum is difficult to be realized, there still exists CO 2 that comes from the residue air in the reactor leading to the generation of C1 product. In this case, we alternatively replace the CO 2 ambience by argon atmosphere in the reactor (light/argon + Cat. + H 2 O), relatively negligible CH 4 and CO production is detected under this inert gas atmosphere in comparison to the generation under CO 2 ambience (Fig. 8c). The minute amount of CO/CH 4 production are virtually the same at these five timeinterval, which might be derived from the unreacted ligand (2-methylimidazole) that adsorbed in the ternary CdS-P25/ZIF-67 (20:3). The MOF structure and the entire ternary catalyst are stable during the photocatalytic CO 2 RR, consistent with relevant reports based on ZIF-67 MOF [47,53,65]. Hence, it is confirmative the carbon source of CO and CH 4 is primarily from exotic CO 2 . As presented by photocatalytic cycle performance of CdS-P25/ZIF-67 (20:3), a comparably insignificant abatement in CO 2 transformation (Fig. 8e) and photoelectrochemical behavior (Fig. 9b,9d) are observed, which might due to the slight decomposition of the organic components. Whereas, the catalyst is able to sustain a satisfactory catalytic activity even over a time range of up to 6 h of illumination (Fig. 8f). The virtually same FT-IR spectra and XRD detection between the CdS-P25/ZIF-67 (20:3) sample before and after use also certify its steady use during the prolonged time catalysis (Fig. 9a and Fig. 9c).

mentions.text: To date, different approaches have been applied for the elimination of dyes from wastewater and all approaches are not feasible equally and also some cause secondary pollution issue, unable to remove the pollutant completely and are costly [22][23][24][25][26]. The RhB is widely used in dyeing, printing, and leather industries, and resultantly, discharged into the environment and cause various health impacts like skin, respiratory, eyes, and nervous system are affected in response to this dye exposure. The RhB dye is water soluble mostly used in textile industry is carcinogenic, highly stable and non-biodegradable under environmental conditions. Therefore, it is need to employ a competent approach to remediate this dye in effluent before discharging in to water [27,28]. Among the alternative chemical processes, photodegradation employing metal oxides under the solar light has proven as an effective approach that is both environmentally beneficial and low-cost. Because the solar spectrum contains a small amount of UV (4%) and a large amount of the visible light (46%), it is important to create innovative effective photocatalyst active under the solar light, that can be accomplished by altering electronic structure and regulating band-gap by substitution [29,30]. For this, an active photocatalyst is required and NPs performed efficient job in this regard [31][32][33]. On the other hand, the catalyst active under solar light irradiation are also regarded economical versus catalysts active under UV light irradiation. The modification (band gap tuning) of NPs with active moieties make material active under solar light. To improve the optical properties doping is best. Attempts have been made to enhance properties of Sr-hexaferrite, numerous cations such as In 3+ , Al 3+ , Cr 3+ , Ga 3+ and cation combinations such as Nb 4+ -Zn 2+ , Ti 4+ -Co 2+ , Ti 4+ -Ni 2+ , La 3+ -Co 2+ , Gd 3+ -Co 2+ , Ti 4+ -Mn 2+ , Ir 3+ -Zn 2+ and Sm +3 -Co +2 have been studied as dopant to enhance the physicochemical properties [34][35][36][37] (Table 1). Particularly, Sr-hexaferrite doped by different cation combinations reflect enhancing electrical resistivity and reducing the magnetocrystalline anisotropy, which exhibits preferable properties for diverse applications. High electrical resistivity materials are most desirable microwave devices applications [6,[38][39][40].

mentions.text: Moreover, the EDS elemental mapping image for NALDH/CN/GA-20 shows the well distributed C, N, O, Ni and Al elements (Fig. S2), which demonstrates that NiAl-LDH, GA and g-C 3 N 4 jointly contributed to the formation of the network framework with ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions. Additionally, the Ni/Al molar ratio was approximately 3 as shown in EDS elemental spectrum (Fig. S2), which is close to the theoretical value for pristine NALDH, and indicated the formation of abundant coupling interfaces in ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions. The content of NiAl-LDH, GA and g-C 3 N 4 in the NALDH/CN/GA-20 composite was further determined by thermogravimetric (TG) analysis (Fig. S3). The actual content of NiAl-LDH, GA and g-C 3 N 4 in NALDH/ CN/GA-20 can be determined as 40 wt%, 37 wt% and 23 wt% respectively. It was consistent with EDS elemental spectrum analysis (Fig. S2). Hydrogen bonding acts a pivotal part in a facile hydrothermal process of NALDH/CN/GA. Hence, infrared (IR) spectroscopy was employed to verify the hydrogen bonding interaction of the ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions in NALDH/CN/GA. NALDH/CN/GA-20 shows a series of peaks in the region of 600-3700 cm -1 , assigned to C-N, N-H, O-H, M-O-M and M-OH characteristic peaks (Fig. S4). As shown in Fig. 2a, the -OH of the interlayer water molecules in NALDH and -NH of uncondensed amino groups in CN exist intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Since the hydrogen bond is formed, the electron cloud density is averaged and the molecular energy decreases, then the vibration frequency shifts to a lower wavenumber in IR [38]. As shown in Fig. 2a, the peak location of OH stretching vibration in NALDH/CN/GA (3423 and 1616 cm -1 ) moves to a lower wavenumber, compared with NALDH/CN (3439 and 1634 cm -1 ). The IR results indicate that NALDH/CN/GA has a relatively strong hydrogen bonding interaction, which contributes to constructs ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions with short-range coupling interfaces. Additionally, in comparsion with CN, the C -N signal at 1240 cm -1 of NALDH/CN/GA was weak due to the intermolecular hydrogen bonds between CN and NALDH. It also confirmed successful synthesis of the ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions in NALDH/CN/GA. Fig. 2b shows the N 2 adsorption-desorption isotherms and the BJH pore-size distribution curves of the NALDH/CN/GA-20 with pore size distribution ranged from 10 to 30 nm, which may be due to the integration of nanosheets leading to the formation of mainly mesoporous structures by steric effect and hydrogen bonding [39,40]. Other catalysts also showed type-IV isotherm and H3 hysteresis loops with the existence of porous structure (Fig. S5), The BET results illustrate that ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions can be self-assembled into network structures with significantly different specific surface area and pore volume (Table 1).

Compared with CN, the PL emission intensities of NALDH/CN were lower (Fig. 4c), which was attributed to the formation of ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions between NALDH and CN with the shorten charge transmission distance, thereby weakening the recombination of photogenerated electron-hole pairs. By introduction of GA, interfacial interaction between NALDH nanosheets and CN nanosheets was more strong, which could efficiently accelerate the transfer and separation of photo-induced charge carriers in the ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions, resulting in NALDH/CN/GA-20 showed the lowest PL emission intensity. Additionally, the NALDH/CN and NALDH/CN/GA photocatalysts exhibited a blue shift compared with CN, which was attributed to the differently intrinsic electronic structures of CN [59,60]. This also indicated the strong hybridized interaction between NALDH and CN, which formed sheet-dependent contact heterojunctions entwined with GA. To further elucidate the effect of ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions on photoexcitation charge separation of NALDH/CN/GA composites, especially NALDH/CN/GA-20, photoelectrochemical characterizations were performed. The charge transfer dynamics for representative samples were investigated by time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) decay spectra (Fig. 4d). Evidently, the average lifetime of the photogenerated charge carries in NALDH/CN/GA-20 (6.01 ns) is more prolonged than that of other samples, of which average lifetime was obtained by substituting the data A1, A2, T1 and T2 in the table into the formula (Table S1). It is well-known that a longer lifetime of electrons and holes implies a high probability for participation in photocatalytic reaction and improved activity [61]. Simultaneously, the NALDH/CN/GA-20 catalyst exhibited the highest photocurrent response after several periods of intermittent irradiation (Fig. 4e) and the smallest arc diameter (Fig. 4f). This was attributed to the ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions entwined with GA, which could efficiently accelerate the transfer, separation of photo-induced charge carriers, and enhanced light absorption performance [62].

As shown in Fig. 5a, pure CN and NALDH exhibited poor CO production, the CO production rate of 1.21 and 1.82 μmol⋅g -1 ⋅h -1 , respectively. The photocatalytic activity of NALDH/CN was clearly improved compared with that of pure CN and NALDH, with CO production rate of 3.71μmol⋅g -1 ⋅h -1 . This might be attributed to the formation of ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions between NALDH and CN, which can decrease photoinduced charge recombination. Furthermore, with the introduction of GA, the effect of ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions on photocatalytic activity of the hybrid system was significantly improved. For NALDH/CN/GA-20, the CO yield rate reached 28.83 μmol⋅g -1 ⋅h -1 , which was 24, 16 and 8 times those of pure NALDH, CN and NALDH/CN, respectively. The introduction of GA as an electronic medium and entwining agent, could furthermore promote charge transfer and coupling interface adhesion of heterojunctions, which enhance the separation of electron-hole pairs and mass transport. Additionally, GA, CN/GA, NALDH/GA, NALDH/CN achieved CO yield of 0.26, 2.30, 1.70 and 18.53 μmol⋅g -1 ⋅under five hours of visible light irradiation, respectively (Fig. S8). Obviously, photocatalytic CO 2 reduction performance of NALDH/CN was higher than that of CN/ GA and NALDH/GA. It illustrated ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions showed more important effects on photocatalytic CO 2 reduction of NALDH/CN/GA than GA. With increasing CN content, the CO production rate of the NALDH/CN/GA hybrid increased, with the maximum value of 28.83 μmol⋅g -1 ⋅h -1 CO obtained by NALDH/CN/GA-20, When the CN content exceeded 20%, the CO production rate decreased, which might be due to the stacking of CN nanosheets. This would lead to the material structure collapsing and the surface active sites being covered. The photocatalytic CO 2 reduction efficiency of NALDH/CN/GA with different CN content was consistent with the PL emission peak strength (Fig. 4c). Notably, the photocatalytic activity of the NALDH/CN/GA-20 was higher than that of previously reported catalysts, of which was applied to conventional CO2 photocatalytic reduction by only using water as reducing agent, as shown in Table 2. Additionally, compares the overall CO and CH 4 evolution rates of all prepared samples. Only NALDH/CN, NALDH/CN/GA-20, and NALDH/CN/GA-25 were produced very small amounts of CH 4 . It was probably attributed to the more suitable E CB level of above three samples than other composites, because the conversion of CO 2 to CH 4 and CO need much differently negative potential (ECO 2 /CH 4 = -0.24 V vs. NHE, E CO 2 /CO = -0.53 V vs. NHE). As shown in Fig. 5b, the activity of NALDH/CN/GA-20 did not clearly decrease, with 91-95% of the original photocatalytic activity remaining after four recycles with more than 100 repeating experiments, confirming favorable photostability. It was attributed to hybrid system with high structural stability and strong interfacial interactions of ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions, as a consequence of the FT-IR spectra without obvious differences for the catalyst before and after use (Fig. S9). The surface photo-voltage spectra was used to further explore photogenerated carrier separation efficiency (Fig. 6a). Compared with SPV signal of NALDH and CN, the signal of NALDH/CN and NALDH/CN/GA-20 was significantly improved. The NALDH/CN/GA-20 has the strongest SPV signal. It may be due to ultratight sheet-sheet heterojunctions between NALDH and CN entwined with GA, which enhanced strong interfacial interaction of heterojunctions by its curly folded layer structure. Thus the catalyst enhances the photogenerated electron capture ability and decreases the photogenerated carrier recombination rate, thus increasing the utilization rate of photogenerated electrons and enhancing the photocatalytic performance [72,73]. To verify that the generation of carbon-based CO or CH 4 was not due to organic residues, Ar was used instead of CO 2 under the same experimental conditions. No CH 4 or CO production was detected after 5 h of light irradiation, indicating that the carbon source was CO 2 . Additionally, A 13 CO 2 isotope labeling experiment (Fig. 6b) was performed using NALDH/CN/GA-20 as catalyst. The peak detected by GC (insetof Fig. 6b) with a signal at m/z 29 in the MS spectrum was attributed to 13 CO, which showed that the CO product originated from CO 2 . In order to elucidate the mechanism of accelerating the separation of charge pairs, we accurately analyzed the semiconductor type, donor density and energy band position of catalysts by the Mott-Schottky method and valence band XPS (VB-XPS). Fig. 7a and b show the Mott-Schottky plots of NALDH and CN catalysts, and the positive slope of NALDH and CN were indicated the n-type semiconductor. The slightly enhanced slope values for NALDH imply the increased donor density compared with CN [74]. More specifically, the flat-band potentials of NALDH (-0.58 V vs. NHE) and CN (-1.05 V vs. NHE) were obtained by extrapolating the Mott-Schottky plots in Fig. 7a and b. The flat-band potentials of NALDH and CN were obvious the relatively negative CB potential compared with that of CO 2 /CO (-0.53 eV vs. NHE), CB electrons in the NALDH and CN can directly reduce CO 2 to CO. To determine the exact CB and VB positions for each component, VB-XPS analysis were measured as shown in Fig. 7c. Herein, the VB edge potentials of NALDH and CN, determined from the intercepts of tangents to the density of states at the Fermi edge, were 1.71 and 1.60 eV, respectively. Based on the band gap energies of NALDH (2.36 eV) and CN (2.70 eV) that were determined in the UV-DRS analysis, the corresponding CB edge potentials were calculated to be -0.66 eV and -1.10 eV, respectively. Both the CB and VB potentials of NALDH were more positive than those of CN. The band structure of NiAl-LDH and g-C 3 N 4 was further determined by ESR analysis for an investigation of the transfer path of light-induced electrons and holes. Fig. 7d showed six characteristic peaks of the DMPO-• O 2 -adduct.

Compared with CN and NALDH, the DMPO-• O 2 -signal intensity of NALDH/CN/GA-20 was significantly increased, which might be due to the transfer of photoinduced electrons from the conduction band (CB) of CN to the CB of NALDH [51]. More importantly, the no characteristic peaks of the DMPO-• OH adduct was observed for NALDH/CN/GA-20, NALDH and CN as shown in Fig. S10, which was in accordance with the potential of its valence band (VB). No ESR signals were detected in the catalysts under dark conditions, which indicated that the spin-reactive species were produced under light irradiation [75]. To investigate groups formed on the catalyst surface during the photocatalytic CO 2 reduction reaction, and predict the intermediates, in-situ FT-IR (ISFT-IR) spectroscopy experiments were conducted on the NALDH/CN/GA-20 catalyst. As shown in Fig. 7e, multiple intermediate products, including HCO 3 * (1370 cm -1 ), b-CO 3 2-(1245 and 1215 cm -1 ), CHO* (1085 cm -1 ), CH 3 O* (1040 cm -1 ), and COOH* (1670 and 1435 cm -1 ) were observed [70,[76][77][78]. Notably, the concentration of COOH* and CH 3 O* intermediates increased significantly under light irradiation, suggesting that COOH* and CH 3 O* were the main intermediates of the CO 2 reduction process [77,79]. By integrating the results above, based on type-II NALDH/CN/GA hybrid system (Fig. 7f), the multi electron series reduction mechanism was proposed to explain the CO 2 reduction pathway as shown in Fig. 8. Upon the visible light irradiation, the electrons on the valence band (VB) of CN and NALDH can be excited into the conduction band (CB). Meanwhile, the formed holes on the VB of NALDH transfer into the VB of CN, and the electrons transfer from the CB of CN to the CB of NALDH. Subsequently, compared with that of CO 2 /CO (-0.53 eV vs. NHE), owing to the relatively negative CB potential (-0.68 eV vs. NHE) and the flat-band potential (-0.58 V vs. NHE) of NALDH, electrons in the NALDH CB can directly reduce CO 2 to CO via HCO 3 * and COOH* intermediates with the multi electron series reduction process [54,79,80]. And the detailed CO 2 reduction process is conducted by a series of equations in the Table S2.

mentions.text: In order to further verify the presence of surface OVs in the samples, EPR spectra of pure IO and ZCS/IO-10 were measured, as shown in Fig. 3g. It can be found that both pure IO and ZCS/IO-10 exhibit OVs signals at the g value of about 2.002 [17]. Moreover, the EPR signal strength of ZCS/IO-10 is much higher than that of pure IO, demonstrating that there are more abundant surface OVs in the ZCS/IO-10 composite, which is in agreement with the results of XPS test. The surface OVs can strengthen the light response, activate O 2 molecules adsorbed on catalyst surface to produce active oxygen species, and act as trapping centers for photoinduced electrons to accelerate the efficient separation and transfer of photogenerated carriers [10,36,37]. Thereby, the fabrication of ZCS/IO-10 composite with great concentration of 4a, the adsorption-desorption isotherms of all the samples showed a typical type-IV isothermal model with H3 hysteresis loops, suggesting the presence of mesoporous structure in the three materials [25,44,46]. The BJH (Barrett-Joyner-Halenda) pore size distribution curves in Fig. 4b further verified that the pore sizes of the three samples were in the range of 2-50 nm. As can be seen from Table 1, the BET (Brunauer-Emmett-Teller) specific surface area of ZCS/IO-10 (120.58 m 2 ⋅g -1 ) is nearly 6-and 3-folds that of IO (23.84 m 2 ⋅g -1 ) and ZCS (43.6 m 2 ⋅g -1 ), respectively, which might be due to the loading of ZCS nanoparticles on the surface of IO [44]. The significant increase in the surface area of ZCS/IO-10 can provide more reactive sites for the photocatalytic reaction, which will lead to an enhancement in the photocatalytic activity [1,44]. Additionally, a decrease in the pore size of ZCS/IO-10 (6.5 nm) can be observed in comparison with that of pure IO (42.60 nm) and ZCS (26.98 nm), which may be due to the good dispersibility of ZCS on the IO surface [1]. In conclusion, the ZCS/IO-10 composite has a larger specific surface area as well as pore volume, which can expose more active sites for adsorption and photocatalytic reactions, and thus improving its photocatalytic performance [44].

Generally, the polarity of the solvent is an important factor influencing the catalytic reaction. In deionized water (DIW) (entry 8), the poor activity might be related to the low solubility of benzylamine in H 2 O. This indicates that Zn 0.1 Cd 0.9 S and In 2 O 3 in ZCS/IO-10 composite are not simply mixed, but formed a heterojunction through intimate contact, which is crucial for the enhancement of photocatalytic activity. mentions.text: The photocatalytic oxidative coupling of different amine substrates were investigated to demonstrate the universal applicability of the ZCS/ IO-10 composite. As shown in Table 4, for the substituted benzylamines (entries 1-7), the selectivity to corresponding imines were in excess of 99.0 % with either an electron-donating or electron-withdrawing substituent in the phenyl ring. Nevertheless, the conversion of amines were evidently influenced by the position of the substituent. mentions.text: Experimental details concerning materials and raw samples preparation were given in Ref. [43]. All samples are synthesized by laser pyrolysis method in a flow reactor where a continuous wave CO 2 laser (λ = 10.6 μm) orthogonally crossed the gas/vapors flows emerging through three concentric nozzles as follows: SnMe 4 /ZnEt 2 vapors and SF 6 /C 2 H 4 gases through the central nozzle, O 2 and Ar gas mixture through the middle one, Ar gas for confinement through the third nozzle. The experimental parameters are presented in Table 1. In the synthesize process SF 6 or C 2 H 4 are introduced as energy transfer agents (sensitizers) because SnMe 4 and ZnEt 2 precursors does not absorb CO 2 laser energy. The interaction between laser radiation and reactants results in a confined sooting flame from which the SnO 2 based nanoparticles emerge and are then collected on a porous filter.

mentions.text: The performance of g-C 3 N 4 , LaCoO 3 and 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 composite was assessed with the production and selectivity of CO and CH 4 , and results are exhibited in Table 1. Utilizing the CO 2 -H 2 O system, CO 2 is efficiently converted to solar fuels. Using pristine g-C 3 N 4 , yield rates of 114.3 and 78.9 μmole g-cat -1 h -1 at the selectivity of 78.9 and 21.1% were obtained. Similarly, selectivity of LaCoO 3 for CO and CH 4 were 79.4 and 20.5% at the production rate 110.4, and 28.5 μmole gcat -1 h -1 , respectively. This confirms that both g-C 3 N 4 , and LaCoO 3 desirable to convert CO 2 to produce CO and CH 4 , however, the yield rate is lesser because of the charges recombination over the surface of each catalyst individually. When LaCoO 3 was coupled with g-C 3 N 4 , the amount of CO yielded was raised over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 composite, but selectivity was lowered as opposed to g-C 3 N 4 because of the higher electron production and the selectivity of CH 4 increased. More attractively, the amount of CH 4 (48.59 μmole g-cat -1 h -1 ) produced was increased over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 composite at the selectivity 26.4%, indicating the photocatalytic activity increases CH 4 production. The production rate of CO over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 of 135.152 μmole g-cat -1 h -1 was achieved, which is 1.18 and 1.2 times greater than when it was yielded with g-C 3 N 4 and LaCoO 3, respectively. Similarly, with a selectivity of 26.4%, a yield rate of 48.5 μmole g-cat -1 h -1 was achieved for CH 4 , which is 1.59 and 1.7 times greater than the selectivity obtained over g-C 3 N 4 and LaCoO 3 , respectively. This resulted in the water gas shift (WGS) response [2], showing that both g-C 3 N 4 , and LaCoO 3 boosted the yield rate because of its enhanced charges separation rate when combined together. This shows that a composite of 15 wt % LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 is promising for selective photocatalytic CO 2 methanation under apparent light irradiation.

For each molecule of CO and CH 4 production, the number of electrons (n) used were 2 and 8, respectively. The light intensity of 20 mW cm -2 at wavelength 420 nm and incident area of 25 cm 2 was utilized for QY measurement. The QY for CO and CH 4 over g-C 3 N 4 , LaCoO 3 and 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 composite is demonstrated in Table 1. Utilizing pristine g-C 3 N 4 , a QY for CO and CH 4 of 0.24 and 0.90% were attained, which was raised to 1.06% and 0.38% using 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 samples, respectively. Likewise, a QY of LaCoO 3 for CO and CH 4 of 0.87 and 0.22% were attained, which were improved to 1.06% and 0.38%, respectively, using 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 samples. This indicates that heterojunction of g-C 3 N 4 with LaCoO 3 improved photon energy usage, enhancing efficient photogeneration electron-hole pairs with their efficient separation of CO 2 reduction to CO and CH 4 . Highest QY of CH 4 production was 0.38% over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 composite, whereas, the maximum QY of CO generation was 1.06% over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 composite was observed. The quantity of QY for CH 4 production over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 was 1.5 and 1.7 folds more than QY of g-C 3 N 4 , and LaCoO 3 , respectively. QY for CO yielded over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 was 1.18 and 1.22 folds more than QY of g-C 3 N 4 and LaCoO 3 , respectively. The significantly improved QY over 15 wt% LaCoO 3 /g-C 3 N 4 was because of higher electron generation due to the controlled composite catalyst, increased electron movement and effective charge transmission rate by LaCoO 3 . This is made possible by their efficient photoelectrical properties as heterojunction photocatalyst.

mentions.text: Moreover, the Pt-GCO-BMO photocatalyst demonstrated a superior photocatalytic performance toward the decomposition of BPA in water. As represented in Fig. 8a, Pt-GCO-BMO displayed higher BPA degradation within 75 min (78.12%) as compared with pure GCO (18.03%), BMO (47.88%) and GCO-BMO (64.52%). Based on first-order kinetic equation ln(C t /C 0 ) = k app t [44,45], the reaction rate constant(k app ) of Pt-GCO-BMO was 16.47 x10 -3 min -1 (Fig. 8b), much higher than that of GCO (0.95x10 -3 min -1 ), BMO (4.71x10 -3 min -1 ) and GCO-BMO (10.72x10 -3 min -1 ), respectively, which further demonstrates the high efficiency of the Pt-GCO-BMO photocatalyst for the application in water treatment. mentions.text: The synthesized binary composite and bare MOF were tested for the photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 using N,N-dimethyl formamide and water (3:1) as reaction medium and triethylamine (TEA) as a sacrificial electron donor under visible light irradiation. At first, the reaction mixture (50 ml) was degassed with N 2 for 30 min followed by CO 2 for one hour with vigorous stirring. Further, the photocatalyst (50 mg) was added to the reaction mixture and the resulting solution was purged with CO 2 for 30 min for saturation. The reaction vessel was equipped with CO 2 -filled balloon and kept nearly 4 cm away from the light source (20 W LED light) for 24 h with irradiated light intensity on the reaction potof 85 w.m -2 . The reaction progress was measured by analyzing the samples after every 4 h intervals by GC/FID(Varian CP 3800) equipped with Stabilwax column. The analysis of gaseous products was done by GC-RGA (Agilant 7890B) using 20μL sample. The analysis of the liquid phase confirmed the selective formation of methanol without any evidence for the formation of formic acid and other possible carbon products. However, there was no possible carbon products such as methane, CO, ethane and ethylene detected in the gaseous phase analysis. The total highest methanol yield was found to be 9264 μmol.g -1 for g-CNQDs@MOF and 1584 μmol.g -1 for NH 2 -UiO-66 MOF after continuous irradiation for 24 h, corresponding to g-CNQDs@MOF (386 μmol. h -1 .g -1 ), compared to NH 2 -UiO-66 MOF (66 μmol.h -1 .g -1 ) methanol formation rate (Fig. 9). For the quantification of methanol yield, a calibration curve was made using the known concentrations of methanol. As shown in Fig. 9, the yield rate of methanol increased almost linearly as a function of irradiation time. The linear increase in the product amount with time was due to the availability of all the active sites on the catalyst surface for CO 2 adsorption and subsequent reduction reaction. With time more and more sites got occupied with the CO 2 and hence the production of the methanol molecules increased with time. But after nearly 16 h, the rate of methanol production was found to be decreased due to the consumption of the available CO 2 molecules as well as adsorption of the product molecules over the active sites of the catalyst surface. With further time, after 28 h it starts to decrease significantly because of the non-availability of vacant active sites as the desorption of product molecules lowered and with time some of the active sites got deteriorated. mentions.text: The textural properties ( Table 1 ) were determined from nitrogen adsorption isotherms at -196 °C. The BET areas and micropore volumes of TS-1-C and TS-1-V (528 m 2 /g and 466 m 2 /g; 0.15 cm 3 /g and 0.14 cm 3 /g, respectively) are consistent with those typically observed in MFI zeolites. Significant differences in external surface area between these two catalysts result from marked differences in crystal size. The TS-1-C is composed of crystals with approximately 200 nm in diameter, whereas the TS-1-V has a crystal size of 1- 2 μm (cf. SEM images, Fig. 2 ). Lam-TS-1 has a significantly lower micropore volume (0.11 cm 3 /g) than conventional TS-1 samples resulting from its layered character. In contrast, its total pore volume (0.34 cm 3 /g vs. 0.22 cm 3 /g) and external surface area (94 m 2 /g vs. 49 m 2 /g and 6 m 2 /g) are higher than those of conventional TS-1 samples. TiO 2 P25 is composed of small ( < 500 nm) agglomerated crystals (Fig. S2, Supplementary Information), with no micropores and with an external surface are of 55 m 2 /g, which is similar to that of TS-1-C. The nature of the titanium species present in titanosilicate zeolites was investigated by the DR-UV/Vis spectroscopy ( Fig. 3 ). Titanium (IV) species in a silica matrix exhibit ligand-to-metal charge transfer absorption bands in range of UV light. Isolated Ti species, which are not connected to any other Ti atom via an oxygen bridge, with tetrahedral coordination (framework Ti species), exhibit an absorption band typically at 205-220 nm, depending on the type of zeolite, more specifically at 205-210 nm for MFI. Conversely, anatase-like domains (containing Ti-O-Ti bonds) absorb at 330 nm. The Rutile phase of TiO 2 exhibits an absorption band at 380 nm, and 5-and 6-coordinated isolates species, attached to the silica framework, exhibit various bands in the range from 220 to 290 nm [16] . In all zeolite samples under study, isolated tetrahedrally coordinated species prevailed, whereas anatase-like domains were detected only in the TS-1-C and likely in lam-TS-1 (cf. shoulder above 300 nm, in Fig. 3 ). The lam TS-1 also contains a considerable share of extra-framework isolates Ti species (bands at 240 nm and 280 nm) [16] . Anatase is the dominant phase in the TiO 2 P25 sample, as shown by the lack of strong absorption above ca. 350 nm.

The affinity of the titanosilicate photocatalysts to CO 2 was investigated by TPD-CO 2 profiling ( Fig. 5 ). The amounts of desorbed CO 2 after saturation (q max CO 2 ) are outlined in Table 1 . CO 2 des- orption at low temperature was observed in the TS-1 based photocatalysts, with the desorption T max ranging from 85 to 94 °C. The interaction between CO 2 and the photocatalyst is thus weak. Nevertheless, Lam-TS-1 bound CO 2 more strongly than TS-1-V and TS-1-C. In contrast, the TiO 2 P25 exhibited a strong desorption peak with T max = 220 °C. The higher the desorption temperature, the stronger the bond between adsorbate and sorbent. The nature of the TiO 2 is different in comparison with the titanosilicate catalysts. That is a reason why the TPD profile is different and in short stronger CO 2 bonding is observed on TiO 2 in comparison with the titanosilicates. The observed profile is in agreement with the findings of Serpone et al. [37] , published in the book: Environmentally Benign Photocatalysts -Applications of Titanium Oxide-based Materials.

The hydrophilicity of the photocatalysts was investigated by TPD-H 2 O profiling ( Fig. 6 ), and the amounts of desorbed H 2 O after saturation at 25 °C (q max H 2 O) are listed in Table 1 . The profiles are qualitatively similar to the above TPD-CO 2 , with a low temperature desorption maximum between 74 and 85 °C. Again, the TiO 2 P25 exhibited another broad maximum at 180 °C, and Lam-TS-1 had a low temperature maximum with a tail up to 230 °C, which is not present in TS-1-C or TS-1-V. TPD-H 2 O confirms the hydrophobicity of TS-1, which is one of its strong features, e.g., in epoxidation with hydrogen peroxide [17] . Lam-TS-1 is slightly more hydrophilic than TS-1-V and TS-1-C because of its silanol groups between layers. Our measurements with saturation at 100 °C confirmed the above observation (Fig. S1 S3, Supplementary Information).

The efficiency of the photocatalytic reaction was also evaluated in terms of an apparent quantum yield (AQY). All parameters needed for the calculations are shown in Table S1, in Supplementary materials, including an example of our calculations. The total apparent quantum yields of each photocatalyst are outlined in Table 2 .

The key steps of the photocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide are adsorption and subsequent activation of the reagents (CO 2 and H 2 O). As shown in Fig. 5 and Table 1 , photocatalysts with a higher affinity to CO 2 , i.e., Lam-TS-1 and TS-1-V, have a higher photoreduction quantum efficiency (PQE). In turn, Fig. Fig. 10 c shows the relationship between the amount of adsorbed H 2 O molecules (TPD-H 2 O) and hydrogen production. The sample TS-1-V had both the highest amount of adsorbed H 2 O molecules and hydrogen production. Concurrently, the lowest amount of adsorbed H 2 O molecules and hydrogen production was observed in the same sample, TS-1-C. These results are in line with previous studies, which have shown that photocatalyst hydrophilicity affects the efficiency and selectivity of photocatalytic processes [49][50][51] .

We confirmed that on irradiation, CO 2 was selectively reduced to CO with no H 2 (detection limit <10 ppb) or other byproducts being detected at all time (Fig. 5). Continuous evolution of CO could be measured, with [Ir-PhCOOH] showing higher activity than [IreCOOH]. The CO turnover numbers at 300 min irradiation (TON CO @ 300 min) of 37 and 51 were measured for [IreCOOH] and [Ir-PhCOOH], respectively. Both showed no sign of deactivation even after 7 h of reaction. The higher activity of [Ir-PhCOOH] corroborates the photophysical characterization, where [Ir-PhCOOH] exhibits a higher extinction coefficient relative to that of [IreCOOH] (Fig. 3), allowing higher absorbance of incoming photons for photocharge generation, as well as the electrochemical characterization that it is capable of more thorough catalyst activation (Fig. 4). Furthermore, the ePhCOOH ligand substituent can enhance the activity in three ways. First, given that the elimination of Cl À from the Ir center is a critical step to generate the eventual active catalyst responsible for CO 2 reduction [18], strong electron-donating power, characteristic of the phenyl ring, strengthens the nucleophilicity of the metal center and hence the catalyst activation. Second, as will be discussed later in this work, the phenyl group assisted in stabilizing the CO adduct on the Ir center in its rate-limiting step. Third, a bulky substituent (e.g. phenyl) at the terpyridyl ligand may also enhance the system lifetime because of the effective steric protection [28]. In the absence of the carboxyl groups, Genoni et al. mentions.text: The CV experiments of Co-PYN5 and Co-N5 were also registered in the presence of 5% 2,2',2''-trifluoroethanol (TFE) under CO 2 in MeCN as solvent and are displayed in Figures S1 and S2. Interestingly, as can be observed, all potentials cathodically shift by about 200 mV and the onset of catalysis now occurs at approx. À1.0 V. Electrocatalytic experiments were carried out by means of bulk electrolysis for both Co-PYN5 and Co-N5 in MeCN with 5% TFE as a proton source at an applied potential of À1.30 V, giving mainly CO and H 2 as products, in ratio of 3.8 and 2.5, respectively (Table S1 and Figure S20).

A typical time profile of [Co-PYN5+g-C 3 N 4 ] system for photocatalytic CO 2 reduction is displayed in Figure 5. Using a [Co-PYN5] of 50 mM and after 8 h of irradiation, 15.4 mmol of CO was detected as the dominant gaseous product, consistent with a 94% CO selectivity and a TON of 77 (Table 1, entry 2). This is in sharp contrast with the electrocatalytic conditions described earlier in homogeneous phase where the CO selectivity is significantly lower. For the Co-N5 catalyst, in the absence of the pyrene group, the species absorbed or in close contact with the surface drastically decreases, giving a TON of 37, which is 2 times lower as compared to the Co-PYN5 in the same conditions (Table 1, entry 6). This comparison clearly manifests that the CH-p interaction significantly promotes the photocatalytic performance. The increased reactivity of the Co-PYN5 versus Co-N5 can also be observed under the same conditions as previously described but in the absence of TFE (see entries 1 and 5 in Table 1), where the reactivity of the pyrene containing complex is 5 times higher toward the formation of CO.

Consequently, only the adsorbed catalytic species, Co-PYN5@g-C 3 N 4 , will be active, and thus, the TON reported here represents a lower limit of the catalyst performance. Indeed, by reducing the [Co-PYN5] to 2 mM (entry 3, Table 1), the TON obtained increases more than 5 times to a value of 396. This indicates that, even at this low catalyst concentration, the amount of Co-PYN5 bonded to g-C 3 N 4 is still very high. It should be noted that the addition of fresh catalyst in the deactivated mixture after photocatalysis could reinitiate the CO formation (Figure S19), indicating the catalyst deactivation during photocatalysis should be a main reason for the ceased CO evolution after 8 h of irradiation.

Further, in order to decouple the equilibrium indicated in Equation 1, the photocatalytic experiments were carried out using CH 2 Cl 2 as the solvent instead of MeCN, where Co-PYN5 is insoluble. In this case, we used the hybrid material Co-PYN5@g-C 3 N 4 suspended in a CH 2 Cl 2 solution in the presence of TEOA under the same conditions. A TON of 533 is reached that is nearly an order of magnitude larger than that in MeCN (Table 1, entry 4) and is among the largest reported in the literature for related systems with no noble metals. Further, an initial turnover frequency (TOF i ) (measured during the first 2 h) of 95 h À1 is obtained that is among the fastest reported in light-induced CO 2 reduction systems using non-noble-metal molecular catalysts and g-C 3 N 4 . For comparative purposes, the performances of other relevant 1), where the interactions with the catalysts and the g-C 3 N 4 semiconductors are based on van der Waals interaction (entry 9 and 13), p-p stacking (entries 11 and 12), and covalent amide bonds (entries 10 and 14). Finally, another feature of our system is that it is also active at [CO 2 ] as low as 0.1 atm, as indicated in the entry 7 of Table 1. This is interesting because, in fuel, oil, and coal combustion, the flue gas [CO 2 ] in dry exhaust gas is within 10%-15% by volume. 49 Overall, the results presented here prove that the CH-p interaction between molecular Co catalysts and the g-C 3 N 4 surface provides the ideal electronic interaction for a successful electronic communication between the catalyst and the light absorber. Figure 6 exhibits an energy diagram containing the main reactions involved, whereas Figure 3 shows a diagram of the electron and hole flow upon illumination. Visible light irradiation of the g-C 3 N 4 surface produces a relatively long-lived, charge-separated excited state (in the ranges of ns), where the positive charge generated at the valence band (VB) is quenched by excess TEOA that acts as a sacrificial electron donor. On the other hand, the electrons at the CB are collected by the molecular Co(II) catalyst undergoing two consecutive reduction events that provoke the transformation of CO 2 into CO, in agreement with the electrochemical results described earlier (Figure 2).

mentions.text: Structural characterization and growth mechanism of 2D/2D hybrid Because the 2D/2D hybrid is a layer-by-layer assembly of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 and Ni-Mn LDH, the two components were first studied in isolation. OVs-Mn 3 O 4 was prepared by the hydrolysis of Mn(COOH) 2 $2H 2 O in MeOH at 180 C (see Supplemental information for details). An X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern reveals that the OVs-Mn 3 O 4 is a tetragonal phase Mn 3 O 4 (JCPDS no. 24-0734) of high purity (Figure S1). In the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra, oxygen peaks at 529.8, 530.2, 531.0, and 532.5 eV correspond to the lattice oxygen, the OH group, the oxygen species chemisorbed on the surface OVs, and the absorbed H 2 O, respectively. 31 The abundance of OVs in OVs-Mn 3 O 4 can be demonstrated by the area percentage (52.40%) of the peak at 531.0 eV that is higher than that of commercial Mn 3 O 4 (25.23%, Figure 1H; Table S1) and from the electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signal at g = 2.000 (Figure S2) that arises from the electrons trapped in the OVs. 32 The Ni-Mn LDH was prepared by the hydrolysis of Mn(COO) 2 $2H 2 O and NiCl 2 in MeOH at 180 C (Ni/Mn = 0.7). As-prepared Ni-Mn LDH is an a-Ni-Mn LDH (JCPDS no. 00-025-4047) of high purity (Figure S1) 33 and has homogeneous elemental distribution according to elemental mapping, including 47.1 wt% Ni, 16.55 wt% Mn, and 36.35 wt% O (Figure S3). Ni-Mn LDH is basically free of OVs, as the O1s peak at 531.0 eV in the XPS spectra is negligible (Figure 1H).

The 2D/2D assembly of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 and Ni-Mn LDH was prepared as a micro-flower through the same hydrolysis reaction at Ni/Mn = 0.3, as confirmed by XRD analysis (Figure S1) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images (Figures 1A-1G and S4). The relative mass ratio of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 to Ni-Mn LDH in the 2D/2D hybrid is $0.53 according to an elemental analysis. The skeleton of the hybrid is Ni-Mn LDH nanosheets (NSs). In the high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) image of the hybrid (Figure 1C), the observed inter-planar spacing of 0.21 nm can be ascribed to the (010) plane of Ni-Mn LDH. 34 On the surface of Ni-Mn LDH, NSs are scattered as many leaf-like Mn 3 O 4 NSs (Figure 1B) that show well-resolved lattice spacing of 0.29 and 0.25 nm ascribed to the (211) and (200) planes of Mn 3 O 4 , respectively. According to high-resolution elemental mapping (Figures 1E-1G), the Ni atoms are segregated in the Ni-Mn LDH NSs and have an average Ni valence (V Ni = 2.2) identical to V Ni = 2.3 for pure Ni-Mn-LDH according to XPS measurements (Figure S5). 35,36 We can further rule out the incorporation of Ni in the Mn 3 O 4 lattice based on that: (1) the XRD peak positions of Mn 3 O 4 in the 2D/2D hybrid are the same as those of pure OVs-Mn 3 O 4 (Figure S1B) without a peak shift and 2) the pure lattice fringes of Mn 3 O 4 are identified in the spherical aberration-corrected TEM (ACTEM) images at the atomic level, and the dark/dot contrast shows that Mn 3 O 4 has a uniform distribution of Mn and is free of Ni (Figure 1D). The O1s XPS profile (Figure 1H; Table S1) and the EPR signal (Figure S2) of the 2D/2D hybrid are analogous to those of the OVs-Mn 3 O 4 , indicating that the Mn 3 O 4 in the hybrid still has abundant OVs. The atomic force microscope (AFM) image (Figures 1I and S6) reveals that within the hybrid, the Ni-Mn LDH NSs with a lateral size at microscale are built of thin sheets (ca. 2 nm) that correspond to 2-3 stacking layers of LDH along the c axis. 33 The leaf-like OVs-Mn 3 O 4 NSs are ca. 3.75 nm in height and have a lateral dimension of ca. 90 nm (Figure 1I). The ultrathin feature of both Ni-Mn LDH and OVs-Mn 3 O 4 allows layer-by-layer adhesion and thus creates intimate contact with them in the 2D/2D hybrid. 10 The assembly of the 2D/2D hybrid undergoes a solid-to-solid phase transition (Scheme 1A) via an amorphous Ni-Mn intermediate, which consists of microspheres and can be identified by time-dependent XRD (Figure S7) and SEM (Figure S8) at 1 h of the synthesis. Phase transformation of the amorphous intermediate starts at >1.5 h, and it generates the OVs-Mn 3 O 4 and Ni-Mn LDH at 18 h (Figure S7). Elemental analysis shows that the chemical composition of the amorphous intermediate is very close to that of the final 2D/2D hybrid (Figure S9), indicating that the amorphous intermediate is the precursor to the final hybrid. Such a phase transition can be described as non-equilibrium crystallization via a metastable intermediate (Scheme 1A), a pathway previously proposed for the growth of Mn oxides in aqueous solution. 37

The binding and activation of CO 2 and H 2 O on the catalyst surface was then further evaluated by setting up the models of and running DFT calculations for Ni-Mn LDH, OVs-rich Mn 3 O 4 , and perfect (OVs-poor) Mn 3 O 4 (Figures 3C and 3D), with the Mn 3 O 4 of the perfect lattice structure used as a surrogate to evaluate the OVspoor Mn 3 O 4 . Previously, the electrostatic interaction between the O atoms of CO 2 and the OVs on the catalyst surface was known to promote the adsorption process. 42,48 Calculations reveal that the CO 2 physically adsorbed on perfect Mn 3 O 4 has an adsorption energy (DE ad-CO2 ) of À0.238 eV (Figure 3B). In the presence of OVs, CO 2 can be chemically bound to OVs-Mn 3 O 4 (Figure 3F), thus giving a lower DE ad-CO2 of À0.306 eV. The unreacted CO 2 on the perfect Mn 3 O 4 has a bond angle of 178.75 and a bond length of 1.19 A ˚but is deformed to 133.53 and 1.37 A ˚on the surface of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 as a result of stronger interactions (Figure 3C). The charge migration between the catalyst and CO 2 can be further characterized by the Bader charge Dq (Figure S20; Table 1), 49 which shows a stronger electron transfer to CO 2 from OVs-Mn 3 O 4 (Dq = 0.685 e) than from OVs-poor Mn 3 O 4 (-0.002 e). The CO 2 adsorbate on OVs-Mn 3 O 4 no longer has the linear symmetry of free CO 2 but becomes more amenable to accepting an electron into its lowered LUMO. 50 The Ni-Mn LDH also has a strong affinity for CO 2 and readily activates CO 2 , but CO 2 attaches to the Ni-Mn LDH surface not with its O atoms but with its C atom through the coordination between C and Ni (Figure 3E). The adsorbed CO 2 has a reduced bond angle of 128.3 and an extended bond length of 1.28 A ˚(Figure 3C). Whereas the configuration of CO 2 adsorbed on the Ni-Mn LDH surface is not radically different from that on the OVs-Mn 3 O 4 surface (133.53 , 1.37 A ˚), the DE ad-CO2 of Ni-Mn LDH (-1.60 eV) is dramatically lower than that of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 (À0.306 eV), which may account for the exceedingly high CO 2 -capture ability of Ni-Mn LDH ($6.13 cm 3 /g) compared with that of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 ($4.08 cm 3 /g).

The strong C-Ni interaction is also associated with a notable electron transfer between CO 2 and Ni-Mn LDH that gives a very high Dq of 0.907 e (Figure S20; Table 1), thus facilitating the one electron transfer to generate CO 2 d-, a key limiting step in CRR. 51 Indeed, the high-resolution image of the charge density of Ni-Mn LDH clearly shows an electron transfer between Ni and CO 2 (Figure 3C). Hence, the Ni element must be contributing to the efficiency of CRR by improving the binding and activation of CO 2 , as well as enhancing the injection of the electron into CO 2 . In fact, according to Peressi et al., 52 CO 2 adsorbed on the surface of metallic Ni is attached to Ni (110) through the carbon atom, which has an excess number of electrons and is negatively charged. In the present calculation, when Ni is removed from Ni-Mn LDH to create a Ni-free model of Mn(OH) 2 (Figure 3C), Dq drops radically to only -0.06 eV (Figure S20). This result is in accordance with the measured catalytic performance of a Mn(OH) 2 sample (prepared by the hydrolysis of MnCl 2 ) whose CRR selectivity is as low as 55.71% and whose efficiency is only V CO = 2.84 mmol 3 h À1 (Figure S21), both notably inferior compared with Ni-Mn LDH (100%, 6.46 mmol 3 h À1 ).

The in situ FT-IR (Figures 4A and S22) spectra well-conform to the DFT calculations and corroborate that the CO 2 adsorbed on the OVs-Mn 3 O 4 and Ni-Mn LDH have distinct configurations. Specifically, the CO 2 on Ni-Mn LDH and 2D/2D show the FT-IR bands at 1,688 and 1,632 cm À1 , which correspond to NiÀCO 2 dÀ and NiÀCO 2 H, 19,53,54 respectively (Figures 4A and S22A). Kuehnel et al. 55 has demonstrated that CO 2 can be bound to Ni via Ni-C interaction in both NiÀCO 2 dÀ and NiÀCO 2 H. 19 In addition, the peak at 1,465 cm À1 corresponds to activated species of CO 2 dÀ . The in situ FT-IR measurement proves, along with DFT calculations, that CO 2 is bound to Ni via Ni-C interactions on Ni-Mn LDHs (Figure 3E) and that the Ni sites activate CO 2 into CO 2 d-. When Ni is absent, the CO 2 on OVs-Mn 3 O 4 gives a FT-IR band at 1,721 cm À1 (Figure S22B) that corresponds to CO 2 in the form of chelating bridged carbonate (c-CO 3 d-), an O-coordination complex. 56 This result conforms to the DFT calculation that CO 2 attaches to the OVs-Mn 3 O 4 surface with the O atoms. The peaks intensities (by deducting the absorbance under dark) change after light irradiation. For 2D/2D, under light irradiation, the intensity of the bands at 1,632 and 1,465 cm À1 decreases remarkably with the elapse of time because the activated species of CO 2 d-can react with the surface proton to generate COOH* and quickly produce CO. 57 With regard to the exquisite CRR selectivity of the 2D/2D hybrid that is derived from Ni-Mn LDH, we also evaluated the hydrophobicity of the catalyst surface, as a hydrophobic surface can repel H 2 O molecules and assist in the localization and delivery of CO 2 molecules. 58 Contact angle measurement reveals that all samples are hydrophilic (Figure S23). From theoretical calculation in Figure 3D, there is no significant change of bond lengths and angles of H 2 O, and this suggests a weak interaction between the catalyst and the surrounding H 2 O molecule. Furthermore, the charge density analysis (Figure S27) reveals that the electron cloud of the catalyst basically does not overlap with that of H 2 O in each model. These results show that perfect Mn 3 O 4 , OVs-Mn 3 O 4 , Ni-Mn LDH, and Mn(OH) 2 all have a close DE ad-H2O and that the H 2 O molecule could be just physically adsorbed (Figure 3D) on all catalyst surfaces without being activated. That is, the adsorption of H 2 O is thermodynamically favorable on all catalysts, and their divergent performance cannot be accounted for by their similar abilities in binding and activating H 2 O. However, a sharp contrast appears when the DE ad and Dq of CO 2 and H 2 O are compared for all catalyst models. Both OVs-poor Mn 3 O 4 and OVs-Mn 3 O 4 have similar DE ad for both CO 2 and H 2 O (Table 1). In the case of Ni-Mn LDH, DE ad-CO2 is 4.2 times DE ad-H2O . In addition, the Dq from the catalyst to CO 2 is also much higher for Ni-Mn LDH (0.907 e) than for OVs-Mn 3 O 4 (0.685 e). Hence, the outstanding CRR selectivity of Ni-Mn LDH is readily accounted for by the high Dq (0.907 e) upon CO 2 adsorption and the marked contrast between its DE ad-CO2 and DE ad-H2O , which is ascribed to the presence of the Ni element in the catalyst.

Generally, without activating the unwanted HER, the OVs in OVs-Mn 3 O 4 promote light harvesting and charge transport, which are both crucial for the enhancement of CRR efficiency. As shown in Figure S14 and Table 1, the presence of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 extends the absorption edge from $600 nm for Ni-Mn LDH to $800 nm for the 2D/2D hybrid, hence preventing the inadequate absorption of visible light, a known limitation for photocatalytic reactions. 22 Furthermore, the 2D/2D hybrid manifests the higher I-t (Figure S18) which should arise from the heterojunction formed between the OVs-Mn 3 O 4 and Ni-Mn LDH, and the resulting stronger charge transfer ability leads to the advanced CRR efficiency. To verify this, a mechanical mixture of OVs-Mn 3 O 4 and Ni-Mn LDH that does not form a heterostructure was prepared and tested as a CRR catalyst. The reference mixture indeed attains a high CRR selectivity of 97.88% comparable to that of the 2D/2D hybrid or Ni-Mn LDH, but it only has a lackluster V CO of 7.60 mmol 3 h À1 (Figure S26). In addition, compared with a mixture of OVs-poor Mn 3 O 4 and Ni-Mn-LDH, 2D/2D (i.e., OVs-Mn 3 O 4 /Ni-Mn-LDH) has a higher I-t and lower PL signals (Figure S17 and S18), revealing that OVs in hybrid could facilitate the charge separation. In fact, a control 2D/2D hybrid containing Mn 3 O 4 of lower OVs concentration (Figure S2) can be afforded by regulating the relative Ni content in the synthesis procedure, and such 2D/2D of fewer OVs had a lower V CO down to 12.87 mmol 3 g -1 3 h -1 . Clearly, the presence of OVs is indispensable to afford a high photocatalytic activity, which boosts the charge carriers transfer and separation kinetics of catalysts.
