mentions.text: Irradiation of aqueous suspensions of titanium dioxide saturated with carbon dioxide by light with l £ 350 nm, which exceeds the width of the semiconductor forbidden band leads to the appearance of gaseous methane in the system (Fig. 2a, curve 1). The rate of methane formation involving porous titanium dioxide is greater than this rate using Degussa (Evonik) P25 titanium dioxide (see Table 1). The differences in activity may be interpreted as a consequence of the porous structure of these samples [4], which facilitates prolonged capture of the reagents in the photocatalyst pores and migration of the photogenerated electrons along the system of contacting TiO 2 nanocrystals, which should reduce the probability of electron-hole recombination. Still another reason for the difference in photoactivity of these materials may be the different phase composition of the photocatalysts.

Table 1 shows that although the rate of reduction of carbon dioxide to methane on mesoporous titanium dioxide is almost double this rate using Degussa (Evonik) P25 TiO 2 , it is still rather low. A possible method to enhance the photoactivity of TiO 2 is incorporating this oxide into metal-semiconductor composites [3]. The irradiation of deaerated aqueous suspensions of TiO 2 in the presence of sodium sulfite acting an electron donor and a number of metal salts such as AgNO 3 , CuCl 2 , or NaAuCl 4 leads to coloration of the reaction mixtures. The color of the composites remains after the inlet of air, washing the residues to remove residual salts, and drying. Nishimoto et al. [6] showed that irradiation of suspensions of TiO 2 in the presence of silver ions leads to change in the color of the solutions, which was attributed to the photoinduced formation of metal particles on the semiconductor surface. Our case also apparently involves photoreduction of the metal ions to give TiO 2 /A, TiO 2 /Au, and TiO 2 /Cu metal-semiconductor nanocomposites. Evidence for the formation of metal-semiconductor composites is found in the X-ray diffraction spectra of the materials obtained. Curve 2 for the TiO 2 /Ag nanocomposite in Fig. 1a shows that it is rather difficult to discern silver reflections on the background of anatase reflections due to the low concentration of the metal and its high dispersion on the TiO 2 surface. Curves 3 and 4 contain weak reflections for gold and copper. The X-ray diffraction pattern of unmodified porous TiO 2 (curve 1) lacks these metal reflections. Additional evidence for the formation of metal nanoparticles is found in the electron microscopy results of the study of TiO 2 /Au and TiO 2 /Ag metal-semiconductor nanocomposites. The microphotographs clearly show the presence of the anatase modification of titanium dioxide as well as nanoparticles of gold (Fig. 1c) and silver (Fig. 1d) on the surface indicated by characteristic interplane distances. The diameters of the metal nanoparticles are in the range 10-15 nm.

Irradiation of aqueous suspensions of the TiO 2 /M composite photocatalysts saturated with CO 2 using ultraviolet light also leads to the appearance of gaseous methane in the system. The data in Table 1 show that the rate of methane formation in a b c d the aqueous suspensions increases in going from pure TiO 2 particles to the metal-semiconductor nanocomposites as well as in the series TiO 2 /Ag < TiO 2 /Au < TiO 2 /Cu.

The need for preliminary accumulation of hydrogen in the system in the photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 to methane may be related to the greater activity of the TiO 2 /Au and TiO 2 /Cu photocatalysts in comparison with TiO 2 /Ag since silver as a modifying additive of titanium dioxide displays less activity in the photocatalytic formation of hydrogen than copper and, especially, gold [12]. However, along with the action of copper particles as an efficient catalyst for the dark steps of the photogeneration of hydrogen involving TiO 2 [4], copper also acts as a catalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to methane in aqueous electrolytes at room temperature [13]. The combination of these factors may presumably account for the enhanced activity of the TiO 2 /Cu nanocomposite in the photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 (see Table 1).

mentions.text: In this work, we also studied the photocatalytic activity of the bimetallic nanoheterostructures in the reduction of CO 2 depending on the sequence of deposition of the metals onto the mesoporous TiO 2 surface. In preparing the composites, we maintained the silver/copper mole ratio equal to 1 : 1.44, at which the volumes of the deposited metals are equal, in order increase the probability of coating of the metal core formed on the semiconductor by the other metal. The TiO 2 /Ag@Cu composite was obtained according to the procedure described above by the photoreduction of the metal ions on the TiO 2 surface in the presence of Na 2 SO 3 with subsequent photoinduced reduction of the ions of each metal, initially depositing silver and, then, copper. The TiO 2 /Cu@Ag composite was obtained by the photoinduced reduction of the excess amount of Cu 2+ ions with subsequent galvanic substitution of copper by silver. The activity of the resultant nanostructures in the photoreduction of CO 2 was compared with the activity of the TiO 2 /Ag/Cu ternary bimetallic nanoheterostructures obtained upon the combined deposition of the metal cations. Table 1 shows that the activity of the nanoheterostructures depends on the sequence of deposition of the metals and increases in the series TiO 2 /Cu@Ag < TiO 2 /Ag/Cu < TiO 2 /Ag@Cu. Enhancement of the activity of the systems with the optimal 1 : 6 Ag/Cu mole ratio was also observed in going from nanoheterostructures TiO 2 /Ag/Cu to structures TiO 2 /Ag@Cu (Fig. 2d).

The peak at 1000 second in GC chromatogram is assigned to CO in this case. There was a clear peak in the profile of m/z = 29 at the same retention time with GC chromatogram, and no peak was observed in the profile of m/z = 28. Therefore, only 13 CO (m/z = 29) was evolved in the photocatalytic conversion of 13 CO 2 over Ni-Al LDH(Cl -). This result clearly indicated that the carbon sources of CO evolved were introduced CO 2 ; therefore, carbon species such as carbonate ions kept in the interlayer of LDH and contaminated organics did not decompose into CO. Fig. 5 shows the temperature programmed desorption profile of Ni-Al LDH(Cl -) which was used for the isotope experiment using 13 CO 2 as substrate. 12 CO 2 (m/z = 44) and 13 CO 2 (m/z = 45) were desorbed from the used photocatalyst at around 573 K, indicating that adsorbed 13 CO 2 species such as carbonate or hydrocarbonate species existed on LDH. This result showed that parts of the introduced CO 2 molecules were adsorbed on Ni-Al LDH(Cl -) during the photocatalytic conversion of CO 2 in an aqueous solution. Accordingly, we concluded that the adsorbed CO 2 species on the surface of LDH, which are derived from the introduced gaseous CO 2 in the gas phase, are reduced into CO under UV light photoirradiation. The elemental analysis revealed that 1.2 wt% of chlorine atoms and 0.6 wt% of nitrogen atoms derived from precursors of hydroxide sheets existed on Ni-Al LDH(Cl -) and Ni-Al LDH(NO 3 -), respectively. We have reported that Mg-In LDH(NO 3 -) exhibited the activity for the photocatalytic conversion of CO 2 in H 2 O, 3.2 mol of CO as reduction product of CO 2 and 17.0 mol of O 2 were evolved after 10 h of photoirradiation [18]. 2. Generally, carbonate ions as charge compensating anions are preserved in the interlayer of LDHs. Our fabricating LDHs in this study also keep large amount of carbonate ions with small amount of residual chloride ions derived from the precursor of hydroxide sheets. Fig. 7 shows the effect of anion addition to the reaction solution on the photocatalytic conversion of CO 2 in an aqueous solution over Ni-Al LDH(Cl -) (Ni/Al = 4). Amount of H 2 evolved as the reduction product of H + derived from H 2 O was increased by the addition of NaHCO 3 and Na 2 CO 3 , although the formation of CO was drastically suppressed. Sayama and Arakawa reported that the addition of carbonate ions or hydrocarbonate ions to an aqueous solution enhance the evolution of H 2 for water splitting [21]. In our case, on the other hand, amount of CO evolved was increased in the presence of NaCl and KCl in an aqueous solution as compared to that in a pure water. The formation of O 2 was not observed in all cases. This results indicated that chloride ions in the reaction solution promoted the photocatalytic conversion of CO 2 to CO over Ni-Al LDH(Cl -). We expect that chloride ion in an aqueous solution act as a hole scavenger in the photocatalytic reaction. Chloride ions should be oxidized by holes generated with the photoexicitation of electrons through two processes. One is that chloride ion is oxidized into chlorine (Eq. ( 1)), and chlorine (Cl 2 ) is disproportionately decomposed into chloride ion (Cl -) and hypochlorite ion (ClO -) (Eq. ( 2)).

mentions.text: We prepared TiO 2 (Degussa P25)-loaded Pt and Cu binary co-catalysts by a stepwise photodeposition technique. Pt nanoparticles were first introduced onto TiO 2 by photoreducing H 2 PtCl 6 in an aqueous suspension, providing Pt/TiO 2 with a Pt content of about 0.9 wt % and a mean size of Pt nanoparticles of 3.1 nm (see Figure S1 in the Supporting Information). Then, copper was deposited onto Pt/TiO 2 under irradiation using CuSO 4 as a precursor, and the samples obtained were denoted as Cu/Pt/TiO 2 -xh, where xh was the irradiation time for the photodeposition of Cu. We found that the variation of the irradiation time changed the content of Cu (Table S1). Figure 1 shows the high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) images for the Cu/Pt/ TiO 2 -xh series of samples. For the Cu/Pt/TiO 2 -1h and the Cu/ Pt/TiO 2 -2h samples with lower Cu contents (0.59 and 1.1 wt %), although the Cu species were deposited on the Pt nanoparticle, the covering of the Pt nanoparticle was incomplete. As the irradiation time reached 5 h (Cu content = 1.7 wt %), the Pt nanoparticle was covered by a shell of Cu layers, forming a complete core-shell structure. The HRTEM image displayed lattice fringes with an interplanar spacing of 0.211 nm for the shell (Figure 1 c), which could be ascribed to the (200) facet of Cu 2 O. This suggests that the shell may be in the state of Cu 2 O. We have estimated the mean size of the core-shell structured particles in the Cu/Pt/TiO 2 -5h sample, and the value is 7.3 nm. It should be noted that the Cu species were preferentially deposited on Pt nanoparticles over these catalysts. We speculate that this is probably because the photogenerated electrons are efficiently extracted onto Pt from TiO 2 . For comparison, a sample with Pt and Cu contents . of 0.90 and 1.6 wt %, which were similar to those in the Cu/Pt/ TiO 2 -5h, was also prepared by a hydrazine-reduction method. TEM measurements suggested that this sample was composed of Pt and Cu 2 O nanoparticles (denoted as Pt-Cu/TiO 2 hereafter; Figure S2).

The photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 with H 2 O over our catalysts provided CO and CH 4 as two main products (Table 1). The formation of H 2 was also observed at the same time. We further confirmed the formation of O 2 over our catalysts (see the Supporting Information for experimental details). These suggest the occurrence of the following reductive reactions through photogenerated electrons and the formation of O 2 by photogenerated holes over our catalysts [Eqs. (1)-(4)]:

Table 1 shows that the loading of either Pt or Cu (existing as Cu 2 O) single co-catalysts onto TiO 2 can promote the formation of CH 4 . The formation of CO was also improved by Cu. The enhanced electron-hole separation through trapping electrons by the noble or coinage metal co-catalyst with a lower Fermi energy level is believed to be a main reason. The increased electron density on the co-catalyst may favor the formation of CH 4 , which requires eight electrons. Our present work further clarified that the formation of H 2 was also enhanced by loading Pt or Cu onto TiO 2 , and such an enhancement was much more significant in the case of Pt cocatalyst. Considering that the reduction of H 2 O to H 2 is a competitive reaction with the reduction of CO 2 to CO and CH 4 , [2c] we have evaluated the selectivity for CO 2 reduction on an electron basis (Supporting Information, experimental details). It becomes clear that the Pt co-catalyst decreases the selectivity, whereas the selectivity for CO 2 reduction increases from 60 to 80 % by loading Cu onto TiO 2 .

Although Cu (existing as Cu 2 O) is a more selective cocatalyst for the reduction of CO 2 , the rate of CH 4 formation over Cu/TiO 2 is lower than that over the Pt/TiO 2 . Our transient photocurrent response measurements showed that the photocurrent for Cu/TiO 2 was significantly lower than that for Pt/TiO 2 (Figure 3), clarifying the lower efficiency of the separation of photogenerated electron-hole pairs in the Cu/TiO 2 catalyst. The combination of Cu 2 O responsible for the selective activation of CO 2 and Pt capable of effectively extracting the photogenerated electrons is expected to increase the photocatalytic activity for CO 2 reduction. However, the use of the Pt-Cu/TiO 2 catalyst, which was composed of Pt and Cu 2 O nanoparticles, did not show synergistic effects for CO and CH 4 formation. The rate of CH 4 formation over this catalyst was even lower than that over the Pt/TiO 2 . The selectivity for CO 2 reduction was also low over this catalyst. On the other hand, the Cu/Pt/TiO 2 -5h catalyst containing core-shell-structured Pt@Cu 2 O nanoparticles demonstrated a significantly enhanced activity for the formation of CH 4 (Table 1). The rate of CH 4 formation over this catalyst was about 28 times higher than that over TiO 2 alone, and was 3.0 and 3.8 times higher than those over the Pt/TiO 2 and Cu/TiO 2 , respectively. The formation of CO over the Cu/Pt/TiO 2 -5h catalyst was also higher than that over Cu/TiO 2 or Pt/TiO 2 . We performed a blank reaction over the Cu/Pt/TiO 2 -5h catalyst. In the absence of CO 2 , the formation of CO and CH 4 was negligible, confirming that CO and CH 4 were formed from CO 2 . The rate of H 2 formation in the absence of CO 2 was 32 mmol g À1 h À1 , only slightly higher than that (25 mmol g À1 h À1 ) in the presence of CO 2 . The transient photocurrent response measurement showed that the Cu/Pt/TiO 2 -5h catalyst exhibited a photocurrent similar to Pt/TiO 2 (Figure 3), indicating that the Pt@Cu 2 O core-shell structure could keep the higher ability of Pt nanoparticles for trapping the photogenerated electrons from TiO 2 . All these observations allow us to exclude the possibility that CH 4 is formed via the hydrogenation of CO 2 or CO adsorbed or formed on the Cu site by the atomic H species generated on the Pt site. [2b, 8] Instead, our results clearly demonstrate that the covering of Pt by Cu 2 O with a core-shell structure suppressed the reduction of H 2 O to H 2 and preferentially accelerated the reduction of CO 2 to CO and CH 4 . The selectivity for CO 2 reduction reached 85 %.

The effects of different cocatalysts loading on Hex-KTO nanoakes towards the CO 2 reduction have then been investigated, including metallic Pt and Ag prepared by photodeposition (Table 1). It has been found that 0.5 wt% Pt loaded on Hex-KTO increases hydrogen yield by three fold compared to bare Hex-KTO and has a negligible effect on CO 2 photoreduction. The results are in agreement with numerous studies, which state that Pt is highly effective only for H 2 production. 35,50 In contrast, Ag loading on Hex-KTO dramatically increases the CO yield but decreases hydrogen production. As shown in Fig. 5, the CO yield is found to be 153 ppm g À1 h À1 when 0.01 wt% Ag was loaded, resulting in a 240% increase compared with the best result without a cocatalyst. Meanwhile, the H 2 yield decreases by 15% to 1135 ppm g À1 h À1 . Addition of 0.05% Ag loading further decreases the H 2 yield by 70% and the CO 2 yield is 1.8 fold higher than that in the absence of the Ag cocatalyst. Further loading of Ag beyond 0.05 wt% decreases both CO and H 2 yields, which might be due to excess silver metal coating which reects photons and reduces light absorption and large silver clusters with less reaction sites. The hydrogen yield decreased with increasing Ag loading.

mentions.text: To obtain more information on the catalysts, HR-TEM was used to observe these nanoparticles. Typical TEM micrographs of the TiO 2 and Ag/TiO 2 nanoparticle catalysts are shown in Fig. 1. From Fig. 1b, the relatively dark points are ascribed to Ag nanoparticles. The silver nanoparticle morphology is irregular spherical particles that have a narrow size distribution, while the transparent regions are assigned to TiO 2 in Fig. 1b. Meanwhile, it was evident that the average particle size of the nanoparticles was 40-50 nm, which was in good agreement with the XRD results calculated from the Debye-Scherrer equation (Fig. S2 †). HR-TEM was used to investigate the interfacial structures between Ag and TiO 2 (Fig. 1c and d). In Fig. 1c and d, the lattice fringes of Ag and TiO 2 showed a surface-junction. The (111) lattice fringe of the Ag nanoparticles was 0.236 nm, and the (101) lattice fringe of anatase was 0.356 nm. These results are in agreement with the previous reports. [20][21][22] The photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 coupled with selective benzyl alcohol oxidation was carried out under ultraviolet light irradiation at 0.1 MPa CO 2 pressure. The main liquid products were determined using GC (FID detector) (Fig. S3 †). This result was also proved by 1 H NMR spectroscopy (Fig. 2). When the reaction was carried out in CO 2 , the CO 2 was reduced to methanol, and benzaldehyde was the main product of the photocatalytic selective benzyl alcohol oxidation, along with traces of benzoic acid and benzyl ether (Table 1). The highest conversion of benzyl alcohol is 10.3% and 10.7%, and the maximum yield of methanol is 21.8 and 20.5 μmol g -1 catalyzed by TiO 2 and ca. 1 wt% Ag/TiO 2 after reacting for 18 hours, respectively. However, when reacting in an Ar gas atmosphere, the highest conversion of benzyl alcohol is only 1.7% and 1.9%, and there is no methanol or other products to be observed when catalyzed by TiO 2 and ca. 3 wt% Ag/TiO 2 catalysts, respectively. The blind test without catalyst (please see Table 1, entry 19) shows that the conversion of benzyl alcohol is very low (0.75%) and that there is no methanol to be observed. These results verified that CO 2 is able to be reduced to methanol coupled with the selective oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde, and that methanol is only produced from CO 2 , catalyzed by both TiO 2 and Ag/TiO 2 .

To obtain more information on the catalysts, HR-TEM was used to observe these nanoparticles. Typical TEM micrographs of the TiO 2 and Ag/TiO 2 nanoparticle catalysts are shown in Fig. 1. From Fig. 1b, the relatively dark points are ascribed to Ag nanoparticles. The silver nanoparticle morphology is irregular spherical particles that have a narrow size distribution, while the transparent regions are assigned to TiO 2 in Fig. 1b. Meanwhile, it was evident that the average particle size of the nanoparticles was 40-50 nm, which was in good agreement with the XRD results calculated from the Debye-Scherrer equation (Fig. S2 †). HR-TEM was used to investigate the interfacial structures between Ag and TiO 2 (Fig. 1c and d). In Fig. 1c and d, the lattice fringes of Ag and TiO 2 showed a surface-junction. The (111) lattice fringe of the Ag nanoparticles was 0.236 nm, and the (101) lattice fringe of anatase was 0.356 nm. These results are in agreement with the previous reports. [20][21][22] The photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 coupled with selective benzyl alcohol oxidation was carried out under ultraviolet light irradiation at 0.1 MPa CO 2 pressure. The main liquid products were determined using GC (FID detector) (Fig. S3 †). This result was also proved by 1 H NMR spectroscopy (Fig. 2). When the reaction was carried out in CO 2 , the CO 2 was reduced to methanol, and benzaldehyde was the main product of the photocatalytic selective benzyl alcohol oxidation, along with traces of benzoic acid and benzyl ether (Table 1). These results verified that CO 2 is able to be reduced to methanol coupled with the selective oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde, and that methanol is only produced from CO 2 , catalyzed by both TiO 2 and Ag/TiO 2 .

The effects of the silver loading content on TiO 2 on the catalytic activity were evaluated as well. Compared to pure TiO 2 , the photocatalytic activity of the ca. 2-6 wt% Ag/TiO 2 nanocomposites exhibited a significant increase (Table 1). Meanwhile, the conversion of benzyl alcohol and the yield of the methanol are both drastically increased when catalyzed by ca. 2-6 wt% Ag/TiO 2 . It was found that ca. 3 wt% Ag/TiO 2 was optimum to achieve the highest conversion of benzyl alcohol (24.6%) and the maximum yield of methanol (40.9 μmol g -1 ) after reacting for 18 hours. When the silver loading content is less than 3 wt%, the photocatalytic efficiency of the catalyst is increased with silver loading content. This could be because the Ag nanoparticles deposited on the surface of TiO 2 can act as photo-induced carrier separation centers. 23 Moreover, a Schottky barrier was formed between the silver and TiO 2 contact region, which improved the charge However, when the silver loading exceeds 3 wt%, the photocatalytic activity rapidly decreases. The conversion of benzyl alcohol and the yield of methanol are decreased from 24.6% to 14.9% and from 40.9 to 14.9 μmol g -1 with the increasing of silver loading content from 3% to 9%, respectively. This is may be because excess silver nanoparticles cover the surface of the TiO 2 activity sites that can absorb UV photons. Therefore, the absorption photon capacity of the catalyst is reduced. The excess silver nanoparticles can also act as recombination centers of electrons and holes, which also results in a decrease of the photocatalytic activity of the Ag/TiO 2 nanocomposites. In fact, it has been reported that the probability for hole capture increases with the large number of negatively charged silver particles on the surface of TiO 2 at high silver loading, which also increases the photo-induced electron and hole recombinations. 25 These results are in good agreement with the photoluminescence (PL) spectra intensity of the photocatalysts shown in Fig. S4. † From Fig. S4, † the PL intensities are decreased with an increase of the Ag loading content when the Ag loading content is less than 3 wt%. When the PL signal intensity is weaker, the photocatalytic efficiency is higher. However, when the Ag loading content exceeds ca. 4 wt%, the PL intensities increase. It is indicated that excess silver deposited on the surface of TiO 2 can act as electron sinks to capture the photo-induced electron and hole pairs. Furthermore, the photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 to methanol coupled with the selective oxidation of various alcohols has been performed over 3 wt% Ag/TiO 2 under the same reaction conditions. The results are shown in Table 2. It is indicated that all of the catalyzing systems investigated were capable of converting CO 2 to methanol and converting the aromatic alcohols to corresponding aldehydes with different yield. The groups on the aromatic ring have an effect on the reaction performance. The electron donating groups on the aromatic ring favor methanol production and alcohol oxidation. For example, methoxybenzyl alcohol can convert to p-anisaldehyde with conversions of 50.3% and 91.7%, and the yield of CH 3 OH is 40.9 and 309.6 μmol g -1 after reacting for 18 and 48 hours, respectively. However, the electron withdrawing groups on the aromatic ring result in a low conversion. The conversion of p-nitrobenzaldehyde to nitrobenzyl alcohol is only 8.4% and 19.8% after reacting for 18 and 48 hours, respectively. The yield of CH 3 OH is low as well (13.6 and 79.5 μmol g -1 ) under the same reaction conditions.

In order to know the stoichiometry of this reaction, the ratio of the formation of methanol and aldehyde has been calculated (the last column in Table 2). The result shows that the ratio will be increased with prolongation of the reaction time. This can be explained by some intermediates that are formed (such as HCOOH, HCHO) in the initial phase. documents.title: Photocatalytic Reduction of CO2 in Aqueous Solution on Surface-Fluorinated Anatase TiO2 Nanosheets with Exposed {001} Facets

tables.caption: Yield of Products under Different ConditionsAmount of Product Yield a (μmol)Upward arrow (↑) represents a significant increased yield relative to that of the control experiment.

mentions.text: If eq 13 is valid, then it is possible to produce methane via the two-electron reduction of methanol. Excess methanol (30 μmol and 300 μmol) was added to the mixture to verify the reaction pathway. The results are shown in Table 3. As expected, an addition of excess methanol had a negligible effect on the yield of CO. In contrast, the yield of methane apparently increased. These results suggest that photoreduction of methanol to methane is a possible route under our experimental conditions. It should be noted that production of formaldehyde and H 2 increased concurrently as a consequence of addition of excess methanol. This is because methanol could act as a scavenger and react with adsorptive hydroxyl radicals (•OH ads ) to produce formaldehyde (eq 18), [78][79][80] leaving more photogenerated electrons to reduce water to form H 2 (eqs 19 and 20).

To further elucidate the mechanism of CO 2 reduction in aqueous solution, we examined the effect of formaldehyde by adding a suitable amount of formaldehyde. Table 3 shows that adding excess formaldehyde had considerable effect on the yield of methanol. At formaldehyde concentrations of 30 and 300 μmol, the methanol yields in aqueous solution were 4.46 and 5.28 μmol, respectively, after 20 h of reaction, ∼4.1-fold and ∼4.8-fold greater, respectively, than those observed in the control experiment. However, the methane concentration in the gas phase increased by no more than 1.1-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively. Thus, there may be a redox equilibrium between methanol and formaldehyde, because of their coexistence in the CO 2 reduction process. Formaldehyde could be reduced to methanol by e CB -, and methanol could be oxidized to formaldehyde by h VB + /•OH ads . The equilibrium acts like a buffer, limiting the rate of the formation of methane from methanol.

tables.caption: Effect of Pt loading on the physical properties of g-C 3 N 4 -Pt composite samples

mentions.text: All chemicals are of analytical-grade and used without further purification. Graphitic carbon nitrides were synthesized by calcining thiourea in a muffle furnace. In a typical synthesis, 10 g of thiourea powder was put into an alumina crucible with a cover, and then the precursor was heated to 550 1C for 2 h at a heating rate of 15 1C min À1 . 24,25 When cooled to room temperature, the yellow solid was collected and ground to fine powders. The g-C 3 N 4 -Pt composites were prepared by using a combined NaOH-assisted impregnation of g-C 3 N 4 with Pt precursors (H 2 PtCl 6 ) and the NaBH 4 -reduction process. 26 Briefly, 1.0 g of the g-C 3 N 4 was put in a 100 mL beaker, and then 20 mL deionized water was added. After ultrasonication for about 1 h, a certain amount of H 2 PtCl 6 aqueous solution was added into the mixture under magnetic stirring. After 1 h, 5 mL of the mixed solution of NaOH aqueous solution (0.5 M) and NaBH 4 aqueous solution (0.1 M) was quickly added into the solution under continuous vigorous stirring for 30 min. Then the samples were collected by centrifugation and washed with deionized water for three times. Finally, the samples were dried at 80 1C overnight. The weight percentage ratios of Pt against g-C 3 N 4 were 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 and 2.0 wt%, which were denoted as Pt0, Pt0.25, Pt0.5, Pt0.75, Pt1.0 and Pt2.0, respectively. The real content of Pt in the samples measured by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES) (an Optima 4300 DV spectrometer, Perkin Elmer) is listed in Table 1.

The specific surface areas and porous structures of Pt0 and Pt1.0 were investigated by nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms. Fig. 4 presents the nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms and the corresponding pore-size distribution curves (inset) of the Pt0 and Pt1.0 samples. According to Brunauer-Deming-Deming-Teller (BDDT) classification, 35,36 the isotherms of all the samples are of type IV, indicating the presence of mesopores (2-50 nm). 37,38 Further observation indicates that the isotherms of Pt0 shift up in contrast to Pt1.0 in all relative pressure ranges, suggesting Pt0 with higher surface areas and larger pore volume. The hysteresis loops of the Pt0 and Pt1.0 samples are of type H3, reflecting the existence of slit-like mesopores due to the aggregation of plate-like particles. This also agrees well with the observed morphology in the TEM images (Fig. 2). 39 The pore size distribution curves (inset) calculated from nitrogen desorption isotherms by the BJH method show that the range of pore diameter is 2-120 nm. Fig. 4 (inset) shows that the Pt1.0 sample has less mesopores and smaller pore volume, because some mesopores were sealed with Pt or other chemical reactants in the process of Pt deposition and NaBH 4 -reduction. 40 Table 1 lists the BET surface areas, pore volumes and the average pore diameter of all samples, indicating that the BET surface areas, pore volumes and the average pore diameter of the Pt0, Pt0.25, Pt0.5, Pt0.75, Pt1.0 and Pt2.0 samples almost remain unchanged due to the low Pt loading amount.

documents.title: Photocatalytic reduction of CO2 on MgO/TiO2 nanotube films

tables.caption: The atomic percent of Ti, O and Mg of different MgO/TNTs films.

mentions.text: The phase structure of the nanotube films was analyzed by the XRD technique. As shown in Fig. 1a, the TiO 2 nanotubes film belongs to a characteristic anatase phase, indicating that the orthorhombic titanic acid nanotubes have transformed to TiO 2 nanotubes completely, which is consistent with our previous work [27]. There still exist some characteristic peaks of metallic Ti at 38.5 • , 40.2 • , 63.1 • , 70.7 • , indicating that only the surface of the metallic Ti foil reacted with NaOH, and the interior still remained as Ti metal. After calcination of TAN immersed in a series of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 aqueous solution and calcined at 500 • C for 4 h, Mg(NO 3 ) 2 and TAN transformed to amorphous MgO and anatase TiO 2 respectively. Although all samples did not appear new peaks, it is obvious that the width of the (1 0 1) plane diffraction peak of anatase (2Â = 25.5 • ) became narrower firstly, and then gradually broader with the increase of concentration of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 . These facts suggested that the crystalline size of the TiO 2 nanotubes increased when being covered with the little content of MgO. Namely, the MgO/TNTs nanotubular structure was more perfect than pure TiO 2 owing to the presence of the covered MgO thin layer. When the concentration of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 is relatively high, broader phenomenon could be ascribed to the high content of MgO formed a large number of particles on the surface of the TiO 2 nanotubes. The characteristic peak of 39.8 • , and 46.2 • in Fig. 1b is ascribed to the (1 1 1) and (2 0 0) plane of the metallic Pt, respectively [28]. That confirms the successful formation of metallic Pt nanoparticles on the surface of MgO/TNTs film, which are consistent with the results from TEM analysis (see Fig. 2e). The morphologies and structure of the series of MgO/TNTs films were shown in Figs. 2 and 3. As can be seen from Fig. 2a, the surface of the titanic acid nanotube (TAN) film showed a porous network structure. After calcination, the nanotubular morphology of TiO 2 was destroyed, and the surface was consisted by many thin nanosheets (shown in Fig. 2b). However, the sample obtained after calcination of TAN immersed in the Mg(NO 3 ) 2 solution have the similar nanotubular structure with the pure TAN (Fig. 2c). And the thickness of the MgO/TNTs was measured to be about 2.1-2.2 m (Fig. 2d). To further observe the morphology of TiO 2 film, some powders were peeled off from the TNTs film, and their TEM images are presented in Fig. 3. Our previous work reported that TAN transformed to anatase TiO 2 nanoparticles completely after calcination at the temperature higher than 400 • C [27]. Observation on the TEM images of MgO modified TiO 2 , we found that the nanotubular structure was kept very well. This indicated that MgO played an essential role to keep the nanotubular structure in the dehydration of TAN. Fig. 3a showed that TiO 2 displayed the uniform nanotube morphology, but a little part of nanotubes destroyed. The actual atomic percentage of Ti, Mg, O elements estimated by EDS analysis was shown in Table 1. The content of MgO increased with the increase of the concentration of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 . As the increase of the amount of MgO, the TiO 2 nanotubular structure was kept better gradually (Fig. 3b). And when the concentration of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 exceeded 0.1 M, MgO nanoparticles began to agglomerate on the surface of the TiO 2 nanotubules (Fig. 3c). Of particular interest is to note that the 0.01-MgO/TNTs sample kept better nanotubular morphology and some MgO existed as thin layer form on the nanotubes as seen in Fig. 3b. The high resolution TEM (HRTEM) images in Fig. 3d clearly show that MgO existed as amorphous thin layers apparently located on the surfaces of TiO 2 nanotubes. The finger spacing of 0.344 nm was indexed to the (1 0 1) lattice plane of anatase TiO 2 [29], which is in agreement with the results obtained from XRD. Moreover, we also found that the layer spacing of the nanotubes decreased to 0.550 nm, this may be due to the shrink of TAN in the processing of high-temperature calcination [30]. As we all known, MgO thin layer plays a critical role in CO 2 methanation, Mg can strongly bind a CO 2 molecule and form a carbonate on the less-stable MgO surfaces and the carbonate that formed on the MgO surface is an important reaction intermediate [31]. Moreover, the coverage of TiO 2 surfaces with MgO might hinder the direct contact of CO or CH 4 with TiO 2 surfaces, reducing the re-oxidization possibilities for CO and CH 4 .

documents.title: Photocatalytic reduction of CO2 over a hybrid photocatalyst composed of WO3 and graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) under visible light

tables.caption: Abbreviations and S BET of hybrid photocatalyst prepared by three kinds of process and their original compound.

mentions.text: Preparation of hybrid photocatalysts g-C 3 N 4 and WO 3 were hybridized in appropriate ratios between 100:0 and 0:100 (wt:wt) by a planetary mill method. The samples which were prepared in g-C 3 N 4 and WO 3 at the ratio of 1:2, 1:1 and 2:1 with a planetary mill, were referred to GW12, GW11 and GW21, respectively. Hybrid photocatalysts of WO 3 and g-C 3 N 4 at the ratio of 1:1 were also prepared by an agate mortar method and sonication method. For the agate mortar method, two kinds of powders were ground by an agate mortar for ca. 20 min. For the sonication method, two kinds of powders were suspended in 20 mL of ion-exchanged water by sonication for 30 min and subsequently stirred for 3 h. Then the sample was separated by filtration, washed with ion-exchanged water several times, and dried in a vacuum drying oven at 60 8C overnight. For the planetary mill method, 1.5 g of each kind of powders and 20 mL of ionexchanged water were added to a 50 mL agate bowl containing 50 g of yttrium-stabilized zirconia grinding beads (Nikkato Co., Ltd., F = 0.6 mm). Then the bowl was placed on a planetary mill (Fritsch Japan Co., Ltd., Planetary Micro Mill pulverisette 7) and the planetary mill was operated at 750 rpm for 10 min. After removing the beads by screening, the sample was separated by filtration, washed with ion-exchanged water several times, and dried in a vacuum drying oven at 60 8C overnight. Denotation of samples names and the hybrid methods are summarized in Table 1.

Fig. 3 shows SEM micrographs of the morphologies of hybrid photocatalysts as well as original g-C 3 N 4 and WO 3 . WO 3 showed aggregated particles with particle size of several hundreds of nanometers (Fig. 3a), while g-C 3 N 4 was plate-like particles with particle size of more than several mm (Fig. 3b). By treatment with a planetary mill, g-C 3 N 4 plate particles were pulverized into particles of smaller sizes (not shown here). In addition, S BET of g-C 3 N 4 was increased after planetary mill treatment (Table 1). This property change agrees with the results of a previous study showing that S BET of g-C 3 N 4 was increased by ball mill treatment due to decrease in particle size [47]. On the other hand, the morphology and S BET of WO 3 did not change after planetary mill treatment. In the sample prepared by an agate mortar and sonication method (a-CW and s-CW), two obviously different morphologies of particles were easily recognized, and they are assigned to g-C 3 N 4 , respectively, because the morphology of WO 3 is quite different from that of g-C 3 N 4 . Agglomerated WO 3 particles were loaded on plate-like g-C 3 N 4 (Fig. 3c and d). In contrast, the mixture condition between WO 3 and g-C 3 N 4 was greatly improved by planetary mill treatment (p-CW) and it seemed that g-C 3 N 4 particles were covered by highly dispersed WO 3 (Fig. 3e). This indicates that pulverized g-C 3 N 4 and WO 3 were highly mixed during planetary mill treatment. These results agree with previously reported results about a similar hybrid photocatalytic system for degradation of pollutants [48].

mentions.text: The XRD pattern (Fig. 2) for g-C 3 N 4 showed its graphite stacking structures. The two diffraction peaks at 2u = 13.18 and 27.48 match well with the (1 0 0) and (0 0 2) crystal planes of layered g-C 3 N 4 [18]. The strong diffraction peak at 2u = 27.48 is a characteristic indicator of layered stacking with a distance of 0.326 nm, and the in-planar repeating tri-s-triazine unit with a period of 0.675 nm can be clearly observed from the diffraction peak at 2u = 13.18, which is consistent with the reported results for g-C 3 N 4 [45]. The average crystal size was calculated by using Scherrer's formula to be 8.8 nm, according to the (0 0 2) peaks in the XRD patterns. The d value for (0 0 2) plane of g-C 3 N 4 and hybrid samples were summarized in Table 2. The difference of d value between original g-C 3 N 4 and g-C 3 N 4 in hybrid samples was hardly recognized. Therefore, we concluded that the structural change of g-C 3 N 4 in the hybrid photocatalysts was not occurred after the three kinds of mixture treatments. FT-IR spectra of g-C 3 N 4 and hybrid photocatalysts were shown in Fig. S2. We observed the typical peaks assigned to g-C 3 N 4 for all samples. The detailed assignments of the peaks were as follows. The characteristic-breathing mode of the triazine units was observed at 820 cm À1 [46]. The peaks attributed to the stretching vibration modes of heptazine-derived repeating units were observed at 1600, 1500, and 1440 cm À1 . The peaks at 1350 and 1280 cm À1 were assigned to stretching vibration of connected trigonal units or secondary amine. These results indicated that the characteristic structure of g-C 3 N 4 was stable even after the mixture process.

mentions.text: XRF analysis of the metallised samples was carried out. The results in terms of Pt and TiO 2 contents are presented in Table 1. In all the cases, the Pt content agrees well with the nominal amount, being close to 0.5 wt%. On the other hand, the estimated amount of TiO 2 in Pt-BiWO-Ti50i also agrees with the expected content.

S BET values are also displayed in Table 1. The coupled Bi 2 WO 6 -TiO 2 sample exhibits a surface area between those of single Bi 2 WO 6 and TiO 2 -P25. According to the calculated values, the photodeposition of Pt does not change the S BET in the platinised materials. Additionally, no change in the pore size distribution was found after platinisation.

The crystallite sizes were calculated from the XRD spectra with the Scherrer equation. The estimated values are collected in Table 1, where very similar sizes can be found for the different samples with almost negligible influence because of the presence of TiO 2 .

By the UV-vis spectra (see Fig. S1 in ESI †), it is possible to see the influence of platinum on the absorption properties, with the appearance of a secondary band in the visible range (λ > 450 nm). This effect has been ascribed to the low energy transitions between the semiconductor and the localised states of the metal clusters. 34 The major influence is found in the Pt-BW sample, which also displays a higher absorption in the visible range, prior to and after platinisation. It might also be observed in Table 1, from the estimated band gap values, that there is a decrease in this value for the BW sample from ∼2.8 to 2.5 eV due to the Pt presence, as also observed by other authors 35 in the PtCl 4 /Bi 2 WO 6 systems. In the case of the BiWO-Ti50i sample, the addition of TiO 2 slightly increases the band gap in comparison with the single Bi 2 WO 6 ; though the platinisation does not induce significant changes.

mentions.text: XRD patterns of raw ZSM-5, TiO 2 , TiO 2 /ZSM-5, Cu-TiO 2 /ZSM-5, and Co-TiO 2 /ZSM-5 catalysts are shown in Fig. S1. For all of the samples, the characteristic peaks at 25.4°, 37.9°, 48.0°, and 54.4° indicate the d 101, d 004, d 200, and, d 211 planes of anatase. Anatase was reported as having a tetragonal structure and a high selectivity for the formation of CH 3 OH [12,13]. Copper and cobalt phases cannot be observed from the XRD pattern, which suggests that Cu and Co species were highly dispersed [14,15] or is due to the low Cu concentration and extremely small Cu clusters [16]. To measure the crystalline sizes of TiO 2 nanoparticles, the d 101 spacing of 25.4° (2θ) for anatase is used, with the results shown in Table 1. It indicates that the doping of Cu and Co species decreased the size of TiO 2 particles, as shown in Fig. 1.

mentions.text: To investigate the effects of Cu and Co deposition with porous ZSM-5 support, four types of catalysts were compared: TiO 2 , TiO 2 /ZSM-5, Cu-TiO 2 /ZSM-5, and Co-TiO 2 /ZSM-5. After 2 h irradiation of the solution, the GC peaks of methanol from CO 2 photoreduction are obtained, as shown in Fig. S4. All of the GC peaks appeared at exactly a 2.46 min retention time and no other GC peaks were detected, suggesting that the methanol is the only obtained product in our study. The yield of methanol increased with the increase in reaction time and the results are shown in Fig. 3. After a 12 h reaction, the concentrations of methanol (CH 3 OH) were 213.18, 318.40, 600.61, and 421.44 μmol L -1 in the solutions where TiO 2 , TiO 2 /ZSM-5, Cu-TiO 2 /ZSM-5, and Co-TiO 2 /ZSM-5 were used as the photocatalysts, respectively. The production rates of the four types of catalysts and the comparisons from selected articles are shown in Fig. 4. The TiO 2 in our study showed the lowest production rate among the four catalysts, with 17.7 μmol g -1 h -1 of methanol. However, it still exhibited high photocatalytic activity when compared to other studies, which may be due to the smaller particle sizes of TiO 2 in our study (4.26-9.90 nm) than commercial ones. With the ZSM-5 support, methanol production was enhanced to 26.53 μmol g -1 h -1 . The improvement may be due to the enhanced dispersion of TiO 2 and improved adsorption of CO 2 on the high surface area of the ZSM-5 substrate [20]. The result is higher than previous studies when other mesoporous materials were used to support TiO 2 . Lin et al. [3] prepared dye-sensitized TiO 2 /SBA-15, which exhibits methanol yield of 0.44 μmol g -1 h -1 . With the addition of Cu or Co species to TiO 2 / ZSM-5, the catalyst showed higher methanol production rates of 50.05 and 35.12 μmol g -1 h -1 , respectively. This was because Cu and Co species can inhibit charge recombination by trapping electrons [21]. However, when there was no ZSM-5 supporting, the photocatalytic activity of Cu-TiO 2 and Co-TiO 2 was much lower (as shown in Fig. S5), which indicatesthat the supporting of ZSM-5 and the doping of Cu or Co species were synergistic. The Cu-TiO 2 /ZSM-5 showed the best photoreduction activity, which may be due to the generation of Ti 3+ that can trap photoinduced electrons and inhibit charge recombination [10]. According to Fig. 3, it is obvious that the methanol formation in our study has exceeded most of the previous studies [2,5,6,14,[22][23][24][25][26]. Only the study of Wang et al. [23] showed a better production rate which may be due to the high light intensity (500 W). Photo energy efficiency (PEE) and quantum yield (φ) of the CO 2 photo-conversion can be calculated (as shown in the Supplementary material) while methanol is considered as the only conversion product in the solution as other products (e.g. methane and formic acid) are too few to be detected. The values of PEE CH3OH andφ CH3OH are shown in Table 2. When Cu-TiO 2 /ZSM-5 was used as the catalyst, the max values of PEE CH3OH and φ CH3OH reached 2.60% and 10.11%, respectively. The values of PEE and φ in our study are higher than the results reported by previous studies [2,4,6,27] which may be due to the high absorption ability of ZSM-5 in our study. In the study of Wang et al. [6], Cu 2 O/TiO 2 composite nanotube was used as the photocatalyst, and a 500 W collimated xenonmercury (Xe Hg) broadband lamp was used as the light source in the study, the maximum photonic efficiency of CO 2 photoreduction can reach 1.731%. Lee et al. [27] used light-harvesting complex assisted Rh-doped TiO 2 photocatalyst to reduce CO 2 when a 300 W xenon lamp (300-1000 nm) was used as the light source, and the total quantum yield was lower than 1.41% for CO 2 photoreduction.

The specific surface areas of Ti-MCM-41materials were approximately around 840-850 m 2 g -1 when Si/Ti molar ratios of Ti-MCM-41 were between 200 and 50. The comparison results are shown in Figure 7. The methane production rate with NaOH solution, 1.96 μmol/g of cat., appears to be the lowest among the three solutions. This may be because when NaOH is reacted with high concentration of CO 2 , it might result in the formation of sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO 3 ) particles and be precipitated in the solution. Figure 6 shows the UV-vis absorption spectra obtained by diffuse reflection of MCM-41 and Ti-MCM-41. mentions.text: The modifying effect of other metal oxides on the photocatalytic activity of the 0.5 wt% Pt-TiO 2 catalyst was further investigated. We found that the modification of the Pt-TiO 2 using basic oxides such as SrO, CaO, BaO, La 2 O 3 and Lu 2 O 3 could also increase the amount of CH 4 (Table S1, ESI †). Over these modified catalysts, the formation of CO was inhibited. The mean sizes of Pt nanoparticles over these modified catalysts were 3.8-4.1 nm, close to that (4.2 nm) over the Pt-TiO 2 catalyst without modification. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface areas of the modified catalysts measured using N 2 physisorption were 43-51 m 2 g À1 , slightly lower than that (55 m 2 g À1 ) of the Pt-TiO 2 catalyst. Thus, the increase in the photocatalytic activity as a result of modification with basic oxides should not be due to the changes in the size of Pt nanoparticles or the surface area of photocatalysts. We evaluated the catalyst basicity by measuring the amount of CO 2 chemisorption. 17 We found a linear correlation between the amount of CH 4 formed and the amount of chemisorbed CO 2 over a series of basic oxide-modified Pt-TiO 2 photocatalysts (Fig. 2). This allows us to propose that the catalyst basicity contributes to the photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 with H 2 O to CH 4 .

The Pt-MgO/TiO 2 catalyst exhibited the best photocatalytic performance in CH 4 formation among the modified Pt-TiO 2 catalysts examined in our work. We further investigated the effect of the content of MgO on the photocatalytic performance. Table 1 shows that the amount of chemisorbed CO 2 increases monotonically with the content of MgO. However, there is an optimum content of MgO for CH 4 formation; the amount of CH 4 increases with increasing content of MgO up to 1.0 wt%, and then decreases with a further increase in the content of MgO. The BET surface area and the size of Pt nanoparticles did not undergo significant changes with an increase in the content of MgO from 0.25 wt% to 3.0 wt%. Thus, there may exist other factors controlling the photocatalytic performance in the Pt-MgO/TiO 2 trinary nanocomposite.

We performed transmission electron microscopy (TEM) studies of the Pt-MgO/TiO 2 catalysts with MgO contents of 1.0 wt% and 3.0 wt%. As displayed in Fig. 3, MgO existed as amorphous thin layers located on the surfaces of TiO 2 crystallites in both catalysts. Over the 0.5 wt% Pt-1.0 wt% MgO/TiO 2 photocatalyst, the interface between TiO 2 , Pt and MgO could be clearly observed in the enlarged image (Fig. 3b). Moreover, because the MgO layer is thin, Pt nanoparticles could be easily d The physical mixture with the same composition as the 0.5 wt% Pt-1.0 wt% MgO/TiO 2 photocatalyst. accessed by the reactants such as H 2 O (or protons) during the reaction. On the other hand, relatively thicker MgO layers were observed over the 0.5 wt% Pt-3 wt% MgO/TiO 2 photocatalyst. The thicker MgO layer could cover Pt nanoparticles (Fig. 3d). This may lead to the decrease in the photocatalytic activity. Thus, the proper location of the three components in the photocatalyst should also determine the photocatalytic performance. This has further been confirmed by the experimental fact that the physical mixture of Pt-TiO 2 and MgO/TiO 2 with the same composition as in the 0.5 wt% Pt-1.0 wt% MgO/TiO 2 photocatalyst exhibited much inferior performances (Table 1). Based on the results described above, we propose functioning mechanisms of MgO and Pt co-catalysts for accelerating the formation of CH 4 in Fig. 4. CO 2 is first chemisorbed on the MgO layer on TiO 2 crystallites. The chemisorbed CO 2 molecule becomes destabilized and its reactivity is believed to be higher than that of the linear CO 2 molecule. 14,17 On the other hand, photogenerated electrons on TiO 2 can be easily trapped by the Pt nanoparticles because of the lower Fermi energy level of the noble metal. It is known that the formations of CO and CH 4 require two and eight electrons, respectively. The enriched electron density on Pt nanoparticles would favour the formation of CH 4 , which is thermodynamically more feasible than the formation of CO. 10b Our result has demonstrated that Pt enhances the photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 to CH 4 but not to CO (Fig. 1). The synergistic effect between MgO, which enhances the density of destabilized CO 2 molecules on the catalyst surface, and Pt nanoparticles with enriched electron density can further accelerate the reduction of CO 2 to CH 4 . Clearly, such a synergistic effect requires the intimate contact of Pt between both TiO 2 and MgO, strengthening the key role of the interface.

documents.title: Photocatalytic reduction of CO2 with H2O to CH4 on Cu(i) supported TiO2 nanosheets with defective {001} facets

tables.caption: Effects of Cu on the physical properties and photocatalytic activity of the samples

mentions.text: Consistent with the XRD result, no nanoparticles corresponding to the Cu species are observed from the TEM or HRTEM images of the Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 sample (Fig. 1c, d and 2a). However, the EDX analysis shows two strong fluorescence signals (Fig. 2b), indicating the presence of Cu. In order to clarify the distribution of the Cu species on the TiO 2 surface, X-ray elemental mapping analysis was conducted, as shown in Fig. 2c-e. The result demonstrates strongly that the Cu species are highly dispersed on the surface of TiO 2 . The Cu contents of the samples were also measured by an ICP-OES method. As shown in Table 1, we can see that the experimental values are close to the predicted values. According to the photodeposition mechanism, the copper cluster produced by the method does not lead to a change of TiO 2 structure. Based on the above mentioned results, we suggest that Cu is not doped into the TiO 2 lattice as ions but that it may be highly dispersed as oxide clusters on the surface of the TiO 2 nanosheets.

The nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms and the corresponding pore-size distribution curves of the bare TiO 2 and the Cu-TiO 2 -x samples are shown in Fig. S4 (ESI †). All the isotherms are of type IV and have similar loop rings (Fig. S4a, ESI †), which indicates the presence of mesopores in the samples. 44 Fig. S4b (ESI †) shows that all the samples exhibit bimodal pore size distributions. The variations of pore size distribution curves may be due to the blocking of some pores of TiO 2 by the deposition of the Cu species. The BET surface areas for the Cu-TiO 2 -x samples are similar to that of the parent TiO 2 , as shown in Table 1.

Since the conduction band potential of TiO 2 is more negative than the reduction potential of CO 2 /CH 4 (À0.24 eV vs. NHE, pH 7.0), 55 it is energetically favorable for electrons from the conduction band of TiO 2 to transfer to CO 2 to initiate the reduction of CO 2 with H 2 O, producing CH 4 . Fig. 6 shows the accumulative yields of CH 4 during the photoreduction of CO 2 in the presence of H 2 O vapor over the parent TiO 2 nanosheet and the Cu-TiO 2 -x samples under simulated solar light irradiation for 4 h. Only methane is detected as a product in the gas mixture of CO 2 with H 2 O vapor with the TiO 2 or the Cu-TiO 2 -x nanocomposites as photocatalysts, which is in line with the previous published work that CH 4 is the main product of CO 2 photoreduction with water vapor. The Cu 2 O content has a significant influence on the photocatalytic activity of the TiO 2 nanosheets. In the absence of Cu 2 O, the bare TiO 2 shows the lowest photocatalytic activity for CO 2 reduction and CH 4 production. When the TiO 2 nanosheets have been modified by Cu 2 O through a photodeposition method, the photogenerated electrons and holes are transferred quickly from the bulk TiO 2 to the interface for the photoreduction of CO 2 due to the formation of an internal electric field. Thereafter, all Cu-TiO 2 -x samples exhibit a superior photocatalytic activity for reduction of CO 2 compared with the parent TiO 2 . Furthermore, Cu 2 O clusters grafted onto the surface of TiO 2 could increase the surface alkalinity of the samples efficiently, and thus, the products will adsorb more CO 2 molecules to promote the mass transfer process in the photocatalytic reaction. This may be another reason for the superior activities of the Cu-TiO 2 -x nanocomposites. To rule out the effect of surface area on the photocatalytic activities, we normalized the photocatalytic reduction rates with respect to the surface areas (Table 1). It can be seen that the order of the normalized rates is the same as the original order. Therefore, the increased activity may be contributed by the physicochemical properties of the samples, such as the enhancement of alkalinity, the enhanced adsorption of CO 2 on Cu + , the higher mass transfer efficiency of CO 2 , and the high separation rate of the photogenerated charge carriers. Among the Cu modified samples, the CH 4 evolution rate follows the order: Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 4 Cu-TiO 2 -1.5 4 Cu-TiO 2 -0.75 4 Cu-TiO 2 -0.5 4 Cu-TiO 2 -2.0 4 TiO 2 . With an increasing Cu 2 O cluster amount from 0 to 1.0 wt% in the composite, the yields of CH 4 are increased gradually because of the enhancement of photocurrent and adsorption capacities for CO 2 molecules. The Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 sample shows the highest activity, reaching 8.68 mmol h À1 g À1 , which is over 30 times higher than that of the parent TiO 2 . However, when the Cu content is higher than 1.0 wt%, the photocatalytic activity is decreased. This may be due to the integrative effects of the Cu 2 O cluster aggregation, the covering of active sites by the excess nanoparticles, and the recombination of charge carriers, even if Cu-TiO 2 -1.5 and Cu-TiO 2 -2.0 have higher CO 2 adsorption capacities.

Furthermore, a set of control experiments was carried out to confirm the photocatalytic process in the photoreduction of CO 2 . As shown in Fig. 7, no appreciable products were detected in the absence of either photocatalyst or light irradiation. It can be clearly found that there is a dramatic decrease in catalytic activity when the reaction is carried out in an anhydrous CO 2 atmosphere, and an inactivation in an N 2 atmosphere. All of these findings illustrate that the reactions over Cu-TiO 2 -x samples are photocatalytic processes. To understand the role of V o , we prepared Cu 2 O-TiO 2 nanosheet hybrid composite samples with a very low concentration of V o through the postannealing of the Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 sample in an air atmosphere. The photocatalytic activity was greatly reduced. In comparison, the difference of the Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 sample with a high concentration of V o before and after the post-annealing process in an N 2 atmosphere was negligible. Additionally, due to the fact that most of the surface V o were produced by the in situ photodeposition process, when the reduction of CO 2 was performed over the Cu 2 O-TiO 2 nanosheet sample prepared by a physical mixture method, it is no surprise that the production rate of CH 4 just reached 0.57 mmol h À1 g À1 . However, if the TiO 2 nanosheet sample was reduced under a H 2 atmosphere to enhance the concentration of V o before mixing with Cu 2 O, it is found that the as-prepared Cu 2 O-TiO 2 nanosheet sample exhibited relatively high activity (2.78 mmol h À1 g À1 ). Moreover, using commercial TiO 2 nanoparticles without surface V o as the catalyst (Table 1), no CH 4 was produced although it can adsorb CO 2 molecules. These results strongly indicate that V o plays a significant role in the reduction of CO 2 .

It is considered that the mass transfer of CO 2 on the catalyst is a preceding step to its photoreduction and plays a key role in affecting the photocatalytic activity. To study the CO 2 adsorption ability of the catalysts, we tested the CO 2 adsorption isotherms of the TiO 2 and Cu-TiO 2 -x samples, as shown in Fig. 8 and Table 1. The comparison of CO 2 adsorption isotherms over the TiO 2 and Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 samples shows that the Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 sample has a much higher adsorption capability for CO 2 than does the TiO 2 sample. The maximum CO 2 uptake for Cu-TiO 2 -1.0 is 8.2 cm 3 g À1 at 1 atm, whereas TiO 2 shows poor adsorption of CO 2 molecules. As seen in Table 1, at 1 atm and 273 K, the CO 2 adsorption capacity of the Cu-TiO 2 -x composite samples increases with increasing Cu 2 O content. By normalizing with respect to surface area, we can see that the increased CO 2 adsorption capacity of the composite samples is not caused by the increase in the specific surface area, but by the content of Cu 2 O species. The Cu 2 O species could enhance the alkalinity of the sample to adsorb more acidic CO 2 molecules, and the formation of Cu 2 O by the photoreduction and in situ photodeposition process could create more V o over TiO 2 nanosheets. The enhanced alkalinity and formed V o could co-promote the adsorption of CO 2 . An increase of adsorption capability for CO 2 over Cu-TiO 2 -x can therefore facilitate the mass transfer process and play an important role in the higher CO 2 photoreduction activity.

mentions.text: UV-visible absorbance spectra and Tauc plots of Ca x Ti y O 3 are shown in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6, respectively. The absorption maximum of catalysts appears at 350 nm, which is redshifted with increasing of titanium component from 0.75 to 1. However, the absorption intensity at 320 nm decreases with increasing titanium component. The band gap was calculated using Tauc equation [31]. A plot of (˛h ) 1/2 versus photon energy (h ) and the intercept of tangent to the X-axis gives the band gap. The band gap of Ca 1.50 -Ti 0.75 , Ca 1.28 -Ti 0.85 , Ca 1.00 -Ti 1.00 , and Ca 0.75 -Ti 1.12 were found to be 3.51, 3.53, 3.44, and 3.45 eV, respectively (Table 2). The band gap of catalysts decreases when the titanium component increases.

The PL spectral measurements (Fig. 7) are used to understand the electron-hole recombination process. The PL spectra of catalysts exhibit a strong signal at 468 nm. The PL intensity of catalysts decreases when titanium component increases. It is attributed to the transition of trapped electron to Ti ions. Generally, new oxygen vacancies are created by metal-doping, the photogenerated electrons in the conduction band initially reached the vacant space and then recombined with the photogenerated holes in the valance band to produce fluorescence emission [32]. The smallest PL intensity is observed for C 1.00 -Ti 1.00 . It means that the electron-hole recombination rate is minimized when the calcium and titanium content are C 1.00 -Ti 1.00 . The decrease of PL intensity is attributed to the defects (regardless of the chemical stoichiometric or nonstoichiometric) generated in the structure. N 2 adsorption-desorption isotherms and BET surface area of Ca x Ti y O 3 are shown in Fig. 8 and Table 2, respectively. The isotherms are similar to type III curves, and hence, the prepared catalysts are nonporous materials [33]. The BET surface area of catalysts increases as titanium content increases except for Ca 1.28 -Ti 0.85 . It indicates the formation of TiO 2 or C 6 H 15 O 3 Ti as shown in Fig. 3. The perovskite structure is perfectly formed in Ca 1.28 -Ti 0.85 and it exists in a higher density state than other catalysts. tables.caption: The BET surface area, pore size, pore volume and surface atomic ratio of 0 #, 2 # and 5 # samples.

mentions.text: Compared with that of unmodified TiO 2 , the particle size of Lamodified samples decreases slightly with increasing the content of La, and BET measurement results (Table 1) support this suggestion. Compared with unmodified TiO 2 , the specific surface areas of the 5 # samples increased from 3.13 m 2 /g to 46.9 m 2 /g. Such effects of La loading on samples are in agreement with the literature [34], which is because that the rutile phase formation may start at the defect sites on surface of anatase, and La 2 O 3 will easily occupy the defect sites of the anatase particles to prevent the anatase transforming into rutile and the increasing of the grains. Moreover, the XRD did not show any lanthanum oxide phase. It may be due to the very small particle size of lanthanum oxide highly dispersed on the surface layer of TiO 2 .

To investigate the surface chemical states and atomic concentration of La-modified TiO 2 , the XPS spectra of La and Ti elements on the surface of La-modified TiO 2 nanoparticle samples (1-5 #) are shown in Fig. 5. It can be obtained from the XPS survey spectrum that 2 # and 5 # La-modified TiO 2 contain 4.1% and 8.4% La 3d, respectively (shown in Table 1). Regarding the La 3d core level spectra (Fig. 5a), it was observed that the splitting of the main peaks of La 3d 5/2 and La 3d 3/2 are at around 834.2 and 851.0 eV, respectively, and the shake-up satellite peaks of La 3d 5/2 and La 3d 3/2 are at 838.5 and 855.2 eV. In comparison with the bonding energy of pure La 2 O 3 (834.9 eV) [38], the slight shift of La 3d 5/2 (834.2 eV) to lower binding energy indicates the formation of La O Ti in the samples [27]. As shown in Fig. 5b, it can be seen that Ti 2p XPS spectra of La-modified TiO 2 is mainly composed of the main peaks of Ti 2p 1/2 at 464.0 eV and Ti 2p 3/2 at 458.2 eV, respectively, which shifts to a lower value in comparison with the reported result [39,40]. Therefore, it can be concluded that a tiny number of La atoms substitute the surface Ti atoms in the form of Ti O La. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements were further carried out on the as-prepared catalysts at room temperature. As shown in Fig. 6, all the La-modified TiO 2 samples gave rise to a strong EPR signal, while almost no signal was seen in the unmodified TiO 2 sample. The EPR spectra of La-modified TiO 2 samples show a paramagnetic signal centered around g = 1.98 (Fig. 6), it agrees very well with g values reported for Ti 3+ ions [41]. It can also be seen from the Fig. 6, 2 # sample gives the highest intensity of EPR signal of Ti 3+ , and further increasing the La loading from 2 # to 5 # did not lead to the enhancement of Ti 3+ , which may because only a certain amount of La can modify the surface of TiO 2 , and excessive La loading induces the accretion of La 2 O 3 on the TiO 2 surface. DFT calculation on the spin density charge and Bader charge analysis of the La-modified TiO 2 further supports the formation of Ti 3+ on the surface (Fig. S3). In combination this with the XRD patterns, XPS spectra, it can be concluded that La does not enter the bulk lattice of TiO 2 , but it modifies TiO 2 in the form of Ti O La.

mentions.text: The pore structure properties of all photocatalysts are summarized in Table 1. All as-synthesized TNTs showed similar values of high surface area (333-403 m 2 /g) and pore volume (ca. 1.2-1.3 cm 3 /g). Surface areas of as-synthesized Mo-doped TNTs were in the order of Mo/T-H > Mo/T-P > T-0 > Mo/T-I, and these values were 6-8 times higher than that of the TNTs precursor material (P25 TiO 2 ). The higher percentage of tube shape in Mo/T-H and Mo/T-P compared to T-0 could be the possible reason for their higher values of surface area than that of T-0. This also indicated that the doping of Mo during the formation of tubular structure (i.e., hydrothermal and acid washing) might help to form better tubular structure and provide higher surface area. On the other hand, when Mo was doped after the tube was already formed (i.e., in impregnation case of Mo/T-I after drying), the Mo species could only be appeared on the surface of TNTs. The porous structure of TNTs included the inner pores of the tube and the interlayer pores of the tube-wall [22,23,29]. Therefore, the Mo-species that accumulated in the TNTs during impregnation process could block these pores and result in the lower surface area of Mo/T-I as compared to pure T-0.

documents.title: Photocatalytically reducing CO2 to methyl formate in methanol over ZnS and Ni-doped ZnS photocatalysts

tables.caption: Characterization results for various ZnS and Ni-doped ZnS samples and the rate of methyl formate formation in the presence of CO 2 and N 2 .

mentions.text: XRD patterns of ZnS, Ni-doped ZnS and NiS loaded ZnS, synthesized by hydrothermal method using TAA as the sulfur source, were depicted in Fig. 1b. Obviously, the diffraction peaks for the three samples matched well with the cubic zinc blende structure of ZnS with lattice constants a = 5.406 Å and b = 5.406 Å (JCPDS No. 05-0566). The peaks were much sharper and smoother than that of ZnS-P or ZnS-I, which indicated samples synthesized by hydrothermal method had good crystalline structure. Fig. 1c displayed the enlarged (1 1 1) diffraction peak for the above three catalysts. Notably, the peak position of 0.3 wt% Ni-doped ZnS was slightly left-shifted compared to undoped ZnS, which might be ascribed to that Ni 2+ inserted into the structure of ZnS and located at interstices or occupied some of the lattice sites of ZnS because the effective ionic radius of Ni 2+ (0.69 Å) [25] was smaller than that of Zn 2+ (0.74 Å) [26]. Interestingly, the peak position of 0.3 wt% NiS loaded ZnS was similar to that of pure ZnS, suggesting that only Ni 2+ incorporated into the ZnS lattice could result in its lattice change. Other photocatalysts prepared by hydrothermal method had XRD patterns similar to that of Fig. 1b, and the average crystallite sizes were further estimated based on the broadening of the (1 1 1) diffraction peak using the Scherrer equation (see Table 1).

BET gas sorptometry measurements were conducted to examine the porous nature of samples. Fig. 2 showed nitrogen sorption hysteresis and the corresponding pore size distribution curve (inset) for the ZnS-I sample. The isotherms exhibited type IV, which was characteristic of mesoporous materials. The pore size distribution curve calculated from the desorption branch by the BJH method indicated a number of pores about 3.4 nm in the sample. The measured Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) area for as-prepared ZnS-I was 126.56 m 2 g À1 and the single-point total volume of pores at P/P 0 = 0.9618 was 0.55 cm 3 g À1 . These results manifested that ZnS-I had nanoporous and hollow nanostructures [23]. BET surface areas of the as-prepared catalysts were summarized in Table 1.

The direct bandgap values of the pristine and 0.3 wt% Ni-doped ZnS samples were estimated from the (ahm) 2 versus photon energy (hm) plot [12,14] as shown in the inset of Fig. 3. The bandgap values of other samples were estimated by the same method and the values were listed in Table 1.

Fig. 4a and b presented the morphology of pure ZnS and 0.3 wt% Ni-doped ZnS prepared by hydrothermal method recorded by SEM image. It could be seen that both catalysts consisted of nanosized crystallite particles, which was consistent with the calculated results by Scherrer equation. Furthermore, a large proportion of nanoparticles agglomerated into anomalistic particles without uniform size. The addition of Ni almost did not change the morphology of ZnS. The energy-dispersive X-ray (EDS) spectrum of 0.3 wt% Ni-doped ZnS was shown in Fig. 4c. The actual Ni content of Ni-doped ZnS from EDS analysis was listed in Table 1.

hydrothermal time led to more agglomeration and smaller specific surface area (see Table 1), contributing to the decrease of photocatalytic activity of ZnS-H36. It was worth noting that the photocatalytic activity of ZnS-I with high BET surface area was inferior to that of ZnS-H24 with low BET surface area, indicating that nanoporous or hollow nanostructure was not significant for photocatalytic activity in present study. These observations suggested that the photocatalytic activity of CO 2 reduction in methanol mainly depended on crystalline structure. Fig. 6 showed the photocatalytic activity of CO 2 reduction in methanol over ZnS with various Ni 2+ doping under irradiation, as well as NiS loaded ZnS for comparison. Remarkably, 0.3 wt% Nidoped ZnS demonstrated the highest activity of methyl formate formation and the corresponding methyl formate evolution rate reached 121.4 lmol g À1 h À1 . The activity was visibly enhanced compared with non-doped ZnS, but when the Ni 2+ doped content increased to 0.5 wt%, the activity became lower. The above results suggested that suitable incorporation of Ni 2+ could improve the photocatalytic activity of ZnS. This was ascribed to that doped Ni 2+ could act as a temporary trapping site of photoinduced electrons and greatly suppressed the recombination of electronÀhole pairs on the surface of the photocatalyst [21,30]. However, the relatively high doping concentrations of Ni 2+ might become the recombination center of photogenerated carriers, resulting in a decrease of photocatalytic efficiency [25,31]. For comparison, the photocatalytic activity over 0.3 wt% NiS loaded ZnS was also evaluated. Apparently, the photocatalytic activity of 0.3 wt% Ni-doped ZnS was almost four times that of 0.3 wt% NiS loaded ZnS, which indicated again that it was Ni 2+ entering the ZnS lattice that possessed the enhanced photocatalytic activity. The NiS on ZnS surface could shield the incident light and facilitate charge recombination because their unmatched energy levels, which resulted in the significant reduction of the photocatalytic activity. Ag 2 S, CuS and Bi 2 S 3 loaded ZnS were also prepared, respectively, and all of them had lower photocatalytic activity than ZnS.

The influence of the photocatalyst quantity on formic acid formation is reported in Table 1. It can be observed that 0.025 g represents the amount of catalyst producing the most significant increase of formic acid production if it is compared with bare TiO2 or higher loadings (0.075-0.300 g). Nevertheless a higher quantity, i.e., 0.050 g, was used in the further experiments to avoid difficulties to reproduce the measurements. mentions.text: The influence of pH of the aqueous solution on the process efficiency for the formation of formic acid was studied by using three different initial pH values (3, 7 and 13) without changing or checking them throughout the experiments. In Table 2, the results of CO2 photoreduction at different initial pH's have been reported. The conversion of CO2 into formic acid increased by decreasing the pH value. The highest conversion (CO2 to HCOOH) observed in this work was 0.65% and this value is reasonable when compared with others reported in the literature (0.2%-0.4%) [42]. It was calculated as ratio of the concentration of formic acid and the concentration of carbon dioxide in water by assuming the solution saturated by CO2 and by considering the relative constant of solubility equal to 1.45 g/L at 298 K. The hydration equilibrium at pH = 3 was negligible, being the constant of hydration equal to 1.70 × 10 -3 at 298 K. This finding can be explained by considering both the role of hole scavengers and the reaction mechanism.

Therefore, analogously to what observed for the photodegradation of 4-nitrophenol (4-NP) [37][38][39] it is essential to photoexcite both the components of the system, i.e., TiO2 and the sensitizer, in order to obtain substantial improvement of the photoreduction of CO2. mentions.text: Structural properties as the crystallinity, the phase composition and the crystallite-size of investigated photocatalysts were examined using powder X-ray diffraction. The XRD patterns of all examined photocatalysts are shown in Fig. 3a. Parent TiO 2 as well as all cerium doped TiO 2 show the diffraction lines corresponding only to TiO 2 anatase h k l reflections. However, in parent TiO 2 besides the main anatase (1 0 1), (0 0 4) and (2 0 0) h k l reflections at 29.4 • , 2. Concerning the possible inhibiting effect of cerium on the growth of TiO 2 crystallites and the TiO 2 phase transformation, which correlates vice versa, our conclusion can be supported by literature [43,44]. Lin et al. [43] justified the stabilization of TiO 2 anatase by surrounding Ce ions based on the formation of Ti O Ce bonds at the TiO 2 -CeO 2 interface. Fang et al. [44] proposed that the CeO 2 clusters preferentially nucleate on the oxygen vacancies within TiO 2 anatase, which forms the interface bridged with oxygen between CeO 2 and anatase. At low Ce contents this occurs preferentially on the oxygen vacancy sites in the bulk of TiO 2 anatase than on its surface, because surface oxygen vacancy sites are preferably hydroxylated and thus filled. With the increasing Ce content the CeO 2 clusters grow, forming cubic CeO 2 crystallites. Hence, the decreasing concentration of oxygen vacancies and the Ti O Ce interface are responsible for the inhibition of structural changes within TiO 2 anatase in TiCe mixed oxides. It is not therefore surprising, that the anatase crystallite-size decreases with increasing Ce content, as it is nicely depicted in Fig. 3b and summarized in Table 2 for the TiO 2 photocatalysts with Ce loading up to 3 mol.%.
