mentions.text: The X-ray photoelectron spectra (XPS) were used to explore the surface properties of Pd 2 Cu/P25. The narrow scan Pd 3d spectrum shows two peaks for spin-orbits 3d 5/2 and 3d 3/2 at 339 and 345 eV, corresponding to the metallic Pd 0 respectively (Figure 3a). Moreover, the deconvolution spectra of Pd 3d show an additional peak for the Pd 2+ , which is attributed to PdO on the surface [36]. Figure 3b shows the narrow scan spectrum of Cu 2p. The binding energies at 937 and 957 eV correspond to the 2p 3/2 and 2p 1/2 spin-orbits, respectively. The Cu 2p spectrum was deconvoluted into four peaks. The two main peaks denote Cu in the metallic state, while the minor peaks denote Cu in +2 oxidation states. Similar to Pd, Cu also exhibited CuO on its surface. Moreover, the peak intensity of Cu 2p was lower than that of Pd, which is in accordance with EDX results. Additionally, Figure 3c,d shows the narrow scan peaks of Ti 2p and O 1s, which are indexed to the typical peaks of TiO 2 (P25). The Ti 2p spectra shows two peaks at the binding energies of 462.1 and 467.8 eV belonging to the 2p 3/2 and 2p 1/2 orbitals, respectively. The deconvoluted O 1s peak reveals two binding energies at 533.5 and 535.3 eV, corresponding to the surface hydroxyl groups and lattice oxygen atoms respectively. Overall, these characterizations confirm the formation of Pd 2 Cu alloy on the P25 support. The amount of metals proportion in the photocatalyst were further confirmed by ICP-AES. For the analysis, the powder of the as-prepared catalyst was soaked in the aqua regia solutions for 6 hours and then mixed with 30wt% HF for overnight. The results were summarized in Table 1.

mentions.text: Results and Discussion g-C 3 N 4 (GCN) is a visible light active and well-known catalyst on which both CO 2 photoreduction and water splitting has been demonstrated. The GCN sample we used in this investigation was obtained from dicyandiamide by heating at 550 o C. The sample is nonporous and its band gap, as reported elsewhere is 2.78 eV. 21 Owing to the lack of conductivity and fast hole-electron recombination, we could measure the photocurrent generation upon the visible light irradiation only upon the addition of conductive carbon black. As seen in Figure 1, exposure to light increases the current owing to the generation of photoelectrons. The effect is small and it could be even underestimated since expose of carbon black itself to visible light itself results in a current decrease due to the movement of electrons to some trapped stated by the provide energy. 21 Interesting, while on carbon black the cycles upon light switching are almost repeatable, in the case of GCN some decrease in photocurrent is measured with an increase in the number of cycles. Based on the behavior of carbon black, a plausible explanation is some instability of GCN surface upon visible light exposure. The elemental composition of GCN surface, determined by XPS, initial and exposed to water, CO 2 and CO 2 and water, all under visible light irradiation, for 24h is presented in Table 1. The traces of oxygen on the surface indicate that GCN is not pure g-C 3 N 4 for which the ratio of C/N is expected to be 0.75. Interestingly, that ratio markedly increases after exposure to CO 2 under light. This is accompanied by an increase in the content of oxygen. Both these trends suggest that both oxidation and surface reduction took place when only CO 2 and the catalyst were in the light exposed vessel. On the other hand, when water and the catalyst were only in the system the C/N ratio decreased. Moreover, the presence of water and CO 2 together resulted in almost unchanged content of the elements. 1S and 2S of Supplementary Information. On C 1s core energy level spectrum for the initial GCN, the contributions at 284.8, 288.0, 289.2, and 293.5 eV are detected. They represent carbon in, C-C bonds. N-C=N or C-N bonds, O-C=O and π ->π * transition, respectively. Interestingly, exposure to light with either CO 2 or water present in the reactor vessels results in a small contribution of C-O bonds which must form as a result of oxidation of carbon in triazine rings. This effect is the strongest for the sample exposed to CO 2 and light. Interestingly, when water is present in the system more carbon atoms are oxidized to O-C=O bonds than to C-O bonds. Moreover, when O 1s spectra are analyzed, upon exposure to water, especially in the absence of CO 2 (sample N 2 LW), the contribution of oxygen in carboxylic/quinones groups increases. The opposite changes are found after only CO 2 exposure in light (sample CO 2 L), suggesting some degree of carbon reduction. The degree of surface reduction is certainly confirmed by the analysis of N 1s core energy spectra (Figure 2). Here the contribution of nitrogen in triazine rings markedly increases. Since this is associated with a decrease in nitrogen which might suggest removal of some amines, likely as result of their oxidation 29 or reaction with CO 2 30 . Interestingly, when CO 2 is present together with water, the changes in surface chemistry, although consistent, are much less pronounced than when the catalyst is exposed to only CO 2 . This suggests some either "screening" or a competitive effect of water when it is present on the surface along with CO 2 . Water by itself, upon visible light irradiation results in minimal changes in the speciation of nitrogen, but it is able to markedly oxidize the carbon atoms of GCN. Changes in the surface chemistry are also seen on the results of potentiometric titration (PT) (Figure 3, Table 1S of Supplementary Information). In analyzing these results one has to keep in mind that the changes reflect the alteration in the amounts of Bronsted acids present the surface in aqueous environment. Here GCN appears as the sample richest in surface groups dissociating in our experimental window. Based on the result of XPS, we linked them to the protonated amines. Their relatively high contribution results in the highest surface pH among all the samples. Expose to CO 2 in light markedly decreases the amount of these groups. This is in in agreement with the XPS results, which showed a decrease in the amount of nitrogen and in amines in general. On the other hand, some carbon atoms got oxidized and this change is reflected in a slight decrease in surface pH as a result of formation of more phenols, which are not very acidic (pK a ~10) (Figure 3). Exposure to water in light (sample N 2 LW) also slightly acidifies surface. Interestingly, it results in a decrease in the amount of acids. This could be due to the contribution of amines decreases and the some carboxylic groups appear on the surface, which are stronger acids than the protonated amines. Exposure of the sample to CO 2 and water in visible light (sample CO 2 LW) results in much smaller decrease in the amount of acids on the surface than when exclusively water ( sample N 2 DW) or CO 2 ( sample CO 2 D) were present.

mentions.text: As in the case of GCN, we have analyzed the changes in CS surface chemistry in aqueous environment by potentiometric titration (Figure 5, Table 2S of Supplementary Information). The changes of sulfur-doped carbon might differ in its origin from those in the case of GCN. Since the carbon is porous, retention of CO 2 on the surface 23,24 and its reactivity with water/carbonate formation must affect our study on surface chemistry alterations. Interestingly, exposure of the CS carbon to water only, either in dark (sample N 2 DW) or in light (sample N 2 LW) decreases the number of dissociating groups in the similar manner suggesting the lack of photoactivity and some reactivity maybe related to hydrolysis of some surface groups. The presence of CO 2 along with water in the dark results in similar changes as those caused by the adsorbed water. On the contrary, exposure simultaneously to light, water and CO 2 (sample CO 2 LW) changed only slightly the number of species detected on the surface. This might be an effect of limitations in CO 2 adsorption in such conditions due to its competition with water for the polar adsorption centers. Nevertheless, CO 2 presence results in a smaller decrease in the number of species detected on the surface in comparison with the situation when only water was present (sample N 2 LW and sample N 2 DW). This is probably due to the contribution of the carbonate and bicarbonate ions, which are formed in the reaction of CO 2 with water. When the sample with water was exposed to CO 2 in the dark (sample CO 2 DW) the numbers of surface groups detected are similar to that when the carbon is exposed only to water, either in light (sample N 2 LW) or in dark (sample N 2 DW). When water is not present and samples are exposed to CO 2 only, either in dark (sample CO 2 D) or in light (sample CO 2 L), a slight acidification of the surface is observed with a decrease in the number of acidic groups, indicating that some strong acids are formed.

mentions.text: Since once again CO 2 must be adsorbed in the pores of the carbon and the volume of the pores is constant, similar changes in chemistry are noticed due to the effect of carbonates and bicarbonates. Moreover, adsorbed CO 2 showed exhibit some chemical reactivity with this carbon surface. 23,24 The previous results analyzing CO 2 adsorption, indicated that in surface reactions carbon got oxidized and some sulfur species were removed from the surface. 23,24 In that study, the sulfur content decreased and the contribution of reduced sulfur increased, which is consistent with our XPS data (Table 4). Thus in the case of this carbon, photoactivity either does not play a role in CO 2 reduction or the chemical reactivity predominates. Based on the similarity of the results obtained when only water or only CO 2 was present, in dark and light, photoactivity seems not to affect to a marked extent the interactions of either CO 2 or water with the surface.

tables.caption: Resistance, resistivity and conductivity of the CS carbon exposed to various environments. N 2 , CO 2 , L, and W refer to nitrogen, carbon dioxide, exposure to ambient light, and exposure to water, respectively, at various combinations of experimental conditions.

mentions.text: Exposure to various environments indeed changed the texture of the carbon and it must be the result of the chemical changes (Figure 6 and 7, Table 3S of Supplementary Information). The most marked alterations in the surface areas are noticed upon exposure to water at light (sample N 2 LW, an increase) and to CO 2 at light (sample CO 2 LW, a decrease). These changes follow the changes in the pore volume. Since water in the dark (N 2 DW) practically does not affect the porosity, obviously some surface activation was noticed upon irradiation and it is linked to photosensitivity. That additional development of porosity in the presence of water at light could only happens as a result of water oxidation reaction in which oxygen is released. It is especially seen in the volume of mesopores where more water could be adsorbed on hydrophilic surface groups than in micropores. It is important to mention that the exposure to CO 2 and water in light (sample CO 2 LW) decreases the porosity much more than the irradiation only (N 2 LW). This is a very interesting observation since the changes in surface chemistry for sample CO 2 LW and N 2 LW are quite similar. A plausible explanation is in the difference is the location of the reactive sites on the surface. If photoactivity in the case of CO 2 LW increased the CO 2 reactivity in terms of reaction 2, in which oxygen from water oxidation was "scavenged" in CO 2 reduction, the surface oxidation by oxygen could be limited. Besides, in parallel reaction CO 2 likely reacted to some extent with reactive carbon at the entrance to small pores. Incorporation of oxygen (oxidation of surface was noticed from XPS results) likely blocks the accessibility of pores to the nitrogen molecule, which is used as a porosity probe. CO 2 in this case could not result in oxidation of sulfonic groups followed by their removal since due to their hydrophilicity, they are likely "screened" by the adsorbed water. Surprisingly, exposure to CO 2 in light (sampleCO 2 L), which caused the most marked changes in surface chemistry probed by XPS, resulted in minimal changes in porosity. Taking into account the mechanisms we propose, even though the decrease in the content of sulfur was supposed to result in an increase of the porosity, surface oxidation by holes and by oxygen from CO 2 reduction, formed new groups at the pore entrances. Thus the accessibility of some pores decreases. These two processes occurred simultaneously resulting in almost unchanged pore volume calculated from the nitrogen adsorption. Contrary to the potentiometric titration results, the XPS results should not be affected by the adsorbed species (the samples were outgassed before the experiments and thus it is assumed that the adsorbed species are removed from the pore system) and therefore the comparison of the surface chemical changes on the surface CS carbon to those GCN seems to be more meaningful than in the case where adsorption in the pore system might play a role. Here the remarkable similarity is in the trend of the observed changes. In both cases exposure to CO 2 under light affects the surface to the greatest extent resulting both in oxidation of carbon atoms and in reduction of oxidation level of heteroatom-containing group. Even though this effect happens on the carbon surface in the dark, there is an indication that photoactivity contributes to this process, especially in the case of GCN. Formed oxygen reacts with carbon atoms causing their oxidation, either on the surface of GCN or that of CS. Water, when on the surface along with CO 2 , limits the direct contact of CO 2 with the surface and inhibit its ability either to be reduced by electron or oxidized by oxygen. Formed CO in the CO 2 reduction process likely reacts with amines of GCN. Since the content of sulfur on the surface of CS markedly decreased, it is likely due to the oxidation of sulfonic acid and sulfones, which result in the release of sulfur as SO/SO 2 . Changes in surface chemistry and the development of porosity in CS carbon could also affect the samples conductivity. The collected results are collected in Table 5. Both, an increase in oxygen groups on the surface and an increase in porosity are expected to decrease the carbon conductivity. Owing to the complex changes in carbon texture and chemistry, the differences in the conductive behavior do not follow a clear tread. Nevertheless, the least conductive are CS-CO2LW and CS-CO2L. While for the former showed the most visible changes in the porosity, for the latter the alteration in surface chemistry were the most pronounced. Thus the electrical measurements show some sensitivity to the changes in the surface features of the materials tested.

mentions.text: Table 1 summarises the main physicochemical characteristics of NaNbO 3 and NaTaO 3 photocatalysts. Chemical analyses indicate a good agreement of the obtained compositions with those pursued in the synthetic method (stoichiometric wt% given in brackets in Table 1), with a small defect of sodium that reveals that there still exists an effect of Na volatilisation in spite of the excess of Na 2 CO 3 used in the synthesis.

Table 1 summarises the main physicochemical characteristics of NaNbO 3 and NaTaO 3 photocatalysts. Chemical analyses indicate a good agreement of the obtained compositions with those pursued in the synthetic method (stoichiometric wt% given in brackets in Table 1), with a small defect of sodium that reveals that there still exists an effect of Na volatilisation in spite of the excess of Na 2 CO 3 used in the synthesis.

X-ray diffraction patterns of the obtained materials (Fig. 1) show their characteristic crystalline structure. 17 Thus, the NaNbO 3 sample is composed of a single phase with an orthorhombically distorted perovskite structure (NaNbO 3 , ICDD PDF # 01-073-0803). This orthorhombic structure (ICDD PDF # 01-073-0878) is also mainly present in NaTaO 3 together with a monoclinically distorted perovskite structure (NaTaO 3 , ICDD PDF # 01-074-2478), with a minor contribution of an additional hexagonal phase (natrotantite Na 2 Ta 4 O 11 , ICDD PDF # 01-084-0810). The results of Rietveld refinement of the powder diffractograms of the above mentioned structures are included in Table 1. The natrotantite phase is present in a ca. 2.5% amount in the NaTaO 3 sample, which contains a ca. 4.5 : 1 orthorhombic/monoclinic NaTaO 3 proportion. Only slight deviations (maximum 0.15%) exist in cell parameters with respect to the reference structures. Large crystal sizes are found in both metallates, as could be expected considering that they were obtained by solid-state synthesis at high temperature. These large sizes are confirmed by TEM images, an example of which is shown in Fig. 2. In agreement with this, both catalysts present low surface areas, with values around 1 m 2 g -1 . In accordance with the synthesis temperature, the nitrogen adsorption isotherms (not shown) are of type-II in both cases, indicating that the solids are not porous and that the specific surface area is due to the external surface of the particles.

The structural characterisation was complemented by Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 3). The bands in the Raman spectra are well matched with those described in the literature for NaNbO 3 18,19 and NaTaO 3 . 20 Typical spectral profiles of perovskite structures, with intense bands in the 100-300 and 400-700 cm -1 regions, are observed. Thus, the NaNbO 3 spectrum shows bands at 125, 144 and 155 cm -1 corresponding to the librational modes of the NbO 6 octahedra. The rest of the observed bands are generated by the internal vibrations of the NbO 6 octahedra, with the triply degenerate F 2u and F 2g modes giving rise to the profile observed in the 170-300 cm -1 region, and the intense shouldered band centered at 605 cm -1 , which is assignable to symmetric stretching modes. The low intensity bands observed at ca. 380 and 435 cm -1 are indicative of a tilting angle between adjacent octahedra that deviates the NaNbO 3 crystalline phase from the ideal perovskite structure, as observed in the X-ray diffractograms discussed above. 21 Also in line with the XRD data for NaNbO 3 , the weak band at 870 cm -1 corresponds to a combination mode in centrosymmetric space goups. 22 Similar assignments can be made for NaTaO 3 . The spectrum presents bands at 140, 160, 204, and 222 cm -1 that are characteristic of Na translational vibration modes, which in the case of NaNbO 3 appear at Raman shifts below 100 cm -1 and are not observed due to the used Rayleigh filter. 18 The bands at 263, 318 and 345 cm -1 can be assigned to the bending modes of TaO 6 octahedra, and those at 453, 499, and 626 cm -1 correspond to Ta-O stretching modes, with possible combination bands appearing at 693 and above 750 cm -1 . This band distribution is in good agreement with the main presence of an orthorhombic NaTaO 3 phase in this catalyst. 23 Fig. 4 shows the diffuse reflectance UV-vis spectra of NaNbO 3 and NaTaO 3 . As expected, the sharp absorption edge for NaTaO 3 appears at a higher energy than in the case of NaNbO 3 . 5,7,[12][13][14][15][16] Their corresponding band gap (E g ) values, included in Table 1, were calculated from Tauc plots considering a direct transition in NaTaO 3 , in accordance with the main contribution of the orthorhombic phase, 24 and an indirect transition in the case of NaNbO 3 . 25 The obtained values are in good accordance with those described in the literature for these phases. [12][13][14][15][16]24,25 The valence band potentials of NaTaO 3 and NaNbO 3 are similar because both consist of O 2p orbitals and the oxygen anions coordinate to Ta 5+ or Nb 5+ ions, which have the same ionic radius. 8 Hence the difference in the band gaps arises from the higher energy (more negative reduction 1). potential) of Ta 5d orbitals, forming the conduction band of NaTaO 3 , with respect to Nb 4d orbitals forming the conduction band of NaNbO 3 . Assuming that the valence band potentials in oxides with metal ions without partially filled d levels lie at 2.94 V vs. SHE within 2% deviation, 8,26 a band potential diagram like that shown in Fig. 5 can be deduced from the E g values obtained from UV-vis spectra.

The structural characterisation was complemented by Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 3). The bands in the Raman spectra are well matched with those described in the literature for NaNbO 3 18,19 and NaTaO 3 . 20 Typical spectral profiles of perovskite structures, with intense bands in the 100-300 and 400-700 cm -1 regions, are observed. Thus, the NaNbO 3 spectrum shows bands at 125, 144 and 155 cm -1 corresponding to the librational modes of the NbO 6 octahedra. The rest of the observed bands are generated by the internal vibrations of the NbO 6 octahedra, with the triply degenerate F 2u and F 2g modes giving rise to the profile observed in the 170-300 cm -1 region, and the intense shouldered band centered at 605 cm -1 , which is assignable to symmetric stretching modes. The low intensity bands observed at ca. 380 and 435 cm -1 are indicative of a tilting angle between adjacent octahedra that deviates the NaNbO 3 crystalline phase from the ideal perovskite structure, as observed in the X-ray diffractograms discussed above. 21 Also in line with the XRD data for NaNbO 3 , the weak band at 870 cm -1 corresponds to a combination mode in centrosymmetric space goups. 22 Similar assignments can be made for NaTaO 3 . The spectrum presents bands at 140, 160, 204, and 222 cm -1 that are characteristic of Na translational vibration modes, which in the case of NaNbO 3 appear at Raman shifts below 100 cm -1 and are not observed due to the used Rayleigh filter. 18 The bands at 263, 318 and 345 cm -1 can be assigned to the bending modes of TaO 6 octahedra, and those at 453, 499, and 626 cm -1 correspond to Ta-O stretching modes, with possible combination bands appearing at 693 and above 750 cm -1 . This band distribution is in good agreement with the main presence of an orthorhombic NaTaO 3 phase in this catalyst. 23 Fig. 4 shows the diffuse reflectance UV-vis spectra of NaNbO 3 and NaTaO 3 . As expected, the sharp absorption edge for NaTaO 3 appears at a higher energy than in the case of NaNbO 3 . 5,7,[12][13][14][15][16] Their corresponding band gap (E g ) values, included in Table 1, were calculated from Tauc plots considering a direct transition in NaTaO 3 , in accordance with the main contribution of the orthorhombic phase, 24 and an indirect transition in the case of NaNbO 3 . 25 The obtained values are in good accordance with those described in the literature for these phases. [12][13][14][15][16]24,25 The valence band potentials of NaTaO 3 and NaNbO 3 are similar because both consist of O 2p orbitals and the oxygen anions coordinate to Ta 5+ or Nb 5+ ions, which have the same ionic radius. 8 Hence the difference in the band gaps arises from the higher energy (more negative reduction 1). potential) of Ta 5d orbitals, forming the conduction band of NaTaO 3 , with respect to Nb 4d orbitals forming the conduction band of NaNbO 3 . Assuming that the valence band potentials in oxides with metal ions without partially filled d levels lie at 2.94 V vs. SHE within 2% deviation, 8,26 a band potential diagram like that shown in Fig. 5 can be deduced from the E g values obtained from UV-vis spectra.

Fig. 7 shows the accumulated amounts of the main reaction products over 15 h of irradiation, compared to those obtained with TiO 2 PC500 (S BET = 165.8 m 2 g -1 ). In all cases, the main CO 2 reduction products are CO, CH 4 and CH 3 OH, together with H 2 coming from the concomitant reduction of water competing with that of CO 2 . Trace amounts of other products like C 2+ hydrocarbons and ethanol are obtained, with similar amounts for different catalysts. Reactions carried out in an argon atmosphere under irradiation gave rise to product evolution of less than 2% with respect to the tests performed feeding CO 2 + H 2 O, indicating that the evolved gases in the presence of CO 2 and H 2 O do not arise from adventitious carbon contamination on the surface of the photocatalysts. In spite of their low surface areas (see Table 1), both NaNbO 3 and NaTaO 3 give rise to product amounts comparable to those with titania, although the production attained with the latter is considerably larger in all cases except for CH 4 . However, if the results are referred to the surface area unit, which would reflect the intrinsic photoactivity of the materials, the production with the synthesised metallates reveals considerable interest. In line with this, the measured PL spectrum of TiO 2 (Fig. 6), with slightly higher intensity than those of both perovskite materials, reveals that the larger net production with titania cannot be explained only in terms of photogenerated charge carrier utilisation.

In the case of using the NS-Ar photocatalyst, the formation rates of acetaldehyde and acetone are significantly increased to 11.5 and 15.0 μmol g -1 h -1 with the selectivities of 32.4 and 67.6%, respectively. mentions.text: In order to further reveal the importance of the composite structure of C-TiO 2Àx @g-C 3 N 4 in CO 2 photoreduction, control experiments employing different TiO 2 -based composites as photocatalysts were carried out under similar conditions (Table 1). When using commercial P25 TiO 2 (entry 2) as the photocatalyst, around 0.0301 mmol g À1 CO was generated, which was about 20fold lower than that of C-TiO 2Àx . When reducing TiO 2 to TiO 2Àx , the generation of CO was enhanced to 0.255 mmol g À1 (entry 3); however, this was still 2.3-fold lower than that of C-TiO 2Àx . These results implied the carbon layer played a positive part in TiO 2 in CO 2 reduction. With TiO 2 @g-C 3 N 4 (entry 4) as the catalyst, made from P25 and g-C 3 N 4 , the yield was higher than bare P25 but was 68 times lower than that from C-TiO 2Àx @g-C 3 N 4 -3. Replacing P25 with titanium isopropoxide as the starting material, the resultant TiO 2 @g-C 3 N 4 (entry 5) exhibited a sharply increased reactivity, with up to 0.274 mmol g À1 CO generation. However, this reactivity was one order of magnitude lower than that of C-TiO 2Àx @g-C 3 N 4 -3. These results illuminated that the carbon layer and excellent light adsorption of TiO 2Àx play a pivotal role in the photocatalysis. Using black TiO 2 nanobelts-doped g-C 3 N 4 (ref. 25) as the catalyst (entry 6), 0.535 mmol g À1 CO was produced, which was 4.6-fold lower than that from C-TiO 2Àx @g-C 3 N 4 -3, revealing a small size of nanoparticles was indispensable. Besides these TiO 2 -based catalysts, the CO generation rate of C-TiO 2Àx @g-C 3 N 4 was one order higher than most the reported TiO 2 -based catalysts and it outperformed any other reported TiO 2 -based material under similar conditions (Table S1 †). 25,37 To further expose the photocatalytic ability of C-TiO 2Àx @g-C 3 N 4 , the CO 2 reduction reaction was performed under the irradiation of whole light (Fig. 5b). Under irradiation of 12 h, around 4.500 mmol g À1 CO was produced by C-TiO 2Àx @g-C 3 N 4 -3. The yields of C-TiO 2Àx and g-C 3 N 4 were 2.900 and 0.600 mmol g À1 , respectively. documents.title: Fabrication of heterostructured UIO-66-NH2 /CNTs with enhanced activity and selectivity over photocatalytic CO2 reduction

tables.caption: The surface area and pore structure for different samples.

mentions.text: Table 1 summarizes the specific surface area and pore size distribution of the samples. CNTs have a BET surface area of 82.10 m 2 /g, while pure UIO-66-NH 2 exhibited a large surface area of 448.7 m 2 /g. It is found that when the content of CNTs is 2 wt%, the specific area of the composite is the highest, as well as the pore volume and average pore size. This inferred that the content of CNTs has an optimal value. The appropriate content of CNTs not only disperse UIO-66-NH 2 , but also increase the surface area, pore volume and average pore size of the composite materials. As increasing the surface area of composites, contact areas between active sites and target substrates are also increased thus causing superior photocatalytic performance. Besides, the studies showed that the increase of surface area could promote the acceptance of electrons and make the photocatalysts have a strong contact with active molecules. Thus the high surface area of composites would be conducive to supplying more reaction sites [62].

Furthermore, we pursued selectivity of HCOOH changes. From Fig. 6(b), when the CNTs loading content changes from 0 to 2 wt%, the yield of HCOOH changes from 1.84 mmol to 18.2 mmol and the selectivity changes from 38.3% to 63.1%. When the CNTs loading content continues to increase from 2 wt% to 5 wt%, the yield of HCOOH has a gradual downward trend, while the selectivity also decreased. When the loading content of CNTs is 2 wt%, the yield of HCOOH and the selectivity reached a maximum value of 63.1%. The selectivity is almost 2 times higher than the pure UIO-66-NH 2 . The improved selectivity is dued to the absence of eNH 2 , the physical adsorption sites and chemical reaction adsorption sites increased, the absorption reaction between CO 2 and eNH 2 enhanced the adsorption capacity of CO 2 significantly, therefore improve the selectivity of HCOOH. This has also been demonstrated by previous reports [68]. In addition, we obtained composite samples through mechanical mixing method and thus demonstrated the advantages of hydrothermal synthesis (Table S1).

As listed in Table S1, the UIO-66-NH 2 /2 wt% CNTs sample was fabricated through hydrothermal method and exhibited higher HCOOH evolution amount (28.8 mmol), which is 2.1 times higher than the mechanical mixing sample (13.6 mmol). The selectivity of HCOOH is also nearly 2 times higher than the mechanical mixing sample. The hydrothermal process induced shaping UIO-66-NH 2 crystals on the surface of CNTs, increased its dispersibility and strengthened the contact between the UIO-66-NH 2 and CNTs. These merits supplied a short pathway for charge transfer and low charge transfer resistance during the photocatalysis process.

mentions.text: The photocatalytic activities of various photocatalysts were evaluated under visible light illumination displayed in Fig. 6. In Fig. 6(a), it is evident that photocatalytic activity of CO 2 reduction increased firstly and then decreased while the generation of hydrogen shows the opposite trend. When the loading amount of CNTs is 2 wt%, the reduction of CO 2 reaches a maximum of 28.8 mmol while the H 2 generation shows a minimal amount of 2.0 mmol. The reduction of CO 2 and evolution of hydrogen are two electrons reaction process. They compete for the electrons in the photocatalytic system at the same time. The detailed data are shown in Table 2, all nanocomposites exhibit superior photocatalytic performance compared to the pure UIO-66-NH 2 which presents the synergistic effect of CNTs in these samples and the fact that CNTs improve the activity and selectivity of photocatalysts. With massive loading content of CNTs, the photocatalytic performance decrease, this is due to the fact that photons are further absorbed and scattered in the existence of CNTs. Besides, the excessive CNTs can play as a kind of recombination center instead of supplying an electron pathway.

documents.title: Extending the visible-light photocatalytic CO2 reduction activity of K2Ti6O13 with the MxOy (M = Co, Ni and Cu) incorporation

tables.caption: Quantitative analysis of secondary phases in the M x O y -KTO samples obtained by the Rietveld refinement

mentions.text: To obtain more quantitative information about the formed impurities in the samples, a Rietveld analysis was performed on each diffraction pattern using the MAUD software. This software uses the RUITA/ RITSA method developed by Wenk et al. [41] for the analysis of diffraction patterns, amount of crystal structure, and phase microstructure, along with the texture and the residual stresses [42,43]. For this calculation, the following parameters were considered. For KTO: a monoclinic crystalline structure, space group C2/m, and cell parameters a = 15. Table 1 summarizes the quantitative analysis of each composite sample, obtained by the Rietveld analysis with their respective residual factors (R wp : index of spectra fitting and R exp : expected error).

From Table 1, it is possible to notice the formation and increase in the concentration of the secondary K-poor phases with the increase of the metal oxide precursor concentration, suggesting K-loss during synthesis in the main K 2 Ti 6 O 13 phase, thanks to the possible introduction of Co, Ni, or Cu cations into its crystalline structure. Furthermore, as a result of the cation introduction a different behavior was observed; for instance, the Cu-loaded samples promoted the formation of higher concentration of the secondary phases, compared to the Ni-or Co-loaded ones. This behavior suggests the easy introduction of Cu cations into the crystalline structure of KTO, promoting the presence of more K ? cations for the grow of the K-poor phases.

In addition, the metal oxide phase concentrations (Co 3 O 4 , NiO, and CuO) were also calculated and summarized in Table 1. However, their concentration is very low (\ 1 wt%) compared to the metallic precursor load, as a result of their introduction into the crystalline structure of KTO, or in the formed potassium titanate impurities. These metal oxides can be present over the titanate surface or intercalated between the TiO 6 tunnels, as other studies have confirmed [44,45].

Table 2 summarizes the cell parameter values obtained from the Rietveld refinement, but only for the K 2 Ti 6 O 13 01-054-0275 phase. In this context, all cations were refined in the 4i position with K and Ti cations varying in the partial occupancy between 0.01 to 0.2%. As seen in Table 2, compared to the bare KTO sample, a significant change in the parameter values is observed due to the presence of the metal oxides. For instance, the Co-loaded samples present a slight increase in parameters a and b, confirming an introduction of Co cations instead Ti 4? ones, as reported in the literature [46]. For that reason, these samples promoted the growth of impurities (K-deficient phases) in lower concentration compared to the Ni or Cu-loaded ones (see Table 1), resulting in the purest samples. An opposite behavior was observed in the Cu-and Ni-loaded samples; as seen in Table 2, with the increase in Ni and Cu precursor in the reactant mixture, a decrease in parameter a and b is evident, resulting in most of the cases in a decrease in the cell volume. As a result of these changes, it is possible to confirm that most of the Ni and Cu cations replaced K ? ones in the tunnels, confirming our previous assumption of the availability of more K cations for the formation of the K-poor phases. In the case of Cu-loaded samples, this behavior has also been reported as the introduction of Cu cations into the structure instead of Ti 4? [47]. For that reason, it is possible to conclude that both phenomena happen simultaneously.

Tables S1 and S2 present the cell parameters calculated from the Rietveld refinement for the K 2 Ti 4 O 9 and the KTi 8 O 13 phases. As can be seen, more noticeable changes are presented in all parameters of both phases as a result of the increase in the metal oxide precursor concentration compared to the K 2 Ti 6 O 13 phase, suggesting a higher introduction of metal cations into the crystalline structure of the impurities (K-poor phases). For example, in the case of K 2 Ti 4 O 9 phase, the parameter a decreased by around 3 A ˚due to the Cu cation doping. These significant changes could be associated mainly with the crystalline structure of the different phases, all of them presented in Fig. S2. From the figure, it is possible to observe that it is more difficult to exchange K ? cations in the K 2 Ti 6 O 13 (Fig. S2a) and in the K 1.28 Ti 8 O 16 (Fig. S2c) phases than in the K 2 Ti 4 O 9 (Fig. S2b) due to the TiO 6 octahedrons arrangement forming closed tunnels, instead of the opened ones as in the K 2 Ti 4 O 9 , where the metal cations exchange is more favored.

An opposite behavior was observed in the Cu-and Ni-loaded samples; as seen in Table 2, with the increase in Ni and Cu precursor in the reactant mixture, a decrease in parameter a and b is evident, resulting in most of the cases in a decrease in the cell volume. As a result of these changes, it is possible to confirm that most of the Ni and Cu cations replaced K ? ones in the tunnels, confirming our previous assumption of the availability of more K cations for the formation of the K-poor phases. In the case of Cu-loaded samples, this behavior has also been reported as the introduction of Cu cations into the structure instead of Ti 4? [47]. For that reason, it is possible to conclude that both phenomena happen simultaneously.

Tables S1 and S2 present the cell parameters calculated from the Rietveld refinement for the K 2 Ti 4 O 9 and the KTi 8 O 13 phases. As can be seen, more noticeable changes are presented in all parameters of both phases as a result of the increase in the metal oxide precursor concentration compared to the K 2 Ti 6 O 13 phase, suggesting a higher introduction of metal cations into the crystalline structure of the impurities (K-poor phases). For example, in the case of K 2 Ti 4 O 9 phase, the parameter a decreased by around 3 A ˚due to the Cu cation doping. These significant changes could be associated mainly with the crystalline structure of the different phases, all of them presented in Fig. S2. From the figure, it is possible to observe that it is more difficult to exchange K ? cations in the K 2 Ti 6 O 13 (Fig. S2a) and in the K 1.28 Ti 8 O 16 (Fig. S2c) phases than in the K 2 Ti 4 O 9 (Fig. S2b) due to the TiO 6 octahedrons arrangement forming closed tunnels, instead of the opened ones as in the K 2 Ti 4 O 9 , where the metal cations exchange is more favored.

mentions.text: In addition, surface area and CO 2 adsorption capacity are vital factors in PCR activity. Therefore, the nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms and CO 2 adsorption isotherms experiments are analyzed. As shown in Fig. S6 and Table S1, Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface areas and pore structure distribution of both samples do not vary much.

To further understand the mechanism of PCR reaction, the conduction band (CB) and valence band (VB) positions of ZnO and ZnO/graphene were analyzed. As shown in Fig. S12, Mott-Schottky (M-S) measurement of ZnO and ZnO/graphene were performed. It can be seen that the flat-band potentials of ZnO and ZnO/graphene are similar and estimated to be -0.58 V (vs. Normal Hydrogen Electrode (NHE) at pH = 7), due to a low loading amount of graphene on the surface of ZnO. In general, the flat band potential is close to the CB of n-type semiconductor [88][89][90]. Therefore, based on the results of M-S plots and UV-vis DRS spectra, we can conclude that the CB and VB potentials of ZnO and ZnO/graphene are -0.58 and 2.62 V (vs. NHE at pH = 7), respectively. The reduction potentials of CO, CH 3 OH and CH 4 are -0.53, -0.38 and -0.24 V (vs. NHE at pH = 7) (Table S2) [1,4,5], respectively, which are significantly positive than that of the CB potentials of ZnO and ZnO/graphene. Besides, the oxidation potential of O 2 and protons produced by H 2 O molecules was 0.82 V (vs. NHE at pH = 7) (Table S2), which is obviously negative than those of the VB potentials of ZnO and ZnO/graphene. Hence, the driving force offered by ZnO and ZnO/ graphene easily reduces CO 2 molecules into CO, CH 3 OH and CH 4 . Moreover, the M-S curve slope of ZnO/graphene is obviously smaller than that of ZnO (Fig. S12), demonstrating that the charge carrier density of ZnO/graphene nanocomposite (3.94 × 10 19 cm -3 ) is higher than that of ZnO (1.79 × 10 19 cm -3 ) [91]. This result suggests that introduced graphene on the surface of ZnO for enhanced the charge carrier density. Besides, the PCR reaction is a multi-electron reduction process. As shown in Table S2, evolution of CH 4 (8-electron reaction process) and CH 3 OH (6-electron reaction process) require more photogenerated electrons than that of CO (2-electron reaction process). Therefore, the yield rates of CO, CH 3 OH and CH 4 are different, and the good selectivity of CO is reasonable by considering the reaction dynamics. In addition, the work function of ZnO and graphene were measured by Kevin probe on the basis of contact potential differences (CPD) [35,61]. Furthermore, based on the previous report [61], there is a positive proportional relationship between the change of the CPD values and the concentration of photogenerated charge carriers for samples before and after illumination. As shown in Fig. 14 and Table 1, the difference of CPD values for ZnO/graphene (459 mV) is significantly higher than that of ZnO (381 mV), indicating the better separation efficiency of photogenerated charge carriers for ZnO/graphene nanocomposite than that of ZnO.

Based on the above results and discussions, we illustrate the PCR reaction mechanism of ZnO/graphene in Fig. 15. The work functions of ZnO and graphene are 4.28 and 5.27 eV, respectively (Table 1 and Fig. 15a.). When direct contact between ZnO and graphene is established, the free electrons will transfer from ZnO with higher Fermi level to graphene with lower Fermi level until equilibrium is built. Concurrently, ZnO exhibits upward interface band bending owing to its loss of electrons. Meanwhile, graphene, as the cocatalyst and electron sink, accepts the electrons from ZnO. After that, Schottky junction is formed at the interface and ZnO has the appropriate band bending (Fig. 15b) [92,93]. When the ZnO/graphene nanocomposite is exposed to light (Fig. 15c), the electrons are excited from VB to CB in ZnO, raising the Fermi level of ZnO from -4.28 to -3.90 eV (Table 1). While Fermi level of graphene is almost unaltered before and after illumination and kept at -5.07 eV (Table 1). This provides enough driving force for photogenerated electrons of ZnO to surmount the Schottky barrier and transfer to graphene rapidly. Simultaneously, the photogenerated holes, located at the VB of ZnO, react with H 2 O to produce O 2 and protons. Besides, the photogenerated electrons trapped by graphene cannot flow back to ZnO due to the existence of Schottky junction, which can effectively suppress the recombination of photogenerated electron-hole pairs [93]. Meanwhile, owing to the short transport distance, intimate contact and good electronic conductivity of graphene, the photogenerated electrons on the graphene side can migrate to the surface swiftly, and readily participate in the reduction of CO 2 . Hence, improved PCR performance can be achieved.

Methanol yields of different nanocrystals are shown in Fig. 9, and Table 1. Kočí et al. have successfully conducted UV light-induced photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 on TiO 2 catalyst in liquid phase. The yield of detectable products in decreased order of H 2 > CH 4 > CH 3 OH >> CO was found. 26,27 We focused on CH 3 OH product in liquid phase since CH 3 OH is regarded as a convenient liquid fuel and raw material for synthetic hydrocarbons and their products. Three samples, above mentioned for DRS and XPS measurements, were evaluated for photocatalytic activity. The system steadily generated methanol with a linear increase in the amount of methanol. The methanol yield over high level truncated particles is higher than those over two other ones. The photocatalytic activity of elongated particles is lowest. It can be concluded that the photocatalytic activity of the synthesized particles increases proportionally with the percentage of {001} facets. To clarify this point, we normalized the methanol yield vs BET surface area as shown in Fig. 9B. The higher methanol yield by truncated bipyramidal particles owes to its homogeneous, crystallinity as well as the presence of {001} facets. The exposed facet is highly absorbed ability with dissociative adsorption and chemically oxidative. 28 Beside that, the enhanced separation of electron and hole which improves the quantum yield, is important factor for remarkable photocatalytic activity of truncated octahedral crystals. 25 The higher methanol yield by truncated bipyramidal particles compared to that by elongated rod-like particles was also attributed to their higher crystallinity. As shown in Fig. 3, the peak intensity in XRD pattern of the elongated rod-like particles is lower than those of two others. This is reasonable due to its low temperature synthesis. mentions.text: Severe environmental pollution has hindered the sustainable development of human society, and photocatalysis is one of the promising highly-efficient environmental decontamination strategy [119,120]. Under light irradiation, a semiconductor generates many electrons in CB and holes in VB; the photogenerated electrons can reduce O 2 to $O 2 À , and photogenerated holes can oxidize OH À to $OH. These active species (h þ , $O 2 À , $OH) can oxidize certain pollutants to CO 2 and H 2 O. Due to its strong redox ability, g-C 3 N 4 /BiOX is very suitable for photocatalytic degradation of pollutants [25]. Table 1 summarizes the list of recent studies on the pollutant degradation by g-C 3 N 4 /BiOX composite photocatalytic materials. g-C 3 N 4 /BiOX is an effective photocatalytic material since it can completely decompose various environmental pollutants under mild conditions [63]. Yang et al. [65] applied a protonation pretreatment of graphite-like C 3 N 4 with hydrochloric acid to induce electrostatic interaction between heterojunctions and increase the tightness of the interface. Such material was successfully used to degrade RhB organic pollutants, confirming an enhanced photocatalytic activity of the heterojunction. g-C 3 N 4 /BiOX was also reported as a good material for the treatment of gas-phase pollutants [26]. Methyl mercaptan (CH 3 SH), a highly toxic and corrosive volatile gas, is widespread in urban garbage, industrial garbage, and sewage environment. Hu [121] et al. used a simple solvothermal method to prepare a solution-state Z-type porous g-C 3 N 4 /I 3--BiOI ultra-thin nanosheet heterojunction using I 3À /I À redox ions as a transport mediator that effectively promote transfer and separation of interfacial charges. The g-C 3 N 4 /I 3--BiOI composite material is applied for the photocatalytic elimination of ppm-level CH 3 SH under visible LED light. Compared with pure BiOI and g-C 3 N 4 , g-C 3 N 4 /I 3--BiOI heterojunction exhibits considerably high photocatalytic activity for the CH 3 SH removal. Besides, g-C 3 N 4 /BiOX is widely used in degradation of liquid pollutants (methylene blue [50], methyl orange [31], 2,4-diclorophenol [122], 4-chlorophenol [52]) or toxic NO [26], and pharmaceuticals pollution carbamazepine (CBZ) [44]. i n t e r n a t i o n a l j o u r n a l o f h y d r o g e n e n e r g y x x x ( x x x x ) x x x H 2 production by water splitting

mentions.text: To confirm the possible variation of crystal structure during the LARP process, XRD characterizations for CsPbBr 3 NPs, GO, FLG, CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs were accomplished. Fig. 2(a) shows the XRD patterns of CsPbBr 3 NPs, GO, FLG, CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs. A peak at 2θ = 12.4 • for GO was shown, which can be suggested as the interlayer spacing about 0.71 nm in GO. [40] For FLG, a peak at 2θ = 26 • can be observed, which corresponds to the spacing of (002) planes of hexagonal phase graphite [42]. The XRD peaks at 2θ = 15.2 • , 21.5 • , 30.4 • , 30.7 • , 34.4 • , 37.7 • and 43.7 • can be identified as the (001), (110), (002), (200), (210), (211) and (202) planes of monoclinic CsPbBr 3 (JCPDS Card No. 18-0364). In addition, as the formation of CsPbBr 3 /GO and CsPbBr 3 /FLG NHSs, the XRD patterns of CsPbBr 3 was still presented, which demonstrated that the crystal structure of CsPbBr 3 would not be altered as the FLG or GO were incorporated in the LARP process. The characteristic peak of FLG was still presented for CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs, which illustrated the decoration of CsPbBr 3 NPs only on the surface of FLG without inserting it into the stacked graphene layers. However, the characteristic peak of GO was absent for CsPbBr 3 -GO NHSs, which may be caused by the decoration of CsPbBr 3 NPs on the surface of GO thin layer to change the interlayer spacing. For a better understanding of the interfacial chemical states, XPS analysis of GO, FLG, CsPbBr 3 NPs, CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs was performed. As shown in Fig. 2(b) and Table S1, for the comparison between the two series (GO/CsPbBr 3 -GO and FLG/CsPbBr 3 -FLG), the C 1s XPS spectra represented a significant decrease in the contributions of C-O (285.97 eV), C=O (287.46 eV) and O-C=O (288.86 eV) as compared to that of sp 2 carbon (284.6 eV). This outcome illustrates that the decoration of CsPbBr 3 NPs majorly relies on the formation of chemical bonds upon the oxygen functional groups on the surface of GO and FLG. Moreover, Cs 3d, Pb 4f and Br 3d XPS spectra displayed shifts toward lower binding energies after the CsPbBr 3 NPs were decorated on GO or FLG, respectively. This phenomenon reveals the strong chemical interaction at the interfaces of CsPbBr 3 /GO and CsPbBr 3 /FLG. [22] This result, together with the TEM, EDS and XRD analyses, confirmed that the current synthetic process could successfully obtain CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs.

Before the particle application of in photoelectric conversions, the interfacial charge carrier dynamics for the CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs are essential to understand by TRPL examination. Fig. 6 shows the TRPL spectra of CsPbBr 3 NPs, CsPbBr 3 -GO NHS and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHS samples. Faster PL decay profiles of CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHS samples than CsPbBr 3 NP sample were observed. For the better comparison, the PL decay curves were fitted with exponential decay kinetics and the fitting parameters were listed in Table 1. The PL decay profile of CsPbBr 3 NPs can be fitted with triple exponential decay kinetics, resulting in 17.6 % of fast component with a lifetime of 7.21 ns (τ 1 ), 68.5 % of the medium component with a lifetime of 49.63 ns (τ 2 ) and 14.1 % of slow component with a lifetime of 154.66 ns (τ 3 ). The fast decay component can be assigned as the radiative recombination of CB electrons and VB holes. In addition, the medium and slow components can be suggested as the radiative recombination of long-lived electron-hole pairs in shallow-trap and deep-trap states of CsPbBr 3 NPs, which is consistent with our previous studies of exciton dynamics of lead halide based perovskite nanostructures. [22] For CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs, the increased amplitude of fast decay component and decreased amplitudes of medium and slow components as compared to CsPbBr 3 NPs were observed. These outcomes indicate that the emergency of additional nonradiative recombination pathways from the electronic interaction between CsPbBr 3 NPs and GO/FLG, confirming the proposed mechanism of the interfacial CT process in CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs in UPS examinations. The intensity-average PL lifetime (τ av ) is calculated and listed in Table 1 1.

mentions.text: The composition of CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs can be easily modulated by controlling the relative amounts of CsPbBr 3 precursors and GO/FLG during the LARP processes. Fig. 3 shows TEM images of CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs with a gradual enhancement in the loading amounts of GO or FLG in the individual precursor solutions. The decorated density of the CsPbBr 3 NPs decreased with an increase in the content of GO and FLG for the both of CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs, respectively. In addition, the cubic-like CsPbBr 3 NPs still can be observed on the surfaces of GO or FLG. The histogram of particle size distribution of CsPbBr 3 NPs in CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs are shown in Fig. S2 and summarized in Table S2. Significantly, the increased particle size and enlarged distribution of CsPbBr 3 NPs on the surface of GO and FLG was observed. This phenomenon can be attributed to that the CsPbBr 3 NPs were in-situ grown on the surface of GO and FLG by LARP process, which would vary the growth process and result in the larger particle or aggregation. [22] Note that the actual compositions of CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs were analyzed and interpreted using TGA. The results are shown in Fig. S3 and summarized in Table S3. Obviously, the in-situ growth of the CsPbBr 3 NPs on the surface of GO or FLG would result in the similar cubic morphology but smaller particle size as compared to the pristine free-standing CsPbBr 3 NPs, which may be caused to the lower local concentration of precursors on the surface of GO or FLG than that in solution. For the comparison between CsPbBr 3 -GO and CsPbBr 3 -FLG NHSs, the component of FLG is higher than GO to achieve the similar morphology in the NHSs, which may be due to the lower specific surface area of FLG (38.7 m 2 /g) than that of GO (142.5 m 2 /g) (the BET analytic results of GO and FLG are shown in Fig. S4). mentions.text: The thermal decomposition performance of the specimens can be analyzed by TG measurement (Fig. 3). When the temperature gradually rises to 800 C, the weight loss of NiO nanosheets is hardly found [40]. The g-C 3 N 4 nanowires have a sharp weight loss arising from about 450 C to 710 C, owing to its thermal decomposition [40]. For the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 composites, the obvious weight loss in the range of 500-650 C reveals the thermal decomposition of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires. Therefore the contents of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires in the heterojunctions can be easily calculated from the corresponding mass loss over 800 C [41], which is well consistent with the feeding amount of g-C 3 N 4 (Table 1). The above TG results indicate that there is no loss of precursors during the synthesis of the composites.

To prove the photocatalytic performance of the as-synthesized NiO/g-C 3 N 4 heterojunctions, the catalytic reduction properties of CO 2 using similar photocatalysts were compared in Table S1. Various composite photocatalysts can effectively convert CO 2 to corresponding products under their own catalytic conditions. Compared with other composites, the as-prepared NiO/g-C 3 N 4 heterojunctions with the yield rates of 2.75 and 1.79 μmol⋅h -1 ⋅g -1 for CO and CH 4 exhibit satisfactory photocatalytic performance of CO 2 , indicating superior candidate as the sunlight photocatalyst.

tables.caption: The BET specific surface area, pore volume, average pore size and band gap energy of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires, NiO nanosheets and the composites.

mentions.text: According to the BJH approach (inset of Fig. 5), the pore diameters of NC-3 are primarily partitioned into two sorts. One is the mesopore at about 5.0 nm from the surface structure of the sample that may be due to gas escape during heat treatment. The other is the micropore of 30-110 nm, due to the disordered aggregation of nanoparticles. As summarized in Table 2, compared with pure NiO nanosheets (S BET ¼ 13.94 m 2 g -1 ), the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 photocatalysts display a sharp increase in specific surface area and pore volume, and a significant decrease in pore size, which can be further confirmed by Fig. S1. And it becomes larger with the increasing g-C 3 N 4 content, which leads to more reaction active sites in the samples. At the same time the CO 2 adsorption over various samples (Fig. S3) indicates the potential application of NC-3 in the photocatalytic CO 2 reduction. The results are in line with BET analysis discussed above.

Fig. 7a exhibits the UV-vis spectra of NiO nanosheets, g-C 3 N 4 nanowires and the composites in the range of 250-800 nm. Single NiO nanosheets display its intrinsic band gap absorption of NiO at wavelength of about 305 nm [52]. However, single g-C 3 N 4 nanowires show an absorption edge situated at visible light range as presented. Furthermore, compared with NiO nanosheets and g-C 3 N 4 nanowires, the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 photocatalysts exhibit a red shift of the absorption edge, indicating the strong visible light response [54]. The band gaps of NiO and g-C 3 N 4 could be reckoned from the formula (αhv) ¼ A(hv-E g ) n/2 [55]. Moreover, the n value is dependent on the transition type of the semiconductor. And n ¼ 1 represents a direct transition, while n ¼ 4 means an indirect transition [55]. The n value for g-C 3 N 4 and NiO is 4 and 1, respectively. According to the above equation, the band gap energies of pure g-C 3 N 4 nanowires and NiO nanosheets are 2.75 eV and 3.46 eV (Fig. 7b) [40,52], respectively. Moreover on basis on the Tauc plots of the NiO/g-C 3 N 4 photocatalysts, the band gap energies of the composites are shifted to a more visible region with the increasing content of g-C 3 N 4 nanowires (Table 2), leading to more efficient use of visible light. For NC-3, the band gap energy is estimated to be 2.98 eV. The low band gap can promote the excitation of more electrons under irradiation, which may be beneficial to enhance the photocatalytic activity.

documents.title: A Ti-OH bond breaking route for creating oxygen vacancy in titania towards efficient CO2 photoreduction

mentions.text: We first carried out DFT calculation to check the dissociation energy of Ti-O and Ti-OH bonds in anatase and hydroxyl-containing titania, respectively. The calculation results are summarized in Table 1. The dissociation energy values for Ti-O in anatase and hydroxyl-containing titania are all about 7 ~ 8 eV, while that between Ti and -OH, both OH B and OH T , interestingly, is much lower at about 3 ~ 5 eV. Therefore, the Ti-OH bond breakage strategy might be a mild way for oxygen vacancy generation in TiO 2 .

Inspired by the calculation results, we prepared a titanium hydroxide precursor TiO x (OH) y , which was then calcined at 600 ℃ in different atmospheres. From the XRD patterns shown in Fig. 2a, we can see that the precursor TiO x (OH) y is amorphous. After calcination at 600 ℃, all the samples are crystallized into anatase structure. Raman spectra in Fig. 2b further confirm the well-crystallized structure in all the samples except for TiO x (OH) y , in which characteristic peaks at 142, 193, 393, 515, 638 and 792 cm -1 can be ascribed to E 1g , E 2g , B 1g , A 1g + B 1g , E 3g and second-order of B 1g at 393 cm -1 photon modes of anatase TiO 2 , respectively [27,28]. The broad weak band in the Raman spectrum of TiO x (OH) y at around 877 cm -1 results from the Ti-OH bond [29], which proves the hydroxide nature of TiO x (OH) y sample. Raman spectra and XRD patterns give the same order of the crystallinity of these samples: Ti-air-N 2 -600 > Ti-air-600 > Ti-N 2 -600 > TiO x (OH) y . This is easy to understand that the longer the calcination period is, the higher the crystallinity of the sample will be. Furthermore, we calculated the crystallite size of the three samples utilizing Scherrer's equation. The fitting calculating results are summarized in Table S1. We can see that the crystallite sizes of Ti-air-N 2 -600, Ti-air-600, Ti-N 2 -600 three samples are 23.1 nm, 20.7 nm, and 14.9 nm, respectively, consistent with the order of their crystallinity. From the TEM images in Fig. 3, we can see that the TiO x (OH) y sample is an aggregation of amorphous nanoparticles. Clear lattice diffraction fringes, mainly presented by the (1 0 1) lattice plane (Fig. 3f), and bright spots in selected area electron diffraction (SAED) image (Fig. 3e inset) of the Ti-N 2 -600 sample demonstrate its well-crystallized structure. TEM images of Ti-air-600 and Ti-air-N 2 -600 shown in Fig. S2 show the similar structure to that of Ti-N 2 -600. These results are in good agreement with the XRD and Raman characterizations. Additionally, the TEM mapping for N only shows background noise (Fig. S13) and no N dopant (0.00 atom%) is detected in EDX spectrum of Ti-N 2 -600.

Interestingly, the sample Ti-air-600 prepared by calcining TiO x (OH) y in air also displays paramagnetic signal. We consider that the oxygen concentration in air is not high enough to refill (oxidation process) the oxygen vacancy sites when OH detaching from the titania structure. In other words, the dynamics of OH detachment is much faster than that of the oxidation process. This phenomenon could also further demonstrate our previous opinion that the OH-detaching for oxygen vacancy generation is a much easier method. While in Ti-air-N 2 -600 obtained by calcining Ti-air-600 in N 2 , the paramagnetic signal (Fig. S3) shows no significant increase compared with Ti-air-600, either. It also agrees with the DFT calculation results. Thus, we could draw a conclusion that the present Ti-OH bond breakage approach can effectively but mildly generate oxygen vacancy in titania. Positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) is a wellestablished technique to investigate defect species and their concentrations [41]. Table 2 gives three positron lifetime components, τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 , in accompanying with relative intensities, I 1 , I 2 and I 3, for Ti-N 2 -600 and Ti-air-N 2 -600 samples. The shortest positron lifetime τ 1 is usually attributed to the free annihilation of the positron in defect-free crystal. While in structure with defects, like monovacancy, positron lifetime τ 1 will be prolonged due to the decreased average electron density [41]. The τ 1 values are 0.217 ns and 0.194 ns for samples Ti-N 2 -600 and Ti-air-N 2 -600, respectively, both of which are larger than the reported τ 1 lifetime, 0.178 ns in defect-free anatase crystal structure and 0.189 ns in P25 structure. Ti-N 2 -600 sample presents a much larger value of τ 1 than Ti-air-N 2 -600 and P25, indicating that higher amounts of small size defects, such as monovacancies (oxygen vacancies), have been created in Ti-N 2 -600. The second positron lifetime component τ 2 is generally attributed to larger size defects such as oxygen vacancy clusters (including dimers, trimers, etc.). The commonly reported τ 2 value for defect-free anatase structure is around 0.364 ns [42], which is quite close to that of the Ti-air-N 2 -600 sample. The lifetime component τ 2 of Ti-N 2 -600 sample is a little larger than those of Ti-air-N 2 -600 and the reported defect-free anatase, implying that there is also a small amount of oxygen vacancy clusters in Ti-N 2 -600. The longest lifetime τ 3 is usually assigned to micropores and the annihilation of ortho-positronium atoms. Besides the positron lifetime, the I 1 and I 2 intensities are also associated with the relative concentrations of bulk and surface defects, respectively [41]. In Table 2, we can see that I 1 is higher than I 2 for Ti-N 2 -600, suggesting surface defects are more dominating than bulk ones. Also, the I 1 /I 2 ratio of Ti-N 2 -600 is slightly higher than those of Ti-air-N 2 -600 and the reported P25, evidencing the larger amount of bulk mono-oxygen-vacancy in Ti-N 2 -600 than Ti-air-N 2 -600 and P25. The ratio of surface-to-bulk defects might achieve a good balance in Ti-N 2 -600, thus increased photoinduced charge carrier concentration in Ti-N 2 -600 has been achieved during the photocatalytic reaction.

mentions.text: TiO 2 was synthesized according to a previously reported method with an amino acid additive. [16][17][18][19][20] Briefly, a yellowish transparent peroxo-titanic acid solution was prepared by the addition of an ammonia solution (2 cm 3 , 28%, Kanto Chemicals Co., Inc.) and a hydrogen peroxide solution (10 cm 3 , 30%, Kanto Chemicals Co., Inc.) to titanium metal powder (2 mmol, Wako Pure Chemical Industries Ltd.). Glycolic acid (3 mmol, Kanto Chemicals Co., Inc.) was added to the yellowish solution of peroxo-titanic acid, as a result of which the solution color changed from yellowish to pale red. Heat treatment at 353 K was carried out to remove excess ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. Finally, a stable titanium complex solution of a yellow-red color was obtained. Then, amino acid (Table S1, † 2 mmol, Kanto Chemicals Co., Inc.) was added to the complex solution. The solution of the complex was diluted to 20 cm 3 using distilled water, placed in a Teflon-lined reactor and sealed in stainless steel autoclaves. The autoclave was heated at 473 K for 24 h for the hydrothermal treatment of the complexes. After that, the autoclave was allowed to cool down to room temperature. The resultant powders were separated by centrifugation and washed with distilled water until the obtained solution had a neutral pH.

A similar tendency is also observed for brookite-type particles.

In order to gain insight into the optical properties of titania powder, the band gap energies of the synthesized materials were studied in detail. The band gap energies can be determined by plotting the modified Kubelka-Munk function [FĲR)E] 1/2 calculated from the optical absorption spectrum vs. the energy of the exciting light (Fig. 6B). The values are given in Table 1. The band gap of brookite synthesized with Lys is at around 3.20 eV, whereas that of rutile is about 3.00 eV.

The photocatalytic activities of the synthesized TiO 2 rutile and brookite were evaluated in terms of photocatalytic CO 2 reduction from aqueous solution under UV-vis (λ > 300 nm) irradiation. The results of the photocatalytic study only refer to rutile and brookite, whose photocatalytic CO 2 reduction were less reported. Table 1 lists the methanol yields, specific BET surface areas and other physical properties of the corresponding samples. The rutile samples include whisker particle R Whisker , 18 nanorod R Glu (Fig. 3c and e), rutile (Fig. 3a) and flowerlike particles with exposed high-index facets R Flower . 20 Under the irradiation of light, brookite samples exhibited a higher activity than those of rutile (Fig. 7). The methanol yields on the brookite samples are in range of 7.08-9.22 μmol g -1 , whereas those on rutile are in the range of 3.14-5.12 μmol g -1 . R Glu (Fig. 3c and e) showed a lower activity with respect to that of the rutile sample (Fig. 3a). Especially, B Lys (Fig. 3d and f) exhibited a remarkable photoactivity with a methanol yield of 9.22 μmol g -1 , that is 1.30 times higher than that on the brookite sample (Fig. 3b).

All the brookite TiO 2 samples exhibited a significantly higher photocatalytic activity than those of the rutile samples, which may be attributed to the nature of crystalline brookite. It has been reported that brookite had a higher photocatalytic activity than those of rutile and anatase. 31 Li et al. also reported that the photocatalytic CO 2 reduction activity of a pure brookite suspension was higher than that of pure anatase or rutile, despite the former having a lower surface area. 31 Our results suggest that the brookite-type TiO 2 has a higher activity than that of rutile with the same morphology and specific BET surface area (Table 1). This may be due to the fact that brookite TiO 2 shows the highest reduction ability, from the evaluation of the conduction band po-tential. 30 The more negative flat band potential is beneficial for CO 2 reduction. We performed the examination of brookite particles after the photocatalytic reaction. The XRD pattern of brookite after the catalytic reaction with light irradiation in Fig. S6 † reveals that a phase transformation does not occur.

The different activity of different rutile samples can be understood from their surface structures. All of the rutile TiO 2 with different shapes investigated in the present study were well-crystallized and well-faceted as shown in Fig. 3 and 4, which was, indeed, the result of a slow growth from a stable titanium-complex. In particular, it has been proved that rutile synthesized from titanium-glycolate grows in the [001] direction with the predominant exposure of {110} facets and {111} facets. 18,20 It is observed that the surface area percentage of {111} facets increases in the order R Glu ≈ R Whisker < Rutile < R Flower , whereas the specific BET surface areas increase in the opposite order (Fig. 8, Table 1). On the basis of the investigation, it is found that that photocatalytic CO 2 reduction activity increases with an increased surface area percentage of {111} facets. For instance, R Glu showed a lower activity compared to that of rutile presumably due to the fact that the former possesses a higher aspect ratio with a smaller percentage of {111} facets. Thus, the methanol yield was found to be strongly dependent on the percentage of the {111} surface.

tables.caption: Chemical analysis, basal spacing, surface properties, and reaction yields of all samples.

mentions.text: Different types of ZnS and CuS photocatalysts (samples 1-4) were prepared via solution method that is described in (Ebrahimi et al., 2016). Sample numbers 5, 6, and 7 were synthesized by co-precipitation of 5%, 10%, and 15%, respectively, of copper acetate with zinc acetate in the precipitation step to investigate its effects on catalytic reduction of CO 2 . According to the optimum properties found in (Ebrahimi et al., 2016), the proportion of CTAB stabilizer to CEC of clay was chosen to be 2.5 (shown in Table 1) to expand the basal spacing of MMT. This will result in higher specific surface area and better adsorption of CO 2 in the bilayer area.

Elemental analysis and other chemical information of catalysts are shown in Table 1. As evident, acid activation increases the surface area and absorption capacity of MMT for CTAB, zinc, and copper. This fact results in higher active surface area available for catalytic reduction of CO 2 and for adsorption of catalyst nanoparticles in the synthesis step of catalyst preparation in both samples. Basal spacing of all samples seems to be uniform, which reveals that the bilayer space depends only on the ratio of CTAB to CEC of clay. Surface area, pore diameter, and pore volume results show that these properties only depend on CTAB to CEC ratio and acid activation; therefore, it could be accordingly deduced that the ZnS or CuS deposition does not affect it. FTIR spectra of sample numbers 2 and 4 are shown in Figure 1. The stretching vibrations of C-H bonds at 2924 and 2851 cm -1 were observed in both samples that confirm the presence of CTA. Substitution of Mg 2+ for Al 3+ is seen in the peak at 792 cm -1 . The 1035 and 3618 cm -1 peaks are due to Si-O and Al-O bonds of MMT, respectively.

The photocatalytic test results of all samples are shown in Table 1. H 2 , CH 4 , and CO were recognized in the GC diagrams. A small amount of other light hydrocarbons was also produced. The proposed reduction reactions of carbon dioxide to CH 4 and CO 2 are as follows. mentions.text: The nonstoichiometric Bi 2 O 2.33 has higher photocatalytic activity than stoichiometric Bi 2 O 3 because oxygen vacancies greatly affect the PEC properties and play a key role in adjusting the PEC performance of the device [ 27 , 30-34 ]. The presence and behaviors of oxygen defects were analyzed by XPS. The O 1 s XPS spectra presented in Fig. 7 show an asymmetry peak at around 530 eV, which indicates that the O 1 s XPS spectra contain two binding energy components. The binding energy peaks at around 529.5 and 530.7 eV are attributed to lattice oxygen (O L ) Bi-O bonds and the oxygen vacancies (O V ), respectively [ 27 , 29 , 35 , 36 ]. The O V /O L sample ratios listed in Table 1 were calculated based on the peak area. In order to extract the peak area more accurately, two Gaussian peaks were used to fit the experimental data of O 1 s XPS spectra. The ratio O V /O L increases with the increase of annealing temperature. It reaches its maximum of 1.79 at 600 °C, then decreases with temperature further increasing to 650 °C, implying that the Bi 2 O 2.33 has the highest oxygen vacancy content. The slight shift in binding energy for samples can be attributed to heat treatment temperature, substantially influencing the creation of defect levels at O 1 s [37] . Additionally, the peak attributed to oxygen vacancies of Bi 2 O 2.33 moves to the low bonding energy, which may associate with the produced Bi 2 + resulting in the variation of coordination environment of the metal cations. As a result, part of the oxygen vacancies (electrons) are bound by Bi cations, verified by the high-resolution Bi 4f XPS spectrum of Bi 2 O 2.33 (as shown in Fig. 8 (a)). Obviously, the binding energy of Bi moves to the low binding energy [ 28 , 38 ], signifying that Bi in Fig. S5. The peaks at approximately 160.8 and 162.0 eV are associated with S 2p 3/2 and S 2p 1/2 of CdS, respectively [ 28 , 39 ]. Moreover, the weak shift of Bi 4f and O 1 s peaks towards lower binding energy for Bi 2 O 2.33 -CdS than that of Bi 2 O 2.33 can be associated with the electronic migration and the "bond" (oxygen vacancies).

tables.caption: Membranes solution compositions

mentions.text: Preparation and characterization of photocatalytic membranes Nafion and catalytic Nafion membranes were prepared following the same procedure reported in [8]. Nafion™ 5 wt.% solution (20 g) was dried at ca. 60-70 °C under stirring; then, Nafion was dissolved in EtOH:H 2 O=50:50 wt./wt. at room temperature under stirring for 1 h to obtain the polymeric solution. Two types of flat sheet membranes were prepared: a Nafion membrane (not including catalyst) and a photocatalytic Nafion™ membrane (Table 1). For catalytic membrane, after a complete polymer dissolution, the catalyst (C 3 N 4 ) was added to the obtained solution and the resulting dispersion was left under stirring for 1 h more. Then it was sonicated for 3 h more at room temperature in order to favor the homogenization of the dispersion. The catalyst-polymer dispersion obtained was then casted in a Petri dish (diameter=7.1 cm) and the solvent evaporation was carried out in a climatic chamber (60±4°C and 12±5% as relative humidity) for about 20 h. The membrane obtained was treated thermally, heating it at 10°C min -1 up to 100°C, then at 0.5°C min -1 up to 120°C, and kept at this temperature for 4 h. No specific investigation on C 3 N 4 loading content was carried out and the chosen C 3 N 4 percentage of 1.23 wt% was the same as before for TiO 2 [8]. In the case of the Nafion membrane, the same procedure was followed but without catalyst dispersion. Then, the flat sheet membranes obtained were detached from the Petri dishes with a small amount of water and then dried at room temperature. The two membrane sides were distinguished as the casting plate-facing and air-facing surfaces.

mentions.text: The N 2 -adsorption-desorption isotherms of the pure TiO 2 , TiO 2 NWs and Au/Ag-NPs modified TiO 2 NWs samples are depicted in Fig. 5. The isotherms of all the samples are similar to the type IV curve with the hysteresis loops which is the characteristics of mesoporous materials. The summary of BET surface area, pore volume and pore diameter of the TiO 2 , TiO 2 NWs and modified TiO 2 NWs samples is depicted in Table 1. BET specific surface area (S BET ) of the pure TiO 2 was 42 increased to 75 m 2 g -1 for TiO 2 NWs. On the other hand, BET surface area decreased to 46 and 48 m 2 g -1 when 0.5 wt.% Au-NPs and 3 wt.% Ag-NPs were loaded onto TiO 2 NWs. This decreased in the BET surface area could be accounted for partial TiO 2 NWs surface covered by the deposited of metal NPs. However, an increased in BET surface area was observed in Au/Ag-NPs coloaded TiO 2 NWs. This increased in BET surface area was evidently due to the Au-Ag alloy supported over the TiO 2 NWs. Similar observations were obtained in BJH adsorption pore volumes. In the case of pore diameter, pure TiO 2 pore diameter was 10 nm, increased to 26 nm in TiO 2 NWs, apparently due to the larger diameter of TiO 2 NWs. A further increased in the pore diameter was observed in Au/Ag NPs loaded TiO 2 NWs seemingly due to deposited Au/Ag-NPs layer over the surface of these materials [31]. X-ray photo-electron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to analyze the chemical states of the elements in Au/Ag-NPs/TiO 2 NWs as shown in Fig. 6. The wide spectrum is presented in Fig. 6(a). Fig. 6(b) reveals the presence of Ti2p peaks namely Ti2p 3/2 and Ti2p 1/2, positioned at 458. 08 and 463.72 eV which corresponds to Ti 4+ or titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ). The Ag3d spectrum confirmed the presence of Ag in the metal state as depicted in Fig. 6(c) [21]. Fig. 6(d) presents Au 4f binding energy values of 82.03 eV (Au 4f 7/2 ) and 88.44 eV (Au 4f 7/2 ) in Au-Ag/TiO 2 NWs, attributed to metallic gold (Au o ). Fig. 6(e) shows the O1s spectrum ascribed to the lattice oxygen O 2 . This was also due to the presence of H 2 O or the free hydroxyl group (O H) on the TiO 2 surface. The spectrum of C 1s with peaks located at ∼284.60 and 588.50 eV corresponds to C C, and C O, respectively as shown in Fig. 6(f).

mentions.text: 0.031 g L -1 of catalyst was here taken as reference for further testing, so focusing on the highest gas phase productivity. Indeed, looking at the products distribution and intending this process as a mean to store solar energy by turning a waste greenhouse gas into useful compounds, we calculated the amount of energy stored in chemical form considering the different products we have obtained. We have taken as basis for calculation the enthalpy of combustion of HCOOH, H 2 and CO and made the calculation for the two extreme cases of catalyst concentration 0.031 and 0.5 g L -1 (Table 2). The amount of energy that is stored is slightly higher for the highest catalyst concentration and increases progressively with this parameter. However, the form of storage is different, as well as the easiness of separation and exploitation, which is likely better in the case of gas products than for the diluted liquid product. It is therefore possible to operate obtaining the highest yield of gaseous products, at low catalyst concentration, or to increase the liquid product yield with higher catalyst amount. In the following, we selected to use the lowest catalyst concentration, since it is more amenable for scale up and it leads to a balanced production of gas and liquid phase compounds, that allow to highlight the effect of the other operating parameters on reactivity. Based on the maximum amount of energy stored as calculated in Table 2 and on the measured irradiance in the UVA region (104 W/m 2 ), we calculated approximately 2-3% energy storage efficiency.
